title: UserArena: Benchmarking Interactive User Simulation for Long-Horizon Shopping Agents
abstract: UserArena introduces a real-world interactive benchmark with long-horizon shopping trajectories and an evaluation framework, alongside On-Policy Trajectory Distillation to improve simulator fidelity for agentic recommendations.

title: HiSTEVE 1.0: Harnessing Human-Interface VLA Agents for Open-World Games
abstract: HiSTEVE is a hierarchical vision-language-action agent that combines long-horizon planning with native keyboard-and-mouse control to perform complex open-ended tasks in Minecraft.

title: RSIHub: A Composable Framework for Agent-Evolution Methods
abstract: RSIHub is an open-source framework that standardizes agent-evolution research by providing shared infrastructure for building, comparing, and extending methods with reusable components and consistent evaluation.

title: RynnUnify: Towards Unified Embodied Brain
abstract: RynnUnify is a 16B unified embodied model that integrates visual planning, physical reasoning, and robot control, achieving state-of-the-art results on long-horizon embodied tasks.

title: Omni-Woodpecker: Hallucination Correction via Evidence-Prior Rebalancing for Omni LLMs
abstract: Omni-Woodpecker is a training-free framework that reduces cross-modal hallucinations in omni LLMs by identifying modality conflicts and rebalancing hidden representations to suppress misleading priors.

title: Every Weight Is a Path of Shared Discrete Decisions
abstract: TWIG represents neural network weights as shared discrete decision paths, unifying compression methods and enabling efficient fixed-weight circuits with optimized discrete choices.

title: Dual Exam: Controlled Evaluation of Multimodal Agents and World Models
abstract: Dual Exam evaluates multimodal agents and world models separately across diverse domains, revealing uneven performance and no coupled success in pilot tests.

title: DirCast: Live Esports Directing and Commentary with a Single Streaming Video-Language Model
abstract: DirCast is a streaming video language model that simultaneously directs live esports broadcasts by selecting cameras and generates real-time commentary using only past context.

title: On-Policy Self-Training: Data-Free Self-Improvement in Large Language Models
abstract: Foundation models can self-improve across text and vision tasks by generating synthetic questions and reasoning traces guided only by high-level topics, without external supervision.

title: DraMaze: A Multi-Agent Pipeline with Future-Aware Memory for Diverse Microdrama Script Generation
abstract: DraMaze improves long-form microdrama script generation by using evolutionary tree search guided by trope memory and backward narrative dependency trees to enhance plot diversity and coherence.

title: FLOMSS: Generative Music Source Separation by Flow Matching
abstract: Flow matching is investigated for four-source full-band stereo music separation, evaluating prediction targets, flow paths, modeling strategies, and consistency constraints with both signal-level and perceptual metrics.

title: MultiAgent-OPD: End-to-End Training of Hierarchical Multi-Agent Systems with On-Policy Distillation
abstract: MultiAgent-OPD jointly trains a hierarchical multi-agent team via on-policy distillation and reinforcement learning, using a frozen teacher for local process supervision to improve end-to-end performance across multiple datasets.

title: MMVistaReason: Toward Open-Data and Post-Training Recipes for Multimodal Reasoning
abstract: MMVistaReason improves open multimodal reasoning through structured data construction, difficulty-aware distillation, and specialized reinforcement learning integration.

title: DuoLM: Fast and Effective Personalized Recommendation with Language Models
abstract: DuoLM accelerates personalized recommendation by combining a compact encoder and ranker with optimized inference, achieving high throughput with minimal quality loss.

title: Kolab: Benchmarking Human-Agent Collaboration in Long-Horizon Workflows
abstract: Kolab is a dataset of professional screen recordings that reveals frontier AI agents overestimate collaboration quality and fail to predict expert adoption of contributions in long-horizon workflows.

title: PaperFormalizer: Author-in-the-Loop Autoformalization of Research Papers in Lean
abstract: Even a carefully proofread paper can leave small gaps in its proofs or its stated assumptions. We introduce PaperFormalizer, a Lean-based agentic pipeline that helps authors find and close such gaps in their own papers and turn each paper into a Lean-verified version. Starting from the LaTeX source, PaperFormalizer transcribes the paper into a dependency graph of statements, audits each statement in natural language for faithfulness, ambiguity and correctness, and then formalizes and proves the statements in Lean against Mathlib, optional domain libraries and the author's personal toolkit. Only the author knows what a statement is meant to say and how a formalization gap in a result is best fixed. The pipeline therefore stops and asks the author whenever a statement admits more than one reading, presents every repair, in natural language and TeX symbols, as a proposal that the author can accept, decline or redirect, and leaves to the author every decision that could potentially change what the paper claims. The output is an annotated and revised version of the paper, a report of the changes, and Lean code in which each declaration is linked to the statement it formalizes. The author's toolkit grows as more papers are formalized, and authors can share their verified papers so that researchers who build on them can reuse their Lean code. By making verified papers practical to produce, PaperFormalizer aims to make research that rests on mathematical proofs more robust. PaperFormalizer runs inside a coding agent (Claude Code or Codex) and is available at https://github.com/Jiyuan-Tan/PaperFormalizer. Papers with Lean code shared by users are available at https://paperformalizer.org.

title: Easy-3Dfy: Object-Level Geometric Composition for Single-Image 3D Scene Construction
abstract: Easy-3Dfy separates object generation from scene layout estimation and uses geometric alignment to combine high-quality 3D objects with spatial understanding for improved scene reconstruction.

title: Speculative Diffusion is a Tale of Two Tradeoffs
abstract: This paper explores trading inference speed for output quality in speculative decoding by jointly adjusting diffusion effort and acceptance leniency to extend the speed-quality Pareto frontier.

title: RoboJudge: Multimodal Language Models as Judges for Embodied Video Generation
abstract: Researchers introduce a benchmark and training dataset to evaluate multimodal language models as judges of physically valid, instruction-aligned embodied video generation, yielding a fine-tuned 9B judge with high human agreement.

title: DISC: Domain-Integrated Similarity Cost for Time-Series Dataset
abstract: DISC is a learnable framework that calibrates and combines time-series dataset similarity metrics to better predict downstream forecasting transfer performance.

title: LoCA: Enabling Multi-Modality in Geospatial Location Encoders
abstract: LoCA is a two-stage pipeline that trains co-aligned multimodal image encoders and uses them as high-rank targets to train location and metadata encoders via contrastive learning, outperforming existing methods across diverse geospatial tasks.

title: Echo: Coupled Action and Task Status Signal Denoising for Vision Language Action Models
abstract: Echo integrates stop and failure signals into a vision-language-action model to guide robot execution and recovery without fine-grained progress labels.

title: Generalized CycleGRPO for Fine-Grained Multimodal Understanding and Grounding
abstract: Generalized CycleGRPO unifies region understanding and localization via reinforcement learning with self-verified cycle consistency across images and videos, improving grounding and temporal distinctiveness without external judges.

title: HoloBoxing: A Simple Recipe for Humanoid Boxing with 7 Minutes of Single-GPU Training
abstract: HoloBoxing learns humanoid boxing by combining a frozen whole-body controller with a compact planner that predicts body-point targets, using imitation initialization and reinforcement learning to refine interaction behavior with minimal additional training.

title: JockeyBench: Evaluating LLM Agents on Horse-Racing Decision-Making
abstract: JockeyBench evaluates repeated event forecasting via Japanese horse racing, finding that reusable predictors improve efficiency but all configurations yield negative average betting returns.

title: A path-following framework on fiber bundle for variational inequalities
abstract: A path-following framework on a fixed-point fiber bundle achieves global linear convergence for variational inequalities with continuous mappings over polytopes without monotonicity assumptions.

title: The fixed-point bundle method over product-of-simplex domains arising from game equilibria
abstract: A fixed-point bundle framework extended to product-of-simplex domains via geometric equivalence yields globally convergent path-following algorithms for Nash equilibrium computation.

title: KANLab: TensorFlow Playground for Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
abstract: KANLab is an interactive browser tool for teaching Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks by visualizing B-spline activation curves, gradient descent, and pruning in a compact 2D setting.

title: LLM2Cert: LLM Synthesis of Certificates with SMT/Lean Verification
abstract: A benchmark of nonlinear dynamical systems and an LLM-driven framework that synthesizes and verifies stability and safety certificates via SMT solvers and proof repair agents achieve substantial verification improvements.

title: What Git Does Not Record: Provenance Legibility in Two AI-Assisted Research Repositories
abstract: Repository traces of AI use in computational research are partially visible and unreliable for measuring involvement, requiring auditable provenance systems.

title: Does LeWorldModel Preserve Local Action Geometry?
abstract: Pretrained LeWorldModel's reproduction of small action effects is evaluated via Gram matrices across perturbation scales, showing scale-dependent sensitivity differences and higher errors than environment references.

title: SliderEdit++: Improved Slider Trajectories in Instruction-Based Image Editing
abstract: SlideBench benchmarks continuous image editing and SliderEdit++ improves slider reliability via trajectory regularization and disentanglement for smoother, faster control.

title: Co-adaptive Rule Routing and Constraining for Structured Knowledge Retrieval
abstract: CoRE jointly learns reasoning rules and constrained evidence retrieval through alternating reinforcement and contrastive learning without predefined query-rule supervision.

title: Predictive Closure: A Set-Level Characterization of JEPA's Feature Selection
abstract: JEPA feature selection depends on predictive relationships between features rather than individual predictability, allowing unpredictable but relationally useful features to be retained and enabling indirect steering of representations.

title: Judging the Justification: Decision Certificate Supervision for Generative Reward Models
abstract: DeCert evaluates and improves generative reward model rationales by assessing justification validity and verdict consistency without reference explanations, yielding stronger preference supervision.

title: FLORA: An Open Model Suite for Scaling Robotics Data Engines
abstract: Flora is an open-source industrial data engine for robotics foundation models that provides captioning, outcome and process reward labeling, and pretraining data curation at scale with high accuracy and low cost.

title: FocusVLA: Future-Intent Guided Dynamic View Routing for Vision-Language-Action Models
abstract: FocusVLA improves robotic manipulation by dynamically routing between global and local camera views based on predicted interaction intent across task stages.

title: Anthropic’s IPO filing reveals its strategy for keeping enterprise customers hooked
abstract: Anthropic is building the same kind of cross-product ecosystem that helped make tech companies like Amazon and Uber enormously sticky, and its S-1 suggests the strategy is working. More than half of customers spending at least $100,000 annually now use both the Claude platform and a first-party app like Claude Code or Cowork, up from about 30% at the end of last year. “The speed and depth of our enterprise customer adoption are powerful evidence of Claude’s position at the frontier of AI,” the S-1, filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday , reads. As of September 30, Anthropic recorded more than 11,900 customers spending at least $100,000; more than 1,900 customers spending upward of $1 million; and about 250 customers spending $10 million or more annually. Anthropic attributes customer momentum to a “significant usage expansion as customers realize the value of deploying Claude across their organizations,” which drove net revenue retention of about 900% as of the end of the third quarter. Throwing shade at the entire legacy SaaS industry, Anthropic pitches Claude as not a “static product that serves a single use case,” but rather “frontier AI with rapidly advancing capabilities” spanning the models, the developer platform, and the applications users interact with directly. “An advance at any layer compounds across all three layers, accelerating the pace at which we can deliver more capable intelligence,” the filing reads, calling this “integrated approach” the reason more customers use both the Claude Platform and first-party apps. The playbook is familiar. Uber began by selling rides but has expanded into food delivery and freight. With AWS, Amazon drew in customers with cloud computing services before expanding those relationships into storage, databases, and other offerings, making the ecosystem increasingly hard to leave. Like those companies, Anthropic doesn’t have to sell each product to a brand-new buyer: A business that starts with the API can deploy Claude Code to their engineers and then Cowork to their broader workforce. Those app users become far more valuable. In the third quarter, the highest-spending 5% of Claude Enterprise customers who used Claude Code spent about 20x as much per month as the average enterprise user who didn’t use the coding tool, per the filing. The finding demonstrates how much room there is for per-user spend to grow, and illustrates why Anthropic is keen to get its applications into the accounts that start with the API. Anthropic said it amplifies that organic diffusion by investing in Applied AI teams. An internal Applied AI team works with startups and enterprises to help place Claude inside customers’ existing technology stacks, and the company recently launched a separate venture with Blackstone and other private equity firms, dubbed Ode with Anthropic, to embed forward-deployed engineers into businesses to build bespoke AI tools with Claude. Anthropic also leans on its third-party distribution partnerships with hyperscalers AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Under what the filing calls a “joint go-to-market approach,” Anthropic holds the direct contractual relationship with customers and pays each cloud provider a fee, which the company says lets it “avoid channel conflict” and “set pricing.” Anthropic’s budding stickiness strategy may become essential as the AI giant seeks to constantly “reinvent our business” by releasing “new classes of products whose aim is to dwarf the economic value of our existing ones.” The company says it will devote less effort than a typical business to “entrenching our current products and business models, and more effort to defining new ones.” The filing also flags headwinds, despite impressive revenue growth of $16.3 billion for the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same period last year. The cloud partnerships that help sell Claude are increasingly seeing Anthropic as a competitor, which Anthropic says could lead to difficulties securing the compute it needs from them. The filing states that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft may prioritize their own requirements or rivals they’ve invested in. Customer concentration is another risk. “Any adverse change in demand from our largest customers … could adversely affect our business and prospects,” reads part of the risk factors section. “As a result, a significant reduction in spending by, or the loss of, one or more of our largest customers, if not offset by new customer relationships or increased business from our other existing customers, could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.” Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

title: SpaceX locks in $40B GPU financing deal with Apollo
abstract: SpaceX has reached a binding commitment for roughly $40 billion in financing for AI chips and related data center equipment, the company disclosed in a regulatory filing Monday . In a statement, SpaceX called the deal the “largest committed GPU financing” . Under the agreement, an entity managed by Apollo Global Management, the New York-based private equity giant, will buy the chips and related server hardware, then lease the equipment to SpaceX. The leases will last about five to five-and-a-quarter years, beginning when each tranche of equipment is delivered, according to the filing. SpaceX expects the deal to close by year-end, subject to closing conditions, with leases starting in the first half of 2027 as the GPUs and related equipment arrive. The financing gives SpaceX another way to fund its rapidly expanding AI ambitions without relying solely on traditional debt markets. “This lease diversifies our funding sources and addresses a notable portion of the funding required to deliver on our growth plans,” SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen said in a statement Monday, noting it is seeing “less than one-year payback periods” on its AI infrastructure investments as it scales compute to power Grok and its cloud services. Apollo said the financing will help deliver Nvidia’s next-generation Vera Rubin chips for SpaceX’s “terrestrial compute buildout.” The financing comes as SpaceX ramps spending to expand its AI infrastructure, alongside its Starlink and launch businesses. The financing follows a blockbuster third quarter for SpaceX’s AI business . SpaceX’s AI segment, which includes the Grok chatbot, the Cursor coding tool, and its cloud compute business, outperformed investor expectations in the third quarter and brought in $7.6 billion of SpaceX’s $14.6 billion in revenue, more than Starlink and rocket launches combined. Capital expenditures also surged to nearly $20 billion, up from $6.9 billion a year earlier, as SpaceX races to expand its compute footprint. CFO Bret Johnsen said on the company’s October 20 earnings call that SpaceX expects to spend $35 billion to $40 billion in the fourth quarter alone. The massive lease comes after a tumultuous stretch in the debt markets for AI infrastructure players, as investors grow squeamish over runaway capital expenditures and limited profits. While SpaceX had no trouble tapping Wall Street, Musk used the $40 billion announcement to take a victory lap over pure-play AI compute rivals. Pointing to SpaceX’s “investment-grade” status and steady cash flow from Starlink and rocket launches, Musk argued on Sunday that debt markets have largely closed the door on companies without major revenue streams outside of AI data centers — spelling trouble for the more than 200 neocloud companies built solely to rent out GPUs for AI workloads. “That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation,” Musk wrote on X . “Some will make it through, but not many.”

title: Anthropic officially files for its public debut
abstract: After weeks of leaked S-1s , Anthropic finally filed for an initial public offering on Monday, setting the stage for one of the most closely watched public debuts in modern U.S. history. Anthropic, which plans to list under the ticker “ANT,” recorded revenue of $16.3 billion for the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same period last year, according to the firm’s latest SEC filing. That revenue came off the back of an operating loss of $693 million, an improvement from the $2.1 billion in operating losses that Anthropic recorded in the first half of 2025. Anthropic’s net loss, however, hit $80.7 billion, which was largely driven by noncash accounting adjustments tied to convertible debt. The company says it “may not achieve or sustain profitability in the future.” The filing also provided more color on the scale of Anthropic’s enterprise business. As of the end of September, Anthropic had more than 11,900 customers spending $100,000 or more annually; 1,900 customers spending $1 million or more; and about 250 customers spending $10 million or more. As previously reported , Anthropic’s governance structure will enable Anthropic’s seven co-founders to maintain control once the company goes public. Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Christopher Olah will make up the “Founder LLC,” which will collectively control 50.1% of shareholder voting power — a move Anthropic says is designed to preserve the company’s AI safety mission, per the filing. Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust, established in 2023 to ensure the company pursues its public benefit mission , will have the authority to appoint most of the company’s board. The governance structure is controversial because it means voting power is not proportional to the founders’ economic ownership, and therefore public shareholders will have little practical control over a company building technology that, by its own admission, poses “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.” Anthropic hasn’t yet disclosed how much it hopes to raise nor its proposed share price.

title: Grok releases the first seven minutes of its AI-generated ‘Odyssey’
abstract: Three months after Elon Musk declared that Grok would release a full-length, “historically accurate” movie version of “The Odyssey,” Grok has published a whole seven minutes, which the company is now calling “Episode 1 of our Odyssey series.” Musk had previously lashed out at Christopher Nolan’s version of “The Odyssey” because Nolan cast nonwhite and transgender actors. And Nolan is, in many ways, a perfect foil for Musk — while SpaceX and Tesla CEO hypes up data centers in space and posts an unending stream of AI-generated content, Nolan has described himself as “a techno-skeptic ” and said that before AI, he’d never seen a technology “so completely rejected by the public.” And while Nolan’s version of “The Odyssey” certainly used plenty of visual effects, it’s primarily a feat of practical filmmaking , with a shoot spanning six countries and a cast and crew of thousands. After its release in July, the film became an extraordinary box office success , selling out Imax screenings for months and becoming the likely front-runner at the next Academy Awards . As for the Grok version of “The Odyssey” (created in collaboration with Wonder Studios and director Dev Walker), well, you can watch for yourself. Watch Episode 1 of our Odyssey series made with Grok Imagine. Let us know in the comments if you'd like a full breakdown of how it was done! Creative collaboration with @WonderStudiosX and director Dev Walker @glumlot_ pic.twitter.com/xpgpkqSCpq — Grok Imagine (@imagine) October 23, 2026 I’ll admit it’s not as spectacularly ugly as I’d expected, and certainly more impressive than other videos that Musk has posted recently. If I didn’t know better, there were moments when I might have thought these were real actors sailing across a real sea. And while I can’t speak to Grok’s historical accuracy, it does seem that some fudging was necessary, since no one’s speaking in ancient Greek. But hey, all the characters come in a Musk-approved skin color, while the narrator uses a British accent that will sound familiar to anyone who’s played a fantasy video game or watched a generic Hollywood epic from the past 25 years. What the footage really lacks is any sense of artistry, inspiration, or human interest. The backstory — delivered via the aforementioned voiceover — seems to go on forever, finally giving way to one bearded face after another, each shouting stilted lines that make Nolan’s questionable dialogue (“Our age of bronze is collapsing!”) sound like Shakespeare. While a few individual shots might provide a reasonable simulacrum of reality, as a whole, the clip feels completely airless, offering viewers no sense of momentum, no reason to care about anyone or anything on-screen. And where I had no trouble paying attention for the nearly three hours of Nolan’s “Odyssey,” I was listlessly checking how much time I had left before the Grok version was even halfway through. If it was a video game cutscene, I would have hit the “skip” button. It’s hard to imagine being interested in another seven minutes of this, much less a full movie’s worth.

title: The RealReal won’t let AI agents hog designer clothing
abstract: News AI Business The RealReal won’t let AI agents hog designer clothing Previous reporting by The Verge found that Meta’s Muse could be used to effectively block other shoppers from purchasing items for hours.﻿ Previous reporting by The Verge found that Meta’s Muse could be used to effectively block other shoppers from purchasing items for hours.﻿ by Mia Sato Oct 26, 2026, 5:30 PM UTC Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images Mia Sato is features writer with five years of experience covering the companies that shape technology and the people who use their tools. The RealReal, a secondhand luxury fashion consignment retailer, said it’s updating its bot defense system, effectively making it harder for AI agents to shop on its site. The change comes days after The Verge reported that an AI agent could be used to take advantage of The RealReal’s item reserve system. On the retailer’s website, an item goes “on hold” and is unavailable for other customers to buy for 20 minutes once it’s placed in a user’s shopping cart. Using Meta’s Muse, The Verge was able to instruct the AI agent to continuously re-add The RealReal listings in a shopping cart as soon as the 20-minute hold had expired, effectively blocking other shoppers from purchasing products for hours or longer. After publication, chief technology officer Luke Friang said in an email that the company had addressed the Muse use case flagged by The Verge ’s story. The RealReal’s bot defense configuration now makes it much more difficult for all agents to log in, add items to cart, and check out, Friang said. Agents will still be able to surface listings from The RealReal and direct Muse users to product pages, Friang said, adding that the company will continue to strengthen protections as AI-powered online shopping evolves. Meta didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Technology companies are selling agents as personalized assistants for billions of people — always-on, compliant entities that will schedule meetings, throw parties, and purchase things for human users. So far, agents and shopping seem to go hand in hand; Meta said in its Q3 earnings call this month that it was the most common use case for Muse so far, and that purchases were over $200 on average. Muse has been a hit for Meta and could signal a turning point for AI agents: The company said 10 million people in the US had downloaded the app in 40 days. But robots shopping for things instead of humans has the potential to upend the balance of the web as we know it. For one, if humans stop visiting websites directly and instead access the web through chatbots, businesses become one step removed from their customers. Retailers — most notably Amazon — have recognized that reality could disrupt their bottom line, especially advertising revenue, and have blocked agents from shopping on their sites. An influx of AI agents accessing consumer platforms could also break or complicate even the most unexpected things shoppers take for granted, like the reserve system of a used clothing website. There is, of course, a realistic limit to how long a person is willing to spend adding and re-adding designer clothing to their shopping cart if they’re indecisive. An agent in contrast does not care. It is perhaps precisely the type of busywork a fashion-forward person might pay an actual personal assistant to do on their behalf. Now, a capability like this is at the fingertips of millions of consumers, and they are just beginning to learn how to take advantage of it. Retailers, too, are playing catch-up. title: Five weird details from Anthropic’s IPO filing
abstract: AI Report Anthropic Five weird details from Anthropic’s IPO filing From conscious AI and ‘catastrophic’ risk to unusual corporate structures and executive perks. From conscious AI and ‘catastrophic’ risk to unusual corporate structures and executive perks. by Robert Hart Oct 26, 2026, 5:10 PM UTC Image: The Verge Robert Hart is a London-based reporter at The Verge covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow. Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for Forbes . Anthropic has finally filed its S-1 prospectus with the SEC, a document designed to give investors a look under the hood of its business, from how much its executives are making and plans for spending its IPO billions to the risks that could derail its ambitions. At more than 300 pages, there’s a lot to unpack, and some of the disclosures have not previously been reported. Here are some of the biggest things that jumped out to us from our first pass: It pays to be an Amodei Sibling co-founders Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei are the two most highly-paid executives at Anthropic, according to the filing. Last year, CEO Dario’s compensation totaled nearly $18 million, most of which came from stock and option awards. President Daniela, meanwhile, received $16.4 million. Admittedly, it is at the lower end of the Big Tech scale , but it is still a tidy sum. And that’s not all. Anthropic also spent $2.75 million on “personal security services” for Dario and $1.29 million for “personal protection, home security, and transportation services” for Daniela. Dario also gets access to a private jet for personal use, which cost the company another $97,055. The company says its success is “highly dependent on the continued service” of its senior team, particularly Dario and Daniela, who “are critical” to advancing the company’s research and mission. Anthropic has some pretty existential risk factors Every S-1 features a long list of things that could go wrong. Anthropic’s is no exception. But alongside standard warnings about competition, regulation, and market shifts, there are some less conventional risks too. For one, Anthropic warns that AI systems could cause potentially “catastrophic” harm, potentially of a kind that could not be underwritten by the entire “insurance industry in the aggregate.” As AI systems become more sophisticated, there’s also the question of whether Claude — or any other AI system — could possess or develop “forms of sentience.” Such a scenario would present some rather unusual business challenges. There’s also the possibility they “may behave in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways” that could damage the company. It’s hungry for compute It’s no secret that Anthropic needs compute, but the sheer scale of its spending is staggering. The filing details billions of dollars of commitments to secure the compute needed to power its AI models, including roughly $3.1 billion per month to SpaceX for access to Nvidia GPUs once all of the planned capacity is delivered, totaling as much as $120.5 billion by 2029. Other commitments include spending $44.9 billion with Microsoft through 2033, at least $114.5 billion with Google through 2033, and $110 billion with Amazon over the next ten years. Anthropic also plans to expand its own “infrastructure footprint,” including overseas, as it faces increasing opposition to data center development in the US. It has a really weird corporate structure Anthropic already has a somewhat complicated corporate structure as a public benefit corporation. But there’s another unusual twist that will allow its seven cofounders to retain considerable control over the company even after it goes public. Through a separate corporate entity called “Founder LLC,” the group will collectively control 50.1 percent of shareholder voting power over key matters. Anthropic says the seven founders “are distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission” of benefiting humanity through responsible AI development. Anthropic names only two rivals There’s no shortage of AI models out there, but when it comes to “direct competition,” Anthropic names just two other developers: OpenAI and Google. Condolences to SpaceX, Meta, and the rest of the AI world. Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. title: Microsoft offers buyouts to 60,000 employees
abstract: Tech AI News Microsoft offers buyouts to 60,000 employees Microsoft’s buyout offer is reaching more of its 223,000 or so employees. Microsoft’s buyout offer is reaching more of its 223,000 or so employees. by Emma Roth and Tom Warren Oct 26, 2026, 3:58 PM UTC Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge Part Of The tech industry’s layoffs and hiring freezes: all of the news see all updates Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to up to 60,000 employees across the US, UK, Canada, and India. In a message to employees , Microsoft chief people officer Amy Coleman writes that this gives staff members “the opportunity to leave Microsoft with financial support and career planning resources” as the company looks to trim staff without another round of layoffs. Sources familiar with the situation tell The Verge that staffers across Microsoft are eligible for the voluntary exit offers, including those in its AI experiences, Copilot, CoreAI, Windows + Devices, Xbox, finance, and human resources teams. Microsoft’s cloud + AI, MicrosoftAI teams, and corporate, external, and legal affairs are partially participating, the sources say. Meanwhile, employees on Microsoft’s marketing, commercial business, discovery and quantum, and security teams aren’t participating. The voluntary exit offers come just months after Microsoft laid off 4,800 employees , a move that primarily impacted its Xbox and commercial sales teams. Xbox CEO Asha Sharma is also planning new rounds of layoffs , according to a report from Fortune . This voluntary exit offer doesn’t target Microsoft’s commercial sales teams, and it’s also very different to the previous voluntary retirement program that the company offered long-serving employees earlier this year . That previous offer was only available to around 9,000 employees, for US employees at a certain employee level whose combined years of service added to their age totaled 70 or more. “The Voluntary Exit Offer is new for us,” Coleman writes in a memo to employees. “We’ll learn from it. At the same time, we’ll keep helping people focus on the work that matters most, build new skills and, where it makes sense, find new opportunities across Microsoft. There is no one-size-fits-all approach for every team or every employee. These are a few of the ways we’re trying to meet different business needs while continuing to create opportunities for our own people to grow and contribute.” In a note posted to Microsoft’s internal HRweb site, seen by The Verge , the company says today’s offer isn’t based on age, length of service, or performance. Microsoft also says it may consider a future voluntary exit offer “where there is a business and workforce need.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. title: Kevin Roose is AGI-pilled. Why aren’t you?
abstract: Today, I’m talking to Kevin Roose, journalist and author of the new book The AGI Chronicles , which details the recent and explosive transformation of the AI industry. Kevin was a longtime New York Times reporter and host of the popular podcast Hard Fork , but he and friend of the show Casey Newton just left the Times to start the all-new tech podcast Machine Gods , which launched last week . Kevin and I talked about launching Machine Gods and what it’s like to go from The New York Times to being an independent creator — and then of course we talked about the book, which is an excellently reported dive into the companies racing to build artificial general intelligence. I wanted to get a sense from Kevin of what it was like to report this, to try and understand these characters and this moment in time, and where it all goes next. Fair warning: This conversation takes a pretty philosophical turn at the end, but I think you’ll find it a really worthwhile back-and-forth. Okay: Kevin Roose on The AGI Chronicles , starting Machine Gods , and where AI goes from here. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Kevin Roose, you are the author of The AGI Chronicles and the cofounder and cohost of the new podcast Machine Gods . Welcome to Decoder . I was listening to the first episode of Machine Gods and you and Casey discussed the fact that technically you have the title of CEO. It’s true. I won the coin flip and we needed someone. When you start a company as we have, you need to list someone as the CEO, I guess, to know who to haul in front of Congress when our first scandal inevitably breaks. So that’s going to be me. It’s funny because you’re a CEO on Decoder . It means I’m going to have to ask you the Decoder questions. [Laughs] Okay. Well, I’ve been a CEO for about five minutes and most days I frankly forget I’m the CEO. Honestly, that tracks with most of the CEOs on the show. They all act like they’ve only done it for five minutes. We’ll come to it. I want to talk about your book. It’s called The AGI Chronicles . It is a meticulously reported book about the main frontier labs and the culture shift they’ve all undergone as AI has come into the forefront and become a much more commercial product in many ways. But let’s just start with Machine Gods . You were a journalist for The New York Times for a long time. Obviously, I think the audience probably knows this, but you and I have known each other for a long time. I will say that since I have known you, your desire to be a YouTuber has been top of mind. You’re just like, “How do I get over there?” And I’ve always been like, “Run, don’t do it.” But you did it. You left The Times , you started your own podcast with our friend Casey Newton. It is the next generation of the very popular podcast, Hard Fork , which was excellent. And I’m excited for you, but what made you take the leap? Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . Yeah, you have been trying to convince me out of this for as long as I’ve been trying to convince myself into it and you have not succeeded because here I am. Yep, I failed. Utterly failed. No, look, I think that for some very good reasons, media companies have long been a little bit wary of going all in on YouTube or any other video platform. The ones that have gone all in have not necessarily come out of that with good feelings about it because there are a lot of– Yeah, they pivot to video and also into death, routinely. Yeah, you pivot to video or you sort of waste a bunch of money doing things that don’t pay for themselves. So, I think there are some structural economic reasons for that, but I also think it’s that there aren’t a lot of institutions that are equipped to make that kind of a long-term bet. I’ve been trying to YouTube-pill people in media for many years, as you know. You’ve been trying to undo the YouTube-pilling on your end, but I just think it’s clearly the most important media platform in the world right now. It’s a place where journalism has not historically had a central place. If you were to look at YouTube as a whole and try to assess what piece of it is dedicated to what you or I would consider high-quality journalism, it’s a vanishingly small part of the overall ecosystem there. So, part of my mission is just to crack that and figure out how to do YouTube and video in general in a way that is sustainable from an economic and a sort of creative standpoint. And then just to experiment and do a bunch of things. This is not a face that needs to be on YouTube. So I’m also hoping to bring some other people in and nail some formats. But I look at what The Verge has done there. I look at what people like Joanna Stern and MKBHD have done there. To me, that is very exciting and it’s a space where there’s a lot less competition than text or podcasts. Machine Gods is a podcast that you’re doing in partnership with NPR, which I want to talk about. But do you think of it as a YouTube product? We want it to be video-first. What that means basically is that we are going to give a shit about what it looks like to a degree that we have not always done. We’re going to try to give people a lot of reasons to want to watch as well as listen. Obviously, we know that there are some people who just don’t like video podcasts and so we want to give the audio audience something that is enjoyable, but this is the direction of things. You can’t do a podcast now without doing video on top of it. So we’re going to try to really embrace that and make a good version of it that is as good as two middle-aged journalists can pull off on YouTube. Truly the future of media is middle-aged journalists pivoting to YouTube. I feel the same way because I’m now making more video and that’s what we’re doing. It’s going to be great. The other reason to leave and to do this — and obviously people know I’m friends with Casey as well, and I’ve been talking to you and him about it for a long time — is that the AI story is here. There is a platform shift. There are new companies, new characters, new ideas to talk about in the world. It’s funny because in that context, usually you get a media shift as well. The way we tell stories or the formats we tell stories usually shifts alongside the thing we are talking about or the technology we’re talking about. Here, YouTube feels like the most solid media foundation that exists. It’s the one that’s the same the most, even though it’s changing and it has YouTube Shorts and now you can A / B test everything, including your own face. But it’s the one that is the most the same. Instagram has undergone some massive change and it feels like that will continue happening. Does it feel like YouTube is the most stable place to build as you’re trying to tell these new stories? It does. I mean, obviously you never want to put all your eggs in one basket. So, we are also distributing video on Apple Podcasts and Spotify and we’re going to be everywhere. But yeah, it feels relatively stable. The question I’m always wondering is what would it take to replace YouTube? Many companies have tried to replace YouTube, but to do that, you would not only have to build an experience that was better for creators and better for users, but you would also have to replicate the entire visual corpus of humanity. You would have to just get 6 million videos from plumbers about how to fix every individual sink and then upload it to that. It’s a really hard thing to displace. It is so ingrained for so many people, and I just think it’s going to keep growing. We’ll come to this when we talk about AI, but a long time ago I asked Google CEO Sundar Pichai, “Well, what are you going to do if there’s no more websites?” And he was kind of like, “Well, we have YouTube.” And there’s just no arguing with that. You sure do. And it is just going to keep growing.

title: Anthropic’s IPO filing lays out a plan to ‘revolutionize every area of human endeavor’ with AI
abstract: AI Business News Anthropic’s IPO filing lays out a plan to ‘revolutionize every area of human endeavor’ with AI The company said it plans to list on the Nasdaq exchange under the ticker ‘ANT.’ The company said it plans to list on the Nasdaq exchange under the ticker ‘ANT.’ by Robert Hart Oct 26, 2026, 1:32 PM UTC Image: The Verge Robert Hart is a London-based reporter at The Verge covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow. Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for Forbes . Anthropic has filed its S-1 prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission, preparing the company behind Claude to beat OpenAI to the punch with an IPO. In a filing with the SEC, Anthropic said it plans to list on the Nasdaq exchange under the ticker symbol “ANT.” The AI company confidentially filed with the SEC earlier this year in June, but the public document reveals more details, as well as the company’s plans for the future in its own words, as well as potential risks for investors and the world. According to the S-1, in the first half of this year Anthropic had an $80.7 billion net loss on $16.3 billion in revenue. As previously reported by the Wall Street Journal based on leaked versions of the document, the majority of that loss is from accounting charges related to notes issued by the company for funding. It also lays out billions of dollars in deals it’s made for access to compute to power its AI, including about $3.1 billion per month to SpaceX for access to Nvidia GPUs once all of the planned capacity is delivered, totaling as much as $120.5 billion by 2029. Other commitments include spending $44.9 billion with Microsoft through 2033, at least $114.5 billion with Google through 2033, and $110 billion with Amazon over the next ten years. Anthropic: We believe that AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history. If managed well, it could rapidly accelerate scientific innovation, greatly increase economic growth rates, bring cures for major diseases within reach, and solve problems that have resisted generations of human effort. Anthropic aims to realize these benefits while navigating and preventing the risks that come with a technological revolution this fast and this powerful. There are four things that we would like any investor in Anthropic to understand: the incredible potential of AI, the risks we must address, Anthropic’s unique approach to building a company and operating in the world, and the ways in which our behavior may differ from that of a purely profit-maximizing company. According to the filing, cofounder and chief executive officer Dario Amodei’s compensation totaled nearly $18 million in 2025, most of which came from stock and option awards. His sister, Daniela Amodei, who also cofounded the company and serves as its president and director, was the second highest-paid executive, receiving $16.4 million in 2025. Anthropic set out a long list of risk factors that could affect its business, including the prospect of its AI models developing “forms of sentience,” “AI-specific taxes,” and unfavorable resolutions to the many ongoing copyright disputes relating to how its models are trained. The company also warned about the risk of “catastrophic” AI-related incidents, and said it was likely no single insurer — “and potentially the insurance industry in the aggregate” — could underwrite such risk. Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. Robert Hart AI Anthropic Business News

title: Can AI help solve the COBOL code crisis?
abstract: AI Report Tech Can AI help solve the COBOL code crisis? The ancient code holding the world together may meet its match in AI. Today is not that day. by Robert Hart Oct 26, 2026, 1:15 PM UTC A computer running COBOL 73, an antiquated computer programming language, awaits taxpayer information entries at the Internal Revenue Service in Austin, Tx., on Friday, June 10, 2022. | Image: Getty Images Robert Hart is a London-based reporter at The Verge covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow. Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for Forbes . What do the IRS, banks, airlines, and government infrastructure around the world have in common? They’re all running on systems propped up by antique computer code that nobody dares touch, lest everything come crashing down. OpenAI thinks it may have a solution. On October 19th, the company touted “substantial improvements” in its latest AI models’ ability to migrate aging software written in older programming languages into modern code, which it claims could help organizations with “maintaining and modernizing older systems.” That’s a potentially massive deal. COBOL, one of the languages highlighted by OpenAI, remains stubbornly embedded in vast portions of the world’s critical infrastructure. And despite decades of efforts to banish it to history, the language has limped on, simply refusing to die. “Nobody in their right mind would use COBOL for a new development project.” It is hard to overstate COBOL’s ubiquity. Short for “common business-oriented language,” COBOL came into being in 1959. Nearly seven decades later, it is still everywhere. According to IBM , COBOL is the foundation for more than 40 percent of online banking systems, supports 80 percent of in-person credit card transactions, and handles 95 percent of ATM transactions. It also underpins many government systems, from Social Security to the IRS to services run by most states . One rough estimate puts the annual cost of COBOL’s inefficiencies to the US GDP at around $105 billion. But replacing COBOL is fiendishly difficult. The same goes for other legacy programming languages, like Fortran, still in use today for everything from scientific computing and weather forecasting to atmospheric and ocean studies and codes critical to nuclear security . These systems are often too important to risk breaking, and many of the programmers who understand them have long since retired or died. For all their impressive advances in modern software development , AI coding tools have struggled to make much headway with these legacy systems. But recent developments suggest that may be changing. In its latest blog post, OpenAI reported promising results migrating COBOL code to more modern programming languages, including C++, Java, Kotlin, Python, and Rust, without changing what the original software does. That last bit is crucial for organizations looking to ditch code like COBOL, and OpenAI acknowledges that “a migration is considered successful only if all tests pass.” In OpenAI’s own tests, GPT-6.1 Sol achieved 87 percent behavior preservation accuracy at low reasoning effort — how many computational steps the model spends analyzing a problem before giving an answer — climbing to 98 percent at higher reasoning. By comparison, at low reasoning effort, GPT-6 Astra scored around 86 percent, GPT-6 Sol just 21 percent, and GPT-5.6 Sol a mere 5 percent. “Rewriting code is not the same as replacing a system.” “These evaluation results demonstrate progress toward more accurate, affordable code migration for teams modernizing the software their businesses depend on,” OpenAI wrote. The company also reported improvements on its models’ ability to build database software in various programming languages, including COBOL. Anthropic also sees an opportunity in legacy systems. In February, it published a step-by-step “code modernization playbook” and pitched its coding agent, Claude Code, as a way to migrate COBOL code into modern languages like Java or Python. It offered no performance benchmarks showing how well Claude Code could perform such migrations, but declared that “the economics of COBOL modernization have shifted.” Shares in IBM, which derives part of its revenue helping companies maintain legacy systems, nosedived following Anthropic’s announcement. Experts who spoke to The Verge agreed that AI tools have made strides in tackling legacy code in recent years. But they cautioned that advances trumpeted by OpenAI this week are a very long way from making it possible to safely replace critical legacy systems built around it. OpenAI spokesperson Oscar Haines acknowledged in an email to The Verge that legacy code “is still far from a solved problem” and said the company is listening to feedback from developers and enterprises and exploring ways to build better tests and continue improving its models’ understanding of coding languages. Anthropic did not provide comment in time for publication. “The evaluations shown by OpenAI don’t address the key difficulty: Breaking up a complex legacy system into smaller units that can be replaced individually.” “Rewriting code is not the same as replacing a system,” said Vadim Zaytsev, an associate professor of software evolution at the University of Twente in the Netherlands. Systems do have a lot of code — Zaytsev said the largest system he’d seen had 250 million lines of COBOL, “definitely not the world’s largest” — but that’s only part of the problem. Code may be written in multiple languages and there’s data, potentially stored in various formats, to consider, he said. There are also technical integrations with other systems and the expectations of the people and organizations to bear in mind. All that complexity means “AI is not playing a major role at the moment in replacing or migrating legacy COBOL systems,” Zaytsev said. OpenAI’s evaluations don’t capture this complex reality either, Arie van Deursen, a software engineering professor at Delft University of Technology in the Netherlands, told The Verge . He described the company’s blog as “superficial,” noting it offered few details about the migration task, while its language benchmark tested models on a relatively simple and well-defined task involving systems similar to those they would have encountered in training. He also stressed the huge gap between maintaining an aging system and modernizing it. “Maintaining is of course a lot easier than modernizing,” van Deursen said, calling the tasks OpenAI used to assess its models “lightyears” away from actual modernization. “The evaluations shown by OpenAI don’t address the key difficulty: Breaking up a complex legacy system into smaller units that can be replaced individually.” The biggest challenge isn’t necessarily rewriting code. “The main challenge is indeed not understanding how the system works,” said Alastair Donaldson, a professor of programming languages at Imperial College London. Such a lack of understanding is a “very common” problem for legacy systems using languages like COBOL, he said, adding that very few people know how to program in them anymore. And while it is everywhere, Donaldson said “nobody in their right mind would use COBOL for a new development project.” “In many cases even minor differences in system behaviour before and after migration are unacceptable.” That makes robust testing crucial, Donaldson said. One approach could be to run the same workflows through the old and new systems to check they behave identically. AI could also document its code translation, ideally allowing humans familiar with the legacy language to review the work. Formal verification, which uses mathematical techniques to computationally verify that code behaves correctly, is another option, said Jacopo Mauro, a mathematics and computer science professor at the University of Southern Denmark.

Explore other styles: General summary Bullet points Basic explainer Today, we’re launching “Polar Peaks”, our third quest in the AI Quests series, created by Google Research and the Stanford Accelerator for Learning to teach students how AI works and how to use it responsibly. AI Quests invites students ages 11 to 14 to step into the shoes of Google researchers to tackle some of humanity’s biggest challenges. More than 400,000 quests have been completed to date, localized to 10 languages. Alongside the new quest, we’re also releasing training modules for teachers. Polar Peaks: A journey to map the human brain In the first two quests, students tackle flood forecasting and eye disease detection, inspired by Google Research’s Flood Forecasting initiative and AI model for diabetic retinopathy screening. Our newest quest, “Polar Peaks,” has students travel to the frontiers of neuroscience and see how AI can speed up scientific research. With the guidance of in-game mentors, students scan and map the neurons in the brain to better understand the game character’s memory loss. They complete tasks like data cleaning and model testing, learning firsthand that AI requires careful human oversight and critical thinking. The quest is inspired by over a decade of our research in connectomics: the science of mapping neural networks in the brain. Upon completion of the quest, students hear from two researchers behind our real-world breakthroughs, including the recent mapping of the complete fruit fly brain, the largest brain map by number of neurons to date. Training modules: Tools for teaching AI literacy Teachers play a critical role in bringing the quests to life and fitting them into their existing classroom curriculum. We’re rolling out new dedicated teacher training modules to help educators reinforce key AI literacy concepts and use AI Quests for learning and discussion. These are launching within the Google AI Educator Series . The modules for Quest #1 and #2 are accessible here . The training module for Quest #3 will follow next month. Earlier this year, AI Quests won a 2026 Webby Award for AI Education, Learning & Training, and Best Global K–12 Learning Solution at the ETIH Innovation Awards. title: Nace AI Releases Drex for Search for AI Agents: 92.05% on BrowseComp-Plus With 12.6 Search Calls
abstract: Nace AI has released Drex for Search , which brings its Drex decision models to document search. Drex for Search is a retrieval layer that helps people and agents find evidence. Coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and OpenCode call it through CLI, SDKs, MCP or REST. In Nace’s evaluation, it scores 92.05% on BrowseComp-Plus with GPT-5, using 12.6 search calls per question. Nace AI frames search as a series of decisions. Drex for Search applies its Drex models to those decisions. Drex scores given options with a calibrated probability each, in 1 forward pass. That makes it cheap enough for every agent step. The release targets classic RAG, which Nace sums up as chunk, embed, top-k, hope. The pipeline breaks in 3 cases: Depth is fixed, so Nace says a million files take as many steps as a thousand. Nace AI tested 9 agent and model pairs on OfficeQA Pro , a 133-question benchmark over U.S. Treasury Bulletins. Key highlights: 6% more answers right, 62% fewer steps, 56% fewer tokens, and 2.3x faster. BrowseComp-Plus asks a deep-research agent 830 multi-hop questions over about 100K fixed web documents. With GPT-5, Nace AI reports: On VisDocAgentBench , an agent finds 1 target page among 2,375 arXiv pages. Drex for Search scores 77.5% R@1 with an open-weight Qwen 27B planner. The best published agent, Claude Opus 5, scores 67.5%. R@1 is 97.5% on direct questions, 77.5% on one bridge, and 57.5% on two. On MADQA , agents answer over 800 PDFs and cite pages. Nace reports 94.7% accuracy with Gemini 3.5 Flash and a page-attribution F1 of 88.2. Its effort calibration (Kuiper) is 6.66. Nace ranks it #1, based on the leaderboard as read on October 20. With open-weight Qwen 27B, Nace reports 93.4%. On EnterpriseRAG-Bench , with 500,000+ internal company documents, Nace reports an overall score of 88.22, which it ranks #3. That is 27.2 points above OpenAI File Search (61.03). Ranks and scores are as published by Nace AI , from leaderboards read October 20, 2026. Drex for Search runs in the Nace API Console , with 4 ways in on one key: Check out the Drex for Search page , API Console , Docs and Hugging Face . Thanks to the Nace AI team for the thought leadership / resources for this article. This article is sponsored by Nace AI. title: Tsinghua AI Open-Sources AKV, a Cache Engineering Server for LLM Agents on SGLang
abstract: Tsinghua University and CUHK researchers open-sourced AKV , a serving system for KV cache engineering in LLM agents. Instead of summarizing old history, agents drop selected KV cache entries and keep reusing the rest. Across 3 models and 4 agent benchmarks, average cost falls 27.7% . Average task score rises 1.7 points. The code is Apache-2.0 licensed and builds on SGLang . AKV is a Tsinghua serving system that lets LLM agents drop and reposition their own KV cache. Context engineering trims or summarizes the text history. Editing that prefix invalidates every later KV state. The retained suffix must then be re-prefilled. Harnesses therefore summarize late and aggressively, which can lose details from middle rounds. Cache engineering leaves the text trajectory untouched. It only changes which KV entries stay visible to attention. Retained entries are reused without recomputation. They can still carry information from dropped messages. In the research paper’s cost analysis, KV cache reads made up 82.4% of total API cost. AKV defines 3 cache operations. Append is the standard update for new tokens. Drop removes selected entries from future attention without changing positions. Repos rewrites retained keys to positions 0 through r-1 using a RoPE rotation . Values stay unchanged, so no hidden states are recomputed. In ablations, adding Repos raised GPT-OSS-120B’s BrowseComp-Plus pass rate from 55% to 62%. The hard part is serving. Identical tokens can produce different cache states under different operation histories. Plain prefix matching could reuse the wrong states. AKV extends SGLang’s radix tree with drop and reposition nodes. It frees dropped KV only when no active request still needs it. Segment-batch attention restores evicted states in 1 prefill pass. The interface is stateless and OpenAI-compatible . Clients send the full message history and two optional fields. drop_message maps a trigger message index to the messages to drop. reposition lists the indices after which positions get compacted. A CachePolicy builds those fields from a trigger, a selector and a reposition rule. Built-in policies are turn-based, token-based or model-based. A CacheTool lets the model call drop_context itself. The main policy is a tool-response rolling drop that keeps the latest 12 tool responses. The Standard baseline summarizes at 96K tokens (192K for MiroThinker). Text Engineering summarizes at 48K. Benchmarks are BrowseComp-Plus , GAIA-Text , SWE-bench Verified and xbench-DeepSearch-2510 . Average pass rate (%) and cost (US cents per task) across 4 benchmarks. Source: Table 1 of the paper . AKV also cuts cost 21.9% versus Text Engineering. The accuracy gap opens on long runs. On BrowseComp-Plus at 96K tokens and above, GPT-OSS-120B scores 37% with AKV. Standard scores 24% and Text Engineering 32%, per the project page . Costs are API-equivalent estimates from published rates. Repositioned tokens are charged at the cache-hit rate, a deliberately conservative choice. Serving tests ran GPT-OSS-120B on 80 long-context SWE-bench Verified tasks. At each method’s peak setting, AKV delivers 1.18x output throughput and 1.53x input throughput. P95 request latency is 1.51x faster. At concurrency 16, Standard’s P95 latency hits 229.90 seconds versus 30.63 for AKV. KV pressure pushes Standard into repeated re-prefill. Per decode step, full-attention time falls from 7.082 to 2.849 ms. On 100 SWE-bench Verified tasks under a GPU budget, AKV reached about 47% pass rate. Standard reached 40.7% and Text Engineering 32.3%. MiniMax-M2.7 refined policies on 20 BrowseComp-Plus tasks, then ran 100 held-out tasks. The iteration-6 policy cut cost 17.8% versus Standard at baseline accuracy. The abstract reports 7.1% savings beyond the expert-designed policy. Exposing cache control as a tool also helped accuracy. GPT-OSS-120B rose from 52.1 to 61.0 on a 100-task subset. MiniMax-M2.7’s cost rose, though, from 5.4 to 5.9 cents. The main numbers come from each project’s own paper and use different setups. They are not directly comparable. Check out the Paper , GitHub Repo and Project Page . title: Nanbeige Releases Nanbeige4.3-33B, a 33B Open Agentic Coding Model
abstract: Nanbeige LLM Lab has released Nanbeige4.3-33B on Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 license. Nanbeige4.3-33B is a 33B dense language model built for agentic coding and office-style ‘cowork’ tasks. The lab sits inside the recruitment platform BOSS Zhipin . It also published Nanbeige4.3-33B-Base for custom post-training. The model supports a 524,288-token context window. In the lab’s own table, it leads 17 of 20 benchmarks against 3 open models near 30B. Nanbeige4.3-33B is the flagship ‘teacher’ model of the Nanbeige4.3 series. The lab’s stated strategy is to build a strong teacher first. It then plans to distill agentic skills into smaller models, starting with Nanbeige4.3-3B. The config.json declares a standard LlamaForCausalLM architecture. There is no expert routing, so all 33B parameters run on every token. The chat template exposes 3 controls. enable_thinking toggles reasoning and is on by default. preserve_thinking keeps reasoning from earlier turns. Nanbeige recommends it for multi-turn tool use and code agents. Passing tools enables tool calling, and an XML call format is recommended. Nanbeige compared the model with Qwen3.8-27B, Muse-Glimmer-30B and Gemma4-31B. Every model ran at its highest thinking effort, with shared hyperparameters and harnesses. All scores in this section are self-reported. It loses 3 of 20 rows. Qwen3.8-27B leads SWE-Bench Pro (61.7 vs 60.3) and GDPval (86.4 vs 84.8). Gemma4-31B leads GPQA Diamond in Nanbeige’s table, 91.3 vs 89.5. The Base model beats Gemma4-31B-Base on all 8 reported tasks. Examples include MMLU-Pro (66.9 vs 59.3) and GPQA (62.0 vs 41.5). *Self-reported by Nanbeige. Competitor values come from each lab’s own Hugging Face model card. Some competitor figures in Nanbeige’s table differ from what those labs publish: Different harnesses explain some gaps. The SWE-Bench Pro pair looks swapped. Treat these rows as provisional until independent runs appear. The model card provides Transformers, SGLang and vLLM recipes. Its server examples use 4-way tensor parallelism with Qwen3 reasoning and tool-call parsers. Recommended agent settings are temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95 and 65,536 max new tokens. Reasoning and chat use temperature 0.6 and 262,144 max new tokens. By arithmetic from config.json, BF16 weights need about 66 GB. The KV cache adds about 208 KiB per token in BF16. A full 524,288-token sequence therefore needs roughly 112 GB of KV cache. At publication, no Hugging Face Inference Provider hosts the model. Check out the model weights , the Base model and the launch post on X . Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter .
