title: The Roadmap to Becoming a Computer Vision Engineer in 2026
abstract: The Roadmap to Becoming a Computer Vision Engineer in 2026 A four-stage technical roadmap for becoming a computer vision engineer, from spatial mathematics and ViTs through 3D neural rendering and edge deployment optimization. By Vinod Chugani on October 26, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence Computer vision (CV) has moved far beyond object detection and image classification. In 2026, CV engineers work at the intersection of foundation models, spatial computing, and embedded hardware, building systems that perceive, reason over, and act on the visual world in real time. The demand for engineers who can operate across this full stack is growing steadily. Autonomous vehicles, robotic warehouses, medical imaging platforms, and spatial computing devices all share a common need: engineers who understand not just model architecture, but the full pipeline from sensor to production inference. This roadmap covers four stages, progressing from the spatial mathematics and foundational vision primitives that everything else depends on, through to edge deployment and hardware-aware optimization. Each stage builds directly on the previous one. Step 1: Spatial Mathematics and Foundation Vision Primitives Every CV system is ultimately a system for reasoning about geometry. Before working with modern vision architectures, you need a working understanding of the mathematics that make visual reasoning possible. The core concepts at this stage include matrix transformations, coordinate frames, projective geometry, and multi-view geometry. These aren't abstract. They determine how a camera maps a 3D world onto a 2D sensor, how two camera views can reconstruct depth, and how coordinate systems relate across sensors in a multi-camera rig. On the implementation side, start building fluency with PyTorch for tensor manipulation, which remains the standard framework for vision research and production. Pair this with synthetic data augmentation pipelines. Albumentations is the most widely used library for this, offering fast, composable transforms that simulate lighting variation, geometric distortion, and occlusion without collecting new data. Feature representation is the third pillar of this stage. Understand the distinction between convolutional backbones (ResNet, EfficientNet) and attention-based backbones. Contrastive representation learning — where models learn by comparing similar and dissimilar examples — has become a standard technique for learning useful embeddings before downstream fine-tuning. Recommended resources: Multiple View Geometry in Computer Vision by Hartley and Zisserman (the canonical reference); Stanford CS231n lecture notes (free online); the PyTorch documentation's tensor tutorial series. Portfolio exercise: Implement a basic stereo depth estimation pipeline using two calibrated images. Visualize the disparity map and document where the estimation fails and why. Step 2: Vision Transformers and Multimodal Foundation Models The shift from convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to transformer-based architectures for vision has reshaped what CV engineers need to know. Vision Transformers (ViTs) process images as sequences of fixed-size patches, applying self-attention across those patches rather than local convolutional filters. Swin Transformers extended this with hierarchical, windowed attention that makes the approach practical for high-resolution inputs. Beyond pure vision models, the more significant development is the emergence of vision-language models (VLMs). Models like CLIP and SigLIP learn joint embeddings across image and text modalities through contrastive training on large web-scraped datasets. The practical result is open-vocabulary understanding: you can query a visual scene with natural language descriptions rather than fixed class labels. This unlocks a class of techniques called open-vocabulary detection. Models like OWL-ViT and Grounding DINO extend this capability to object localization, letting you detect any object described in text without retraining on labeled examples of that object. The Segment Anything Model 2 ( SAM 2 ) from Meta takes a different approach, offering promptable, zero-shot segmentation for both static images and video streams. A user or upstream model provides a point, bounding box, or text prompt, and SAM 2 produces a high-quality segmentation mask without task-specific training. Understanding how these foundation models work, where they fail (domain shift, fine-grained distinctions, rare objects), and how to compose them into pipelines is the central skill of this stage. import torch from PIL import Image import requests from transformers import AutoProcessor, AutoModelForZeroShotObjectDetection model_id = "IDEA-Research/grounding-dino-tiny" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForZeroShotObjectDetection.from_pretrained(model_id) image = Image.open("scene.jpg") text_prompt = "a red forklift. a safety helmet." inputs = processor(images=image, text=text_prompt, return_tensors="pt") outputs = model(**inputs) This runs open-vocabulary detection using a text prompt against a scene image, with no task-specific training required. Recommended resources: An Image is Worth 16x16 Words (the original ViT paper); the Hugging Face Transformers documentation for hands-on model loading; Meta AI's SAM 2 repository and paper. Portfolio exercise: Build a zero-shot object detection demo using Grounding DINO. Test it across three different domains (indoor scenes, outdoor scenes, a specialized domain like medical or industrial) and document where the open-vocabulary approach breaks down. Step 3: 3D Vision, Neural Rendering, and Spatial Perception As CV systems move from image understanding to spatial reasoning, the skill set expands significantly. This stage covers the representations and algorithms that let systems understand and reconstruct the 3D world from 2D inputs. The primary 3D representations you'll work with are point clouds, voxel grids, and signed distance fields (SDFs). Each has different memory characteristics, computational costs, and downstream application fits. Point clouds are the natural output of LiDAR sensors and structure-from-motion pipelines. Voxel grids offer regular spatial structure at the cost of memory. SDFs represent geometry as continuous functions, enabling differentiable rendering. Depth estimation is the entry point for most 3D work. Depth Anything (v2 in particular) is the current leading monocular depth estimation model, producing relative or metric depth maps from a single RGB image without any additional sensors. Neural rendering has developed rapidly. Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) learn to synthesize novel views of a scene from a set of posed images. 3D Gaussian Splatting offers a faster, more memory-efficient alternative that has largely displaced NeRFs for real-time applications, enabling interactive novel view synthesis on consumer hardware. Spatial perception, relevant for robotics and autonomous systems, requires understanding Visual Odometry (VO) and Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM). These techniques let systems estimate their own position and build a map of their environment incrementally using only camera inputs. import numpy as np import open3d as o3d # Load point cloud from depth map and camera intrinsics depth = np.load("depth_map.npy") fx, fy, cx, cy = 525.0, 525.0, 319.5, 239.5 h, w = depth.shape u, v = np.meshgrid(np.arange(w), np.arange(h)) z = depth x = (u - cx) * z / fx y = (v - cy) * z / fy points = np.stack([x, y, z], axis=-1).reshape(-1, 3) pcd = o3d.geometry.PointCloud() pcd.points = o3d.utility.Vector3dVector(points) o3d.io.write_point_cloud("output.ply", pcd) This reconstructs a 3D point cloud from a depth map using known camera intrinsics, a technique used in depth-sensor pipelines, robotic mapping, and augmented reality (AR) applications.

title: Building Your First AI Agent in Python with the OpenAI Agents SDK
abstract: Building Your First AI Agent in Python with the OpenAI Agents SDK Build your first AI agent in Python with the OpenAI Agents SDK, adding web search, Python tools, conversation memory, and tracing in a simple end-to-end workflow. By Abid Ali Awan , KDnuggets Assistant Editor on October 26, 2026 in Python Building an AI agent in Python is now much simpler than it used to be. With the OpenAI Agents SDK , you can create agents, connect tools, maintain conversation state, and run multi-step workflows without building your own tool-calling loop from scratch. In this tutorial, we will build a practical research agent that can search the web, call a custom Python function, remember previous messages, and decide when to use each capability . What Is an AI Agent? A standard large language model (LLM) application usually follows a simple flow: Prompt — Model — Response The model receives a prompt, generates an answer, and stops. An AI agent adds tools and an execution loop : User — Agent — Tool if needed — Agent — Final Response Instead of only generating text, the agent can decide whether it needs to take an action first, such as searching the web, calling a Python function, or retrieving information from memory. With the OpenAI Agents SDK, the Runner manages this process automatically. It sends the request to the model, executes any requested tools, passes the results back to the agent, and continues until the agent produces a final answer. This ability to reason, use tools, and continue working across multiple steps is what makes an agent different from a basic LLM application. Set Up the Project Before we build the agent, let's create a clean Python environment and install everything we need. Create a Python project with uv : mkdir first-ai-agent cd first-ai-agent uv init uv add openai-agents Or install the package with pip : pip install openai-agents Set your OpenAI API key: export OPENAI_API_KEY="your-api-key" On Windows, export works in Git Bash. In Command Prompt or PowerShell, you can use: setx OPENAI_API_KEY "your-api-key" Build Your First Agent Now we can turn a few lines of Python into an agent that decides when it needs fresh information from the web. Create main.py : from agents import Agent, Runner, WebSearchTool agent = Agent( name="Research Assistant", instructions=( "You are a concise research assistant. " "Use web search when current information is required." ), tools=[WebSearchTool()], ) result = Runner.run_sync( agent, "What are the latest developments in Python?" ) print(result.final_output) Run it: uv run main.py Output: As of **September 14, 2026**, the major Python developments are: - **Python 3.14 is the latest stable feature series**; the newest maintenance release is **3.14.7**. It adds officially supported free-threaded builds, deferred annotation evaluation, template string literals (`t""`), ... - **Python 3.15 is nearing release**: the final release is scheduled for **October 1, 2026**. ... For new projects, **Python 3.14.7** is currently the safest default. WebSearchTool() is a hosted OpenAI tool, so the model can decide when it needs current information instead of you manually calling a search API. For example, our run correctly identified Python 3.14.7 as the current stable release. Add Your Own Python Tool Web search is useful, but agents become much more powerful when they can also interact with your own Python code. Add a calculation tool: from agents.decorators import tool @tool def calculate_total( price: float, quantity: int ) -> float: """Calculate the total cost of an order.""" return price * quantity Then give it to the agent: agent = Agent( name="Assistant", instructions="Help with research and calculations.", tools=[ WebSearchTool(), calculate_total, ], ) Test it: result = Runner.run_sync( agent, "I need 14 GPUs costing $2.49 each per hour. " "What will they cost per hour?" ) print(result.final_output) Output: 14 GPUs x $2.49/hour = **$34.86 per hour**. The SDK automatically uses the function name, arguments, type hints, and docstring to create a tool schema the model can understand. You do not need to manually define JSON schemas or write the tool-calling loop yourself. Tip: Write clear docstrings because they help the model understand what a tool does and when it should use it. Adding Conversation Memory A useful agent should not forget everything the moment the next message arrives, so let's give it conversation memory. To make the agent conversational, add a session: from agents import SQLiteSession session = SQLiteSession( "user_1", "conversations.db" ) Then pass it into each run: while True: message = input("You: ") if message.lower() in {"exit", "quit"}: break result = Runner.run_sync( agent, message, session=session, ) print("Agent:", result.final_output) Now try: The second request automatically receives the earlier conversation, so the agent understands what "the latest version" refers to. Because we used a file-backed SQLite database, the history can also persist after restarting the program. For larger applications, the SDK also provides session backends for systems such as Redis, SQLAlchemy, and MongoDB . How the Complete Agent Works At this point, all the pieces come together: The agent decides what action to take , the Runner executes the agent loop and any requested tools , and the session preserves conversation history between requests. Here is the complete main.py : import os import sys from agents import Agent, Runner, SQLiteSession, WebSearchTool from agents.decorators import tool @tool def calculate_total( price: float, quantity: int ) -> float: """Calculate the total cost of an order.""" return price * quantity def main() -> None: if not os.environ.get("OPENAI_API_KEY"): sys.exit( "Error: set the OPENAI_API_KEY environment variable first." ) agent = Agent( name="Assistant", instructions=""" Help the user with research and calculations. Use the available tools when necessary. """, tools=[ WebSearchTool(), calculate_total, ], ) session = SQLiteSession( "user_1", "conversations.db" ) try: while True: try: message = input("You: ") except (EOFError, KeyboardInterrupt): print() break command = message.strip().lower() if command in {"exit", "quit"}: break if not command: continue try: result = Runner.run_sync( agent, message, session=session, ) except Exception as exc: print( f"Agent error " f"({type(exc).__name__}): {exc}" ) continue print("Agent:", result.final_output) finally: session.close() if __name__ == "__main__": main() This gives us a small but complete conversational agent with web search, a custom Python tool, persistent memory, basic error handling, and a continuous chat interface . The Agents SDK also enables tracing by default , which is especially useful once your workflows become more complex. Traces let you inspect the model calls, tool usage, handoffs, and other steps taken during an agent run. You can inspect these traces in the OpenAI dashboard to understand how the agent reached its answer, which tools it selected, and where problems occurred. This makes tracing particularly useful for debugging tool-calling behavior and improving agent instructions. Final Thoughts Building your first AI agent is less about creating a complex autonomous system and more about giving a model the ability to take useful actions . In this guide, we started with a simple agent, added web search , connected a custom Python tool , introduced persistent conversation memory , and brought everything together in a complete application with tracing and error handling. That foundation is enough to build surprisingly capable workflows. From here, you can gradually add APIs, MCP servers, guardrails, handoffs, more specialized tools, and additional agents as your application grows. The pattern stays the same: give the agent the right tools, let it decide when to use them, and let the Agents SDK handle the execution loop .

title: 7 Advanced Python Design Patterns for Data Scientists
abstract: 7 Advanced Python Design Patterns for Data Scientists Learn seven design patterns for data science code, from Strategy and Adapter to Command and Proxy, each matched to the pressure it solves, with the Python shape it takes and the caveat that keeps it honest. By Nahla Davies , KDnuggets on October 26, 2026 in Python Most training functions start out small and readable. Give one six months in a shared repository, though, and it accumulates model-specific conditionals, data-source branches, a hand-rolled cache check and logging calls to three destinations. No single line is wrong. The function has simply absorbed another branch every time the project changed, and now every caller inherits the whole pile. KDnuggets has already covered Python patterns for intermediate data scientists , where pipeline, factory and decorator handle the everyday cases. This article starts where that guide stops: seven patterns, each matched to one pressure that shows up once a notebook becomes code other people depend on. One rule of restraint applies to everything below. If nothing else will ever call the code, a pattern is ceremony, and a plain function remains the better tool. Patterns pay for themselves only when they remove a source of change that keeps coming back. Pattern Recurring pressure Python shape Main caveat Strategy A branch per metric or validation policy evaluate(y_true, y_pred, scorer) takes a callable Stateless behavior should stay a plain function, not a class Adapter Model APIs and output shapes that differ by library One local Protocol plus a thin wrapper that reshapes outputs Translates the interface only; semantics still pass through Template Method Sibling experiments copying the same run order ABC owns run() ; subclasses fill selected hooks Inheritance couples variants; prefer Strategy for free mixing Observer Training loop hard-wired to loggers and dashboards Frozen event dataclass sent to a list of callbacks Order, errors and cost must stay explicit as callbacks grow Command Runs that must queue, retry or travel Frozen dataclass with IDs and execute(runner) Seeds, data and code versions still need explicit identifiers Facade Five imports and a setup dance for one task One task-level method that delegates to components Keep it thin or it becomes the new monolith Proxy Expensive model or dataset loaded before it is needed Same predict() contract; _load() runs once on first use Invalidation, thread safety and load failure need decisions Table 1. All seven patterns mapped to the pressure each one answers, the Python shape it takes, and the caveat that keeps it honest. Original reference table created for this article. All seven shapes verified on Python 3.10. Pattern set per the classic catalog; guidance summarized for this article. 1. Swap Evaluation Logic With Strategy An experiment runner that picks scoring with if metric == "accuracy" grows a new branch for every metric the team adopts. Strategy removes the branching by making the scoring behavior a value the caller passes in: def evaluate(y_true, y_pred, scorer): return scorer(y_true, y_pred) evaluate(y_true, y_pred, accuracy) # 0.6 evaluate(y_true, y_pred, recall_pos) # 0.667 Both calls run against the same five predictions, but the runner never learns which policy it executed, and that ignorance is the payoff. Each scorer can now be tested on its own, and adding a new one means writing a function rather than editing the experiment. Strategy also gets confused with Command often enough that the line is worth drawing here. Strategy gives the caller interchangeable ways of doing the same job right now, while Command, further down this list, packages one operation with its arguments so the work can run later or somewhere else. The caveat comes from Python itself. A strategy with no state should stay a plain callable like the scorers above, because a class only earns its place once configuration or related methods need to travel with the behavior. 2. Normalize Model APIs With Adapter Evaluation code that checks which library produced a model has already leaked an interface problem downstream. The fix is one local contract, written as a typing.Protocol , plus a thin wrapper around anything that fails to match it: class Predictor(Protocol): def predict_proba(self, X) -> list: ... class LegacyAdapter: def __init__(self, model): self._model = model def predict_proba(self, X): scores = self._model.score_rows(X) return [[1 - s, s] for s in scores] The legacy model exposes score_rows() and returns bare scores, so the adapter reshapes them into the two-column probability format everything downstream expects. Once that wrapper exists, switching libraries no longer means rewriting the evaluation layer. Protocol carries a warning of its own here. Its checking is static, and decorating it with @runtime_checkable only makes isinstance() test for attribute presence, meaning a class whose predict_proba takes the wrong arguments still passes the check. The bigger danger sits one level deeper, at the semantics. An adapter translates an interface and nothing more, so differences in class order, decision thresholds or calibrated versus uncalibrated probabilities pass straight through it. An adapter that papers over those is a bug generator wearing a compatibility costume. 3. Fix the Experiment Skeleton With Template Method Closely related experiments tend to copy their orchestration from each other, and the copies drift. Template Method fixes the lifecycle once, in a base class built on abc , and lets subclasses fill in the steps that legitimately vary: class Experiment(ABC): def run(self): self.load() self.fit() self.evaluate() self.save() @abstractmethod def fit(self): ... A tree-model subclass implements fit() and inherits everything else, so running it executes load, fit, evaluate and save in that order, every time, for every variant. Nobody overrides run() , because the stable skeleton is the entire point. The orchestration that used to be copied between sibling experiments now lives in exactly one place, and consistent cleanup and reporting come along for free. What the pattern gains through inheritance it also pays for through inheritance, though. Every variant stays coupled to the base lifecycle. The moment steps need to change independently or combine freely, they belong in Strategy objects composed at runtime rather than in a deeper subclass tree. 4. Broadcast Run Events With Observer A training loop that calls the experiment tracker, the console, the dashboard and the early-stopping check by name has four reasons to change that have nothing to do with training. Observer flips the dependency, so the loop emits one immutable event and a list of callbacks decides what happens next: @dataclass(frozen=True) class EpochEnded: epoch: int loss: float for cb in observers: cb(EpochEnded(epoch, loss)) Two observers with separate jobs show why this works. A console logger formats each event into a line, while a best-score tracker keeps the lowest loss it has seen, and neither knows the other exists. Adding a dashboard writer later just means appending one callable to the list, with the training loop untouched. Freezing the event matters more than it looks, too, since any observer that tries to mutate it gets a FrozenInstanceError instead of silently corrupting what the next observer receives. The trouble with Observer arrives at scale. A visible list of three callbacks is easy to reason about, but event order, error handling and per-event cost all need explicit answers before this grows into an invisible event bus nobody can trace. 5. Package Reproducible Runs as Commands Some runs should not execute the moment somebody thinks of them. A sweep might need to wait for overnight capacity, and a run that produced an interesting result last week might deserve an exact repeat today.

title: Expanding Claude for Nonprofits
abstract: Today, we're releasing the Claude for Nonprofits plugin, a set of skills and connectors built with ~30 nonprofits. It helps teams set up Claude responsibly with their organization's context and policies, supports fundraising from research through reporting, and takes on the operational work that stretches small teams. We're also planning to extend Claude Corps (opens in new tab) , our program for placing early-career fellows in U.S. nonprofits, through a partnership with Taproot (opens in new tab) . As a public benefit corporation, Anthropic has a responsibility to make sure our products are accessible and useful to organizations working on the world’s hardest problems. Last December, we launched Claude for Nonprofits (opens in new tab) with discounts of up to 75%, connectors for Blackbaud, Candid, and Benevity, and a free AI Fluency course built with GivingTuesday. More than 25,000 nonprofits now use Claude in their work. Most of those organizations are small, local operations: more than 75% of them have fewer than 10 Claude seats. We think today's update will have the biggest impact on these organizations. Katherine Rodrigues, who leads AI Transformation at the International Rescue Committee (IRC), explains how Claude helped spot a spike in pneumonia cases and mobilize their response. We’ve spent the last year working directly with nonprofits to meet their needs. We expanded nonprofit plans to the same models as our standard Team and Enterprise plans, lowered the Team plan minimum to orgs with as few as two people, and included Claude Code in nonprofit plans at no additional cost. And during the United Nations General Assembly in September, we launched a new discount of ~90% for verified nonprofits in low- and middle-income countries, bringing standard Team seats to $3/user/month. Cost is only one barrier. Nonprofits told us two others stood in the way: a lack of people with the skills to put AI to work, and a lack of tools built specifically for how nonprofits operate. Too few people with AI skills . Claude Corps is placing 1,000 early-career fellows in at least 400 US nonprofits to build with Claude alongside their teams. Hosts include a wide variety of organizations, from large organizations to small, local teams, including food banks, art museums, and veteran support organizations. We’re now planning to extend this program through a partnership with Taproot, which would match nonprofits with experienced pro bono consultants for shorter, project-based work. A growing group of partners can support nonprofit adoption, including Accenture, Boston Consulting Group (BCG), The Bridgespan Group, Civis Analytics, Deloitte, fusionSpan, Idealist Consulting, Myridius, SapienAI, Slalom, v4c.ai, and Vera Solutions. And for teams getting started on their own, we’re hosting two live webinars: Claude for Nonprofits: An Admin's Guide to Data Handling and AI Use Policy (opens in new tab) , for admins, on November 10, and Claude for Nonprofits: A Staff Guide to Making Claude Useful on Day One (opens in new tab) on November 12. Too few tools built to meet nonprofits where they’re at. We built the skills we're releasing today with the nonprofits in our Design Partner Circle. It includes ~30 organizations, from small teams serving one region of the United States to international organizations operating in dozens of countries, working on education, economic mobility, health, humanitarian response, and more. Many are funders themselves. This fall, fundraisers, operations leads, and chiefs of staff at many of these organizations tried early versions of our skills on real work and told us what wasn't working. We brainstormed, iterated, and updated our solution based on what we heard. What's in the plugin We’re starting with three areas nonprofits told us were most urgent, especially as year-end fundraising picks up. Extend your team Many nonprofits told us the same thing: there are more jobs to do than people to do them, so everyone covers several roles at once. Claude extends your team, so a small staff can work like a bigger one and spend more of its time on the mission. Marketing: plan a campaign sized to your team’s bandwidth, teach Claude to draft in your organization’s voice, and get a second read on your content before it goes out. Hiring and people: build a job post with an interview guide and scoring rubric, plan a new hire's first 90 days, and answer staff questions from your own handbook. Board and leadership : see what skills your board is missing, draft outreach to the candidates you have in mind, get new members up to speed with an orientation packet, and plan the deck for your next meeting. Set up Claude responsibly: security, governance, and context Claude works best when it has your organization’s context, including your mission, programs, workstreams, communication principles, and policies, and when your staff have clear rules for working with it. Start by asking Claude to: Map your organization . Claude asks where you keep each kind of record, like donor data, grant files, finances and policies, and, with memory on, saves that map for each person. It then offers to connect the tools it can't reach yet. Every other skill in the plugin reads the map first, so Claude knows where to look and you don't have to point it to the same source for each task. Check what your AI policy allows . Staff can ask "Can I use Claude for this?" and get the answer based on your organization's own AI policy. (No policy yet? See the Claude Academy tutorial below.) Fund your mission Fundraising is the lifeline for nonprofits, and it matters even more toward the end of the year. It's also time-intensive and process-heavy, which can be challenging for small organizations. The plugin supports the full fundraising lifecycle, freeing up your team's time for the irreplaceable human work, like managing relationships and deciding which opportunities to pursue. Find the right funders and grants. Research donors, foundations, companies, and surface open grants, with sources cited. Decide what to pursue . Forward an RFP and get a breakdown on eligibility, requirements, and what it would take to compete. Write proposals and reports . Turn an RFP into a requirements list and a first draft built from your own material. Grant reports include sources for their figures. Keep relationships warm . Get a brief before a funder call, a write-up and thank-you note after, and donor updates in your voice. Ask how to re-engage donors and receive a stewardship plan. Where nonprofits are seeing impact “For Start Early, AI is a tool that supports the people who carry out our mission. Claude first helped our staff save time on tasks like formatting. The nonprofit skills take that further, offering a vision of how AI can support whole workflows instead of single tasks. That gives our teams a strong starting point and opportunity for more time to focus on advancing outcomes for children and families.” Stella Owings, Senior Project Manager, Start Early “Good investor engagement starts with understanding what a funder is working toward. The nonprofit skills in Claude have been a helpful administrative tool, helping us find funding opportunities, connect a funder’s goals to our programmatic work and pull relationship history from our CRM. This allows our team to spend more time on strengthening the relationships that advance StriveTogether’s mission of helping every child succeed from cradle to career.” Amanda Jenkins, Senior Manager, Development, StriveTogether “We built Rumi with Claude so every teacher can have a coach in their pocket. Turning a national curriculum into a year of daily lessons used to take expert teams years. Our agents now do this in a week, then coach teachers daily in their own language. 95% of teachers rate the lesson plans as useful. We support 16,000 teachers and 418,000 learners across 6 countries, and Rumi is open source so others can use it too.

title: GHARP: Real-Time Gaussian Head Animation from Large-Scale Reconstruction Prior
abstract: research area Computer Vision conference Asian Conference on Computer Vision (ACCV) content type paper published October 2026 GHARP: Real-Time Gaussian Head Animation from Large-Scale Reconstruction Prior Authors Ali Benlalah*, Sepehr Johari*, Patricia Vitoria*, Armin Kappeler*, Artem Sevastopolsky, Alexander Jung, Gabriele Fanelli, Kevin Mader, Manuel Breitenstein, Claudia Plüss, Jan Rüegg, Simon Biland, Thomas Etterlin, Dmitry Kostiaev, Mathias Deschler, Brian Amberg, Sebastian Martin View publication Copy Bibtex We present GHARP (Real-time Gaussian Head Animation from Large-scale Reconstruction Prior), a method that animates 3D human heads in real time from a few input images of a subject and a driving expression signal. We decouple the problem into an identity stage that builds a representation of the subject’s geometry and appearance offline, and an animation stage that predicts expression-dependent residuals on top of it at runtime. This separation offers a favorable trade-off with respect to fidelity, quality and runtime: the identity stage can be expensive while the animation stage runs a lightweight network, optimized for mobile devices. Our method performs animation in a semantically structured latent space of a pretrained reconstruction model, where expression changes remain spatially contained, making residual prediction efficient. This reconstruction prior provides a consistent spatial layout, allowing fusion of multiple input views into a compact, fixed-size canonical Gaussian representation. While this two-stage design improves the runtime-quality trade-off, it still inherits a problem common to all expression-driven avatar methods: expression codes describe only the face and thus omit body pose and clothing position, making these regions underspecified in the input. The animation network faces an ill-posed mapping and resorts to averaging over conflicting body appearances, producing blur and temporal flicker. We address this with a body alignment network that learns to align the person’s body in the target image with the input reference images, removing the ambiguity from the training signal. Our method achieves state-of-the-art quality on the Ava-256 benchmark while running up to 13× faster on an A100 GPU with 8× fewer Gaussians. * Equal Contributors Related readings and updates. Large-Scale High-Quality 3D Gaussian Head Reconstruction from Multi-View Captures May 8, 2026 research area Computer Vision conference ECCV We propose HeadsUp, a scalable feed-forward method for reconstructing high-quality 3D Gaussian heads from large-scale multi-camera setups. Our method employs an efficient encoder-decoder architecture that compresses input views into a compact latent representation. This latent representation is then decoded into a set of UV-parameterized 3D Gaussians anchored to a neutral head template. This UV representation decouples the number of 3D Gaussians… Read more HUGS: Human Gaussian Splats December 7, 2023 research area Computer Vision Recent advances in neural rendering have improved both training and rendering times by orders of magnitude. While these methods demonstrate state-of-the-art quality and speed, they are designed for photogrammetry of static scenes and do not generalize well to freely moving humans in the environment.
