title: How NVIDIA Minerva Turns Telemetry Chaos Into Peak GPU Yield
abstract: AI Factories are some of the most technologically complex operational environments ever created. Hundreds of thousands of GPUs, NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet scale-out, scale-across and scale-in fabrics, NVIDIA NVLink scale-up fabrics, distributed schedulers, and multi-week training runs operate in continuous lockstep.These layers function as one production system even when different teams own their telemetry. In synchronous distributed training, a job advances at the pace of its slowest rank. One degraded GPU, interface, storage device, or switch path can waste useful time across many healthy resources. The failures that hurt yield are often subtle: A GPU runs a few degrees hotter than its peers. An NVMe device loses performance only under sustained load. A switch generates a pause-frame storm that looks like dozens of unrelated symptoms. None of these signals necessarily crosses a static threshold. Together, they create stragglers, extended step times, and delayed checkpoints. Diagnosis becomes harder because the evidence is split across teams. Network operators see interface counters and fabric events. Compute operators see node and GPU health. ML teams see changing step times, failed jobs, or unstable inference latency. Each view is accurate, but the relationships between them remain hidden. Triage becomes a chain of dashboard searches and cross-team handoffs, which can turn a contained fault into hours or days of lost production time before the affected node or fabric path is identified. This post covers how NVIDIA Minerva, an AI-native AIOps platform designed around AI factory topology and workloads, addresses these operational gaps. NVIDIA Minerva collects telemetry across the stack, maps infrastructure to active jobs in a dynamic knowledge graph, applies purpose-built machine learning, and correlates dependent symptoms into high-fidelity incidents. An AI agent-powered assistant and MCP server connected to external agentic tools give operators a conversational path through the same live evidence. The goal is practical: preserve effective GPU hours and keep model training moving. Why conventional monitoring breaks at AI factory scale Rule-based monitoring assumes that a known metric crossing a known boundary indicates a known condition. That model works for clear failures. It struggles with so-called “gray failures,” where a component stays available, and the relevant issue may appear only under load or in comparison with peers. Absolute thresholds can miss the shift. Aggressive thresholds often add warnings during normal workload changes, leaving the on-call engineer to decide which deviation matters. Scale adds alert amplification. One physical fault can produce interface errors, RX (receive) pause frames, congestion indicators, GPU utilization changes, and slower job progress. These observations describe the same dependency chain, but separate dashboards or alerts present them as unrelated events. The on-call engineer receives a volume of alerts and needs to manually correlate the alerts, determine the signal from the noise, analyze the root cause and the jobs exposed to it. For operations, the workload is the unit that matters. Teams need to know which job is affected, which resources it occupies, where those resources sit in the physical and logical topology, and how current behavior differs from a healthy baseline. That context must remain current as jobs start and stop and as nodes are drained, replaced, or returned to service. Without it, a healthy component dashboard can coexist with poor job throughput and offer no explanation. Building a live model of infrastructure and jobs Figure 1. The NVIDIA Minerva AIOps observability platform Solving these challenges requires end-to-end visibility across the AI Factory. NVIDIA Minerva ingests metrics, logs, and topology from GPUs, Spectrum-X and NVLink switches, SuperNICs, DPUs, storage, NVIDIA NCCL, schedulers, and AI workloads. Auto-discovery supplies the relationships that raw telemetry lacks. The resulting knowledge graph maps infrastructure, scheduler, and workload elements, then updates those relationships as the environment changes. It can span multiple data centers and support navigation from a factory-wide view to an individual interface. The topology graph is the key to changing the investigation path. Starting with an anomalous interface, an operator can identify its node, the fabric path it serves, current job placement, and nearby components in the same failure domain. Starting with a job ID, an ML engineer can trace the workload through GPU, host, NIC, switch, and log evidence. Network and compute teams can start from an infrastructure event and see the affected jobs, or conversely see an affected job and investigate the cause using NVIDIA Minerva. Everyone works from the same current causal map instead of reconciling separate inventories. Detecting gray failures with purpose-built machine learning NVIDIA Minerva processes billions of metric and log data points per hour with supervised and unsupervised models developed for AI factory infrastructure and workloads. Supervised detection identifies known critical error patterns and can associate recognized conditions with specific remediation guidance. Unsupervised models cover behavior with no predefined signature. They learn normal patterns for a hardware or logical component and compare it with the relevant peers. Peer comparison matters because a measurement can look acceptable in isolation and still be anomalous in context. Sustained errors on a network interface may look normal in isolation but compared to other interfaces, they stand out as anomalous. A GPU temperature may remain within specification while running substantially hotter than sibling GPUs under the same load. Multivariate models can combine temperature, power, clocks, utilization, and workload state to detect that degradation before the component fails outright. Logs receive similar treatment. NLP-based anomaly detection surfaces previously unseen patterns, while supervised matching identifies known critical errors. A detection can feed scheduler workflows so an affected node is drained before another job lands on it or at a safe point between checkpoints. Collapsing event storms into actionable incidents Figure 2. The NVIDIA Minerva Topology Graph Topology-aware correlation connects detection to operator action. The correlation engine’s algorithms leverage the knowledge graph to determine which events share a dependency path. Downstream symptoms are then grouped as one incident instead of competing for attention. The result is less alert noise and more context. NVIDIA Minerva can collapse redundant events and related metric series into a single signal with affected topology and workloads attached. NVIDIA testing shows significant reductions in notified events and tickets for supported scenarios. Operators still need to determine the root-cause using other capabilities provided by NVIDIA Minerva, but they begin with a much smaller search space. Once NVIDIA Minerva creates a high-confidence incident, teams can consume it through the platform UI or existing workflows. Agentic debugging Correlated evidence still requires interpretation. NVIDIA Minerva includes a native AI agent called Sherlock which is grounded in live telemetry and the knowledge graph, so an operator can ask why a specific job slowed during a particular interval, which components changed state, or whether other nodes share the same failure domain. Sherlock enables network ops, compute ops and site reliability engineering (SRE) teams to query the system for root-cause-analysis in human language. Sherlock can present supporting evidence and recommend remediation without requiring every operator to know the exact metric, dashboard, or query language. This gives less experienced operators a route to domain knowledge that has traditionally required escalation to a specialist.

title: How NVIDIA Mission Control 2.5 Brings Autonomous Recovery to Kubernetes
abstract: Training large-scale AI models on thousands of GPUs is a high-stakes operation where monitoring and automation must be built-in to optimize cluster resiliency and uptime at scale. This concept isn’t new to data center operators who have measured mean-time-to-repair (MTTR) and mean-time-between-failure (MTBF) long before AI factories existed. Now the stakes are higher. Modern AI factories run distributed training jobs across hundreds of nodes for days or weeks, and at this scale the operating model changes: hardware anomalies, software errors, network timeouts, and resource contention must be managed proactively to keep workloads on track. Traditional approaches that rely on manual intervention, static checkpointing, and reactive monitoring simply don’t scale when organizations are running dozens of these concurrent multi-node workloads in shared infrastructure. This is why software services, like the autonomous recovery engine offered in NVIDIA Mission Control , are critical to scaling production AI. Previously, the autonomous recovery engine, which can detect, diagnose, and recover from anomalies across the stack, was limited to high-performance computing (HPC) workloads leveraging Slurm . As a part of Mission Control 2.5, this service is now extended to Kubernetes-based workloads managed using NVIDIA Run:ai . This post demonstrates how this latest version of Mission Control brings its integrated resiliency framework to Kubernetes workloads, helping AI factory operations move from reactive operational maintenance to proactive, self-healing infrastructure. Built-in resiliency services The vision behind Mission Control’s autonomous recovery engine is simple: AI factories should be self-healing systems where failures are detected instantly, recovery decisions are made intelligently based on workload context and failure type, and jobs resume automatically with minimal disruption or wasted compute. The goal is to understand what failed, isolate anomalies and tag them for maintenance, and return workloads to productive compute with as little wasted time as possible. Figure 1. In an AI factory, recovery automation should move nodes out of risky or stranded states and back into productive, schedulable compute as quickly as possible to prevent lost work and missed opportunity costs There are two services that make up the autonomous recovery engine: autonomous job recovery autonomous hardware recovery Because true self-governing resiliency is best understood as a control loop rather than a single recovery feature, the autonomous recovery engine then works with the workloads scheduler (HPC or Kubernetes) providing an integrated three-layer framework where each component plays a distinct but coordinated role. For this post, we’ll be focusing on scheduling Kubernetes-based workloads. Figure 2. The three components of NVIDIA Mission Control 2.5’s autonomous recovery engine: the Kubernetes scheduler, the autonomous job recovery service, and the autonomous hardware recovery service The three roles in the loop Let’s start with the Kubernetes workload placement layer. In Mission Control, NVIDIA Run:ai is the Kubernetes default scheduler and included as a part of the software. It manages the Kubernetes-based AI workloads, queues, policies, and schedules the jobs onto available capacity. The autonomous job recovery service provides the workload-context layer. It watches running jobs, tracks where each job is executing, and uses failure history and job topology to classify what kind of recovery path makes sense. The resource manager integration determines how that guidance becomes a restart, retry, re-queue, or placement action. The autonomous hardware recovery service is the infrastructure-health layer. It monitors nodes and GPUs, removes anomalies from scheduling when needed, and runs diagnostics or remediation so hardware problems do not keep spreading into new jobs. Keeping these responsibilities separate is what makes the model portable. The autonomous job recovery service doesn’t need to repair hardware and the hardware recovery service doesn’t need to understand every training framework. Finally, the scheduler can steer workloads toward ready capacity without waiting for a root-cause diagnosis. Failure paths in action The following scenarios show how the control loop behaves differently in Mission Control depending on the failure signal detected by its autonomous recovery engine. Scenario 1. Hardware fault during training A distributed training job is running across a pool of GPUs when one GPU starts to fail. The symptom may appear first as ECC errors, a hung worker, or a communication timeout in the job. The important thing is what happens next: recovery splits into two parallel tracks. The autonomous job recovery service captures the job context and identifies the suspect node or GPU. The Kubernetes scheduler integration then moves workload recovery forward either by restarting or rescheduling the job. Figure 3. When a hardware anomaly occurs during a training run, NVIDIA Mission Control is able to restart the job on other healthy nodes while hardware remediation continues At the same time, the autonomous hardware recovery service isolates the problematic node, records the reason, and starts diagnostics. That hardware path can continue even after the workload is already moving again. Figure 4. The autonomous hardware recovery service in NVIDIA Mission Control makes the node unschedulable and auditable. Polling then locks triage and starts diagnostics The value of this path is reduced downtime. The workload doesn’t wait for root-cause analysis before recovery begins, and the faulty node is not accidentally handed to the next job. Scenario 2. Transient software fault Not every job failure should trigger hardware remediation. A training worker might exit, hit a recoverable timeout, or lose coordination for a moment even though the underlying node is healthy. In this path, the autonomous job recovery service uses job context to avoid overreaction. If the failure history looks transient, the system retries according to scheduler policy instead of quarantining hardware that doesn’t need repair. While NVIDIA Run:ai may express that recovery differently from how it is handled for Slurm, the intent is the same: return the workload to productive execution without unnecessary hardware remediation. The autonomous hardware recovery service keeps monitoring in the background, but it stays out of the recovery path unless new evidence points to hardware. Figure 5. NVIDIA Mission Control takes into consideration that some job failures are software errors and do not need hardware remediation. In this case, retryable software failures restart automatically and repeated failures are surfaced The value of this path is restraint. The system restores the workload without creating unnecessary operator noise or shrinking the scheduling pool. Scenario 3. Hardware degradation caught early The autonomous hardware recovery service in Mission Control can also detect infrastructure degradation before it becomes a job failure. A node may start showing repeated GPU health warnings, connectivity problems, or other signals that make it risky for future scheduling. In this path, the autonomous hardware recovery service can remove the node from scheduler eligibility proactively and start diagnostics before an AI training job lands there. The autonomous job recovery service may never need to respond, because the faulty capacity is removed from circulation before it disrupts a workload. Figure 6. With NVIDIA Mission Control’s autonomous hardware recovery service, suspect hardware is kept out of the scheduling pool while diagnostics and remediation run In this case, Mission Control’s Kubernetes-based scheduler benefits from a cleaner pool of usable resources.

title: Fleet-wide computer vision lifecycle at the edge with SageMaker SDK v3
abstract: Fleet-wide computer vision model lifecycle management is a problem that shows up the moment a quality inspection proof of concept succeeds. One camera and one model work fine. Then the plant asks for the same result on 40 lines, each with several cameras, and every camera sees the world differently. Each has a different angle, different glare off the same stainless surface, and different ambient light depending on which bay door is open. In production deployments we have worked on, a single model trained on pooled footage underperforms enough individual cameras that each camera ends up with its own fine-tuned model. Now the real problem is no longer training one model well. It’s training, evaluating, versioning, and shipping thousands of them without a human in the loop for each one. This post updates the pattern introduced in the 2023 series Build an end-to-end MLOps pipeline for visual quality inspection at the edge for the current Amazon SageMaker Python SDK v3. It replaces the since-deprecated Amazon SageMaker Edge Manager with Amazon SageMaker Neo for edge optimization. I walk through a dual-branch Amazon SageMaker Pipeline that trains an anomaly detector and a defect classifier per camera, with quality gates that block underperforming models. An in-pipeline SageMaker Neo compilation step ensures every registered model ships with a device-optimized artifact, and an AWS Step Functions orchestration layer paces fleet training. You deploy everything with the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK), and a full pipeline run on synthetic data costs about $0.07 in compute. The complete sample is available in the aws-samples GitHub repository . The following diagram shows the sample’s fleet-wide model lifecycle. An orchestration layer queues re-training requests and limits concurrent work. A per-camera training pipeline prepares data, trains and evaluates an anomaly detector and a classifier, and produces versioned model artifacts for edge devices. Figure 1: Solution architecture The training half is a single SageMaker Pipeline, parameterized by camera, that runs 13 steps per execution. Three entry steps run in parallel: Preprocess, Fetch Latest Anomaly, and Fetch Latest Classifier. The pipeline preprocesses that camera’s images and fetches the camera’s most recent approved model for each branch, then trains two models. The first is a small convolutional autoencoder that learns what normal product looks like and flags anomalies by reconstruction error. The second is a ResNet18 classifier fine-tuned to confirm the defect. Each branch exports its model to ONNX, evaluates the exported artifact against held-out data, and passes through a quality gate. Past the gate, the model is compiled with SageMaker Neo for the configured edge target, and only then registered in the SageMaker Model Registry. As a result, every approved package has a device-ready compiled artifact. Packages carry the camera ID as metadata, and each branch’s warm-start fetch filters on it, so re-training always resumes from that camera’s own history. The orchestration half paces the fleet. Re-training requests land on an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue, and an AWS Lambda function starts a Step Functions execution per request. Each execution acquires a slot through a DynamoDB semaphore before starting its pipeline, so a burst of requests drains at a steady rate instead of all launching at once. Completions publish to Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS), and operational failures reach the same topic through an Amazon EventBridge rule with the original error preserved. The output of the system is versioned, quality-gated, per-camera model artifacts. The Model Registry holds the portable ONNX, and S3 holds the Neo-compiled build of that model, which is a device-optimized shared library loaded by the DLR runtime rather than ONNX. Both are ready for whatever delivery mechanism your plant uses. To deploy the sample you need the following: Previous CLI versions fail with a cloud assembly schema mismatch against recent versions of aws-cdk-lib . No service quota increase is needed. The orchestration layer admits at most five pipeline executions at a time by default, which keeps concurrent SageMaker training jobs inside the standard account quota. If you deploy to an AWS Region other than your CLI default, set all three of AWS_REGION , AWS_DEFAULT_REGION , and CDK_DEFAULT_REGION on the deploy command itself rather than in your shell profile, for example, AWS_REGION=us-east-2 AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-2 CDK_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-2 cdk deploy --all . The CDK CLI, Boto3, and the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) resolve the Region from overlapping but not identical variable sets, and a mismatch produces confusing partial deployments. Prefixing the command sets all three for that invocation only, so your own default Region is left unchanged. The code in this section is excerpted from the CDK application in the repository rather than a standalone script, and it runs during cdk deploy, when the stack synthesizes the pipeline definition. Environment setup and the deploy commands come later, under Deploying and running the sample. SDK v3 reorganized the SageMaker Python SDK into modular packages, and the imports show the new shape of the library: Installing sagemaker>=3.0.0,<4 pulls in sagemaker-core , sagemaker-train , sagemaker-serve , and sagemaker-mlops as separate packages. Training configuration that v2 spread across Estimator constructor arguments now lives in typed config objects passed to ModelTrainer . This is the anomaly branch’s trainer, verbatim from the sample: anomalib_input_data wires four channels ( train , validation , test , pretrained_model ) from upstream step properties, and run_prefix scopes every S3 path to the pipeline execution ID so concurrent fleet runs never collide. Both are in the repository. Two v3 behaviors matter when the pipeline lives inside a CDK application, and neither appears in the changelog as a breaking change. First, SDK v3 validates the pipeline’s execution role against live IAM while building the pipeline definition. This validation happens at synthesis time rather than execution time. A CDK app can’t create the role and the pipeline in one deployment, because the role doesn’t exist yet when the SDK validates it. This is separate from cdk bootstrap, which provisions the CDK toolkit resources once per account and Region and might already be done in your account. The sample’s own two-phase deploy is driven by a context flag that happens to share that name. An initial pass with -c bootstrap=true creates the role, bucket, and ECR repository, and the second pass synthesizes the pipeline against the now-existing role. The role Amazon Resource Name (ARN) embedded in the pipeline definition must also be a concrete string, not an unresolved CDK token. Second, the v3 role validator simulates ECR pull permissions without a resource ARN, so an execution role scoped to a single ECR repository fails validation even though it would work at runtime. The sample’s role carries a broader ECR grant for this reason. Lastly, one v3 habit the sample uses: constructing the pipeline with PipelineSession(default_bucket=your_bucket) routes SDK-managed uploads, such as step code, into the pipeline’s own bucket, so every artifact lives in one place and the execution role’s permissions cover a single bucket. (Granting the role access to the SDK’s default bucket works too. This approach is tidier.) Every trained model is evaluated before registration, and the evaluation runs against the exported ONNX artifact rather than the in-memory PyTorch model. That distinction matters: the artifact you gate is the artifact you ship, so an export problem can never slip a broken model past a healthy-looking training run. The anomaly branch gates on AUROC of at least 0.8.

title: Groundhog Day for AI agents: Prompt caching patterns for using OpenAI models on Amazon Bedrock
abstract: Every time you spin off your agent, it has to re-read its whole life story before performing an action. Here’s how to make it remember without having to feed it the same context again. In the movie Groundhog Day , Bill Murray’s character re-lives the same February 2 every day. He wakes up to the same song playing on the radio, in the same inn, and the same small town, again and again for what some movie fans estimate to be 34 years. Nothing he accomplished the day before carries over unless he works it out again from scratch. AI agents live in a version of Groundhog Day. Every time an agent takes a step (calls a tool, reads the result, decides what to do next), it has to send the model its entire story so far to maintain continuity: the tool definitions, the instructions, every previous tool call, and every result. The model only predicts the next token based on the input you provide. It has no internal memory between requests, so it must read all of it again. By turn 20 of a coding session, the model re-reads turns 1–19, and it’s you who pays for every one of those tokens, again and again. Prompt caching breaks the cycle. The service stores your input prompt (instructions, tools, and content) and reuses it on the next request, at a fraction of the input price. In this post, I walk you through an agent’s life, from its first turn to when it gets new tools and spawns helpers. Along the way, I show you how prompt caching keeps costs down and keeps agents responsive and consistent. Before talking about caching, it helps to look at what a typical agent’s first invocation to the large language model (LLM) contains: What an agent sends to the model, turn after turn if you don’t set up caching: Figure 1: What an agent sends to the model on every turn When a model reads a prompt, it first does a write called prefill . During prefill, it processes every input token and builds its key and value vectors (also known as key-value, or KV), which form the model’s working state. This happens before the model writes its first token. Prompt caching saves that state, which contains the system prompt, tools, content, history, and so on. When a later request starts with the same input tokens (that is, the same text), the prompt caching service loads the saved state instead of computing it again. It then processes only what is new in the next payload to the model. Prompt caching can be implicit, where Amazon Bedrock selects where the reusable prefix ends, or explicit, where your code marks that endpoint using prompt_cache_breakpoint . You can use both approaches together, and we recommend doing so. Figure 2: Turn 1 saves the prompt prefix up to the breakpoint, and turn 2 reuses it and pays full price only for the new question Implicit or explicit, and why do we need both? For agentic workloads, implicit caching lets Bedrock choose what to cache as the conversation grows. With explicit caching, you can mark shared content, such as tools and instructions, for reuse across sessions and when spinning up helper agents. You don’t always need both forms of caching, but combining them gives you a reusable starting point while Bedrock manages the growing conversation automatically. New sessions can also reuse that shared starting point while each conversation builds on its own cached history. In this post, we start with the first turn, then show how to carry cached content through later turns, new tools, and across subagents. The first win is to cache the static part of the prompt: the tools and instructions that stay the same across requests. These examples use your existing Amazon Bedrock client, TOOLS , and task . Replace the shortened INSTRUCTIONS string with your real policies and examples. The reusable prefix must reach 1,024 tokens to qualify. When caching static content, use explicit mode: choose where the saved prefix ends. The prompt_cache_key tells the service which requests are meant to share a cache. We come back to how to use it when we get to reading the cache in new sessions. In one of our tests using explicit caching, the roughly 4,000-token tools-and-instructions prefix wrote 4,120 tokens on the first request and read those 4,120 tokens on later requests. The task (or user request) comes after the cache boundary, so this doesn’t trigger a write to the cache. Keep in mind that prompt caching works only when you pass exactly the same text. Make sure that the agent’s instructions and tool lists are serialized the same way every time. Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and other forms of tool delivery need to be indexed to make sure they stay consistent. Keep anything that varies, such as the date, the user’s name, or a request ID, after the cached instructions. As the content grows and varies (different tools and content), use implicit mode to let the service follow the conversation. Here, the first request has no explicit marker. Its latest eligible message is the user’s task, so the automatic breakpoint comes after that task and covers the tools, instructions, and task together. The mode is shown explicitly in the following example for clarity, even though implicit is the default. Setting store=False leaves conversation history in your application. It doesn’t disable caching. This is useful when the next turn continues the same task. A different task doesn’t match the prefix through the old task, and the implicit write doesn’t necessarily create a separate entry for only the tools and instructions. Use an explicit marker there when you need that shorter shared prefix to be reusable across tasks. Use both when the agent needs a shared starting point and a growing history. Start with the marked developer block in the following code example and call the function ask_with_implicit_cache . The request-level mode stays implicit. The block-level marker adds an explicit save point after the instructions. The service can also save through the latest eligible message. This keeps the shared prefix available while the conversation grows. The model requests tools by name and supplies their arguments. Your application must execute them. execute_function is a helper you build to route those requests to the matching Python functions and return their results. The following loop uses this helper to run each requested tool. It appends the model’s output and all tool results to the history list, then sends that list again until the model returns a final answer. In implicit mode, Amazon Bedrock can reuse the unchanged prefix and cache the added content through the last tool result. Keep earlier messages and the initial TOOLS unchanged. For follow-ups, append a new user message and call the helper again. Keep earlier messages unchanged so their cached endpoints remain available. Rolling breakpoints: Each turn reads everything before it Figure 3: Rolling breakpoints, where each turn reads everything before it and writes only its own tool result For a separate explicit-only run, recreate the two-message history from the combined Hello cached world example. This loop wraps tool results in input_text blocks and marks the final result in each batch. Earlier markers stay in history . See the current lookup rules for long conversations. GPT-6 Astra tied for the best implicit result in this six-turn workload: about 62 percent lower input cost than running without caching. Explicit rolling breakpoints saved about 61 percent on the same model. Both reused more history as the conversation grew. These are workload results. Measure your own agent’s savings. Figure 4: Input cost of every caching setup on GPT-6 Astra, relative to no caching Sometimes an agent’s tool list changes, or new tools get added. Keep the initial list stable: adding, removing, or reordering definitions can invalidate the cached prefix. Choose the approach that fits how the tool becomes available.

title: Build agentic retrieval on a Managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with CDK
abstract: This post builds enterprise agentic retrieval on a Managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK). To see why that’s worth building, it helps to start with where ordinary Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) breaks down. Most RAG systems start the same way: they embed the question, fetch the nearest chunks from one index, hand them to a model, and return the answer. One retrieval, one generation. For a large class of questions that’s the right design, and there’s no reason to build anything more complicated. It fails in a recognizable way. Ask a question whose answer spans two corpora, and a single retrieval returns half of what the model needs, which is worse than returning nothing, because the answer comes back fluent and incomplete. Ask a question where the right source depends on the question , and a single index has no mechanism to choose. Ask a question that needs a second look at the corpus after seeing the first result, and there is nowhere for that second look to happen. Enterprise agentic retrieval answers all three by putting a reasoning agent in the loop. The agent decides whether to retrieve, which knowledge base to consult, and whether to go back for more before it composes an answer. This is the direction Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases have evolved. With the launch of the Managed Knowledge Base, retrieval is no longer a single embed-and-fetch call. It has become an agentic capability: multi-turn planning, tool-driven retrieval, and grounded, cited answers. The AgenticRetrieveStream API offers this as a first-class service feature rather than something you assemble yourself. That works, and it also introduces a genuinely harder operational problem. A single-shot pipeline is a function you can reason about by reading it. An agent that reasons and retrieves in a loop takes a different path on every question. By default you can see neither the path it took nor whether the answer it produced was any good. Observability stops being a nice-to-have and becomes the only way to know the system works. In August 2024, Build an end-to-end RAG solution using Knowledge Bases for Amazon Bedrock and the AWS CDK deployed the single-shot design as a CDK application: an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) corpus, an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless collection and index, a knowledge base, and a data source, provisioned as CDK stacks whose order you sequenced by hand. Three things have changed since it was published. This post builds that system: an agent that routes across two knowledge bases, retrieves through the Gateway, and returns a grounded, cited answer, with every layer of its behavior instrumented, as a single AWS CDK application in Python. One command deploys all of it, and CDK derives the order. If you read the 2024 post , the path from an Amazon S3 bucket to the knowledge base will look familiar, and everything after it is new: the vector store is gone, the retrieval is agentic, and roughly half of what the app provisions exists to tell you what the agent did. If you didn’t, this post stands on its own. The services at play and the path one question takes through them: the agent decides whether to retrieve and which knowledge base to consult, the Gateway exposes each knowledge base as a tool it can call, the Managed Knowledge Bases search and cite, and the loop repeats as many times as the question needs. Everything the agent does along the way lands in Amazon CloudWatch. Figure 1: The services involved and the path a single question takes through them Before the walkthrough, it helps to establish three things: what makes retrieval agentic, why the Managed Knowledge Base is the right foundation for it, and why observability and evaluation belong in the design rather than bolted on later. Classic Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) does one retrieval and one generation. Enterprise agentic retrieval puts a reasoning agent in the loop: it decides whether and what to retrieve, can retrieve several times to refine, chooses which knowledge base is relevant (semantic routing), and only then composes a grounded answer with citations. With the Managed Knowledge Base, this is a first-class service capability, the AgenticRetrieveStream API performs the multi-turn planning, executes the retrieval, and returns a cited answer, rather than an orchestration layer you build and maintain over a raw vector search. That produces better answers on complex questions, but it also produces a more complex system to operate, which is exactly why observability and evaluation are built in from the start. Amazon Bedrock now offers a Managed Knowledge Base (Type: MANAGED): Amazon Bedrock manages the ingestion, storage, indexing, and retrieval for you, including embedding and reranking with service-managed models by default, so there is no vector database to provision, scale, or patch . This differs from a Customer-managed (DIY) Knowledge Base, where you choose and operate the vector store (for example, Amazon OpenSearch Serverless) yourself. Two differences matter most for this solution: Because agentic retrieval and the AgentCore Gateway connector are available only on the managed knowledge base, it is the natural foundation for enterprise agentic retrieval. It also means Amazon Bedrock manages the storage and indexing for you, so there is no OpenSearch Serverless collection or OCU capacity to provision in this design. The customer-managed option remains the right choice when you want to select and operate your own vector store, for example to reuse an existing OpenSearch Serverless collection or to meet specific data-residency, tuning, or compliance requirements. For enterprise agentic retrieval, the managed knowledge base is what makes the capability possible. An agentic system that returns an answer isn’t enough for production. You need to see how it behaves (latency, call volume, token usage), how good the retrieval and answers are, and you need those signals continuously. This solution ships two CloudWatch dashboards spanning seven layers of telemetry, plus two forms of evaluation (on-demand and continuous), all provisioned by the same CDK application. The grounding, citations, and evaluation layers also support responsible use. Cited answers trace back to their source passages so responses stay auditable, and the faithfulness and correctness scores let you catch answers drifting from their sources rather than finding out in production. Any infrastructure-as-code tool can create these resources. CDK earns its place here for a reason specific to this architecture: the four stacks are densely cross-referenced . The Gateway needs both knowledge base ids. The agent needs the URL and ARN for the Gateway. The dashboards need the KB ids, the Gateway ARN, and the agent runtime id, seven values crossing stack boundaries, each one a dimension on a metric or a target on a connector. Written as raw templates, that is a set of stack exports and cross-stack lookups kept in agreement by hand, plus a script that deploys in the right order and threads outputs forward, and both drift the moment anything is renamed. In CDK you pass the construct, and the export and the dependency edge are derived from that one act of passing it. The 2024 solution had three stacks and a mostly linear dependency chain. At four stacks with seven values crossing between them, the difference stops being stylistic. Here is the path a single question takes through the system, end to end. It’s worth a slow look, because the rest of the post walks through it left to right. The following diagram traces the end-to-end agentic retrieval workflow. A user’s question enters the agent on the AgentCore Runtime, which routes it through the AgentCore Gateway to one of two AgenticRetrieveStream tools, one per managed knowledge base, financial and weather, each ingested from Amazon S3.

title: Import AI 478: Math for alignment; ProgramBench; and Mirendil shows what RSI means
abstract: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. How math could help alignment: …What the “industrialization of mathematics” means for safety… AI safety startup Resolution (formerly known as Sequent, Import AI 461 ) has published work on how it has automatically formalized some mathematical statements related to statistical learning theory. Specifically, the team has autoformalized the resolution of singularities, which they believe “lays the groundwork for further automated research into the relationship between loss landscape geometry and generalization.” How they did it: I’ll skip over the math and concentrate on how they did it, which gives us some broader lessons for how people are using AI systems to push on the frontier of knowledge. A Resolution researcher “started by working with agents to develop two plans: a high-level, human-interpretable version and a detailed (112-page) plan divided into atomic steps that closely followed the existing literature,” they write. The researcher “then deputized an orchestrator agent to carry out the plan, spinning up agents to do pen-and-paper math, write Lean, and handle support functions like checking that things were staying on track… the execution phase required little scaffolding beyond the initial plan and some agent skills distilled from earlier internal autoformalization efforts.” $135k for math formalization: The work took about a week, taking “on the order of 100B input tokens (90% cache reads) and about 300 million output tokens (totaling an estimated $135,000 in token spend), and produced about 600k lines of Lean.” Now that they’ve done this, they’ve been able to accelerate some other aspects of their research: “We have already seen both benefits from autoformalization in using this library to extend parts of singular learning theory. Formalizing resolution of singularities lets us automate more of the theory, for example, to better understand sampling, and that understanding is what lets us shape how models learn, which is the goal of what we call patterning”. Why this matters – perhaps the math boom will help us make safe AI: Though frontier mathematics often seems disconnected from immediate advances in other fields, posts like this highlight how the two might converge. The key point here is that AI is making it possible to do things that were previously so unbelievably expensive and human-time-intensive that very few people did them and you couldn’t easily integrate them into the research roadmap of a startup – but that has now changed. “We expect the coming industrialization of mathematics to make possible a new, rigorous science of research automation,” Resolution writes. Read more: Formalizing Hironaka’s Resolution of Singularities (Resolution) . Agents can build programs from scratch: …ProgramBench goes from 0% to 18.5% performance in a few months… In a reminder of the blistering pace of AI progress, Claude Opus 5.5 (xhigh) has got a score of 18.5% on ProgramBench, a very hard benchmark that came out in May of this year – and when it came out, every tested model scored 0%. What ProgramBench is: ProgramBench tests out how well AI systems can rebuild software programs based on being given a compiled program and its documentation. Tasks include building things like language interpreters (PHP, Lua, tinycc), databases (DuckDB, SQLite), media and compression utilities (FFmpeg, zstd, xz), and developer tools (ripgrep, fzf, jq). It was very hard until it wasn’t: When it came out, the best scoring system was Claude Opus 4.7 with 0% resolved (fraction of the 200 tasks where all tests passed), and 3% almost (fraction of the 200 tasks where >95% of tests pass). Compare that to today, when Claude Opus 5.5 gets 18.5% resolved and 70.5% (!!!) almost. Why this matters – the era of ephemeral software cometh: In 2027, huge amounts of software will be built via AI systems end-to-end autonomously developing whatever they need to do for whatever tasks they’re being put to. Evals like ProgramBench give us a sense of how rapid the pace of progress is here, given we went from 0% earlier this year to 20% now. My expectation is ProgramBench is saturated by the end of 2027 (where I define saturated as some very high score on resolved, though as with most benchmarks it’s likely there’s some kind of noise ceiling here, so it might not strictly be 100%). Read more: ProgramBench: Can Language Models Rebuild Programs From Scratch? (arXiv) . OpenAI illustrates why locking down AI systems is harder than you think: …Securing smart agents is like catching greased pigs… Here’s a nice post from OpenAI going over some of the things they discovered when they recently used their AI systems to ‘red team’ their own internal controls. The post goes over a number of the escapes and vulnerabilities that OpenAI’s agents found. There’s one particular example about communicating which is worth studying in detail because it tells us something about the wild cunning complexity of these systems. What they did and what they found: OpenAI “asked agents in separate microVMs, created and managed by OpenAI’s sandboxing software on shared host machines, to exchange synthetic secrets without the use of network connections or shared writable files—something that our systems are meant to prevent,” the company wrote. “The agents found a way to communicate using the processor’s cache: a small, fast memory that holds copies of data that applications have recently accessed. Reading data from the cache is faster than retrieving it from main memory, and the agents used this timing difference to communicate. One agent encoded information by evicting selected data from the cache. Another timed how long it took to reload that data, using the difference between fast and slow reads to recover the message. Once the agents agreed on a protocol for encoding and decoding these signals, they could exchange the synthetic secrets without changing a shared file or opening a network connection”. In a related attack, an agent “alternated between continuous writes and inactivity, while another measured the resulting timing differences and used those differences to decode the signal”. During this attack the agent’s chain of thought read as: “Could create acoustic modem-like signal … using continuous writes vs idle.” Why this matters – fighting agents is very difficult : AI systems are increasingly creative, very fast, and have the ability to stay focused on a task and keep trying things. Fighting AI systems is akin to ensuring no leaks in a pipe with water flowing through it; at some point if you increase the pressure of the water (e.g., the intelligence and volume of the AI system), then the water will burst through the pipe. Read more : Securing our frontier model training environment (OpenAI blog) . What RSI looks like – one person pretrains a decent model from scratch: …Mirendil reveals what AI R&D optimization can do… In a sign of how massively augmented AI research is getting, a single researcher at AI R&D startup Mirendil has trained a decent coding model by themselves. The announcement of Mirendil-Base is the first major output from the startup and is less a technical breakthrough and more a proof-of-concept for how AI development could work in the future – a single human working in partnership with AI can build systems that would have taken teams of ten or more people to do a year ago. What they did: Mirendill-Base is a pretrained LLM “built by one researcher in 3.5 months, with less than $10m in compute,” Mirendil writes. “This includes all the research and small-scale experiments it took to get there, as well as the final training run.” All the code was written from scratch on top of libraries like PyTorch and JAX, and the model learned only from publicly available data.

title: OpenAI and Anthropic cut their LLM prices by up to 80% within a few months. Why?
abstract: Let’s look at a quick timeline of the major LLM model announcements from both OpenAI and Anthropic over the past few months. All pricing numbers provided are input MTok / output MTok / cache read MTok . OpenAI announced GPT-5.6 Sol and Luna. Sol is the direct successor to GPT 5.5 at the same price of $5 / $30 / $0.50 , while Luna is a small model specifically designed for cheaper use cases at $1 / $6 / $0.10 . They also announced a Terra model that’s in between those two models, but few cared about it. Anthropic announced Claude Sonnet 5, which Anthropic claimed to be closer to their Opus models, but feedback was mixed. Notably, it had launch pricing of $2 / $10 / $0.20 which was initially supposed to be temporary but would go up. Anthropic announced Claude Opus 5, which was a long-awaited major-version update given the impact Opus 4.5 had on the rise of agentic coding, at a price of $5 / $25 / $0.50 (similar to GPT-5.6 Sol). Although some of the provided benchmark results surprisingly exceeded those of the much larger Fable 5, real-world feedback was more mixed. OpenAI announces that they cut the price of GPT-5.6 Luna by 80% (???) to $0.20 / $1.20 / $0.02 . Model quality vs. Cost-per-task for GPT-5.6 Luna after the massive price reduction. Top-and-left is better, and if OpenAI didn’t do the 80% price cut, it would have lost to DeepSeek V4 Pro. via OpenAI Anthropic announces the temporary Sonnet 5 price cut for the launch is now permanent. OpenAI announces that they are cutting the price for GPT-5.6 Sol by ~20% ( $4 / $20 / $0.40 ) for the next three months. Anthropic announced Fable 5.1 at a price of $10 / $50 / $0.25 , which, in addition to having strictly better benchmark performance in all areas than Fable 5 from June at $10 / $50 / $1 , cut the cache read cost by 75%. When using agents for coding, cache read costs are the vast majority (96% - 99%) of the total token expenditure as the cache is what contains the entire previous conversation each turn. Additionally, the cache tends to be hit around 90 - 100% of the time (varies by the infrastructure of the LLM inference provider). Taken together, a 75% reduction in the cache read cost correlates to a 70-75% reduction in the cost of using the model—obviously notable, even if cache costs are typically a footnote! OpenAI announced GPT-6 Astra, which is similar in size to Fable 5.1 and has similar pricing at $10 / $50 / $1 but without the lower cache read cost. Astra’s model performance is indeed comparable to Fable. OpenAI announced GPT-6 Sol at at a shocking price of $2 / $10 / $0.20 that halves the input and output price relative to the temporarily-discounted GPT-5.6 Sol! They simultaneously released GPT-6 Luna also at half the input and output price ( $0.10 / $0.50 / $0.01 ) of the previous version. On the same exact day , Anthropic announced Claude Opus 5.5, where it’s explicitly stated “Opus 5.5 requires less compute to serve than Opus 5, and its pricing reflects that”. Its price of $4 / $20 / $0.20 is much lower in total than Opus 5’s due to a 20% input/output cost cut and a larger cache read cut, resulting in a total cost reduction of 40-60% for a model that’s even better than Fable 5.1 (I have quite a lot of things to say about Opus 5.5, but that’s for another post). It turned out that GPT-6 Sol was a dud performancewise, so a week later OpenAI announced GPT-6.1 Sol, which surprisingly has comparable performance to Astra (can confirm after personal use), but OpenAI casually cut the cache price in half ( $2 / $10 / $0.10 ) matching Anthropic’s 5%-of-input cache read cost, making this model family cumulatively 75% cheaper. Overall, starting from the release of the GPT-5.6 model families in June to now, the cost of using these popular LLMs has cratered, which is not something I would have expected a year ago. These price cuts also apply to model usage from subscription agentic harnesses such as Codex and Claude Code . More importantly, these models do not appear to have cut any corners in terms of output quality to achieve their price cuts. Data from Vercel’s AI model gateway supporting the decreasing cost-per-token trend to 43.3% of the April 2026 cost. However, aggregate spend has been increasing because the models are getting better faster than they’re getting cheaper! via Vercel From the timeline above, there is a clear tit-for-tat between Anthropic and OpenAI, and it is reasonable to assume that these particular price cuts from OpenAI and Anthropic are in reaction to each other. However, no one cuts prices by 80% unless there is some externality in play. So, what gives? If you have been testing agents with new LLMs as they are released, it can be very difficult to differentiate them outside of subjective vibes. Since last November that launched the hypergrowth of agentic LLMs, models have become more of a commodity where it’s trivial to try a new model on your codebase with just a toggle in a harness like OpenCode and Zed Agent , or a different API endpoint string through OpenRouter , and as a result there is little moat. Additionally, there are many competitors—not just large companies like Google and Meta —who can provide models which are sufficient substitutes and therefore allow pricing pressure. For open weight models, let’s take another look at DeepSeek Flash V4.1 , which also recently released an updated 1017 variant . OpenRouter at this point is the place you go for open-weight models. Retrieved October 24th, 2026. The original DeepSeek V4 Flash 0420 was released in April 2026 at a price of $0.14 / $0.28 / $0.0028 and went megaviral as a result, especially as OpenAI didn’t have a small-class model for simple tasks at the time. That $0.0028 turned out to be the key, as a cache read proportion of 2% is substantially lower than the 5%-10% of the OpenAI and Anthropic models above, which makes the effective cost even lower than what is advertised. I suspect the 80% GPT-5.6 Luna price cut in July was meant to specifically compete with these smaller open-weight models. Now, the new DeepSeek Flash V4.1 1017 model performs significantly better than DeepSeek Flash V4 benchmark-wise ( 45 on the Artificial Analysis index vs. 24 ) and the cost from DeepSeek remains similar at $0.15 / $0.60 / $0.003 . Note the operative words “from DeepSeek”. On OpenRouter, any inference provider can list a model that they host, and when a user hits the OpenRouter API, the request is routed to one of those models—it’s routed to any available model by default for load balancing but the developer can specify preferences such as “lowest price” in the API request. Back in May, I noted that there were 13 distinct providers hosting DeepSeek V4 Flash on OpenRouter. For the updated 1017 variant, there are now 29 distinct providers . Providers for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 sorted by cache read cost. Retrieved October 24th, 2026. However, looking at the effective input costs (which account for the interaction between cache read costs and cache hit rates), many distinct providers are close costwise. Effective costs by endpoint, with Cloudflare and DeepInfra within 10% of DeepSeek’s cost. Despite the fact that these models are the cheapest, note that these models only have a minority of the total token share. Retrieved October 24th, 2026. OpenAI and Anthropic will have to differentiate from these open weight models with higher-quality models—they are currently doing a good job with that particularly with Opus 5.5—but they need to keep doing that, which is why billions of dollars are being invested into R&D. Open-weight models are catching up fast: just a few days ago, Moonshot AI announced Kimi K3.1 Pro which has comparable performance to Opus 5.5 (Kimi at 55 vs. Opus 5.5 at 58 ) at half the input/output price and the same cache read cost ( $2 / $10 / $0.20 ).

title: How to teach with Databricks Free Edition
abstract: You can run a full data or AI course on the same platform enterprises use in production - for free, with no cloud contract, no license to manage, and nothing to install. Databricks Free Edition is a perpetually free version of the platform; each student signs up individually and works entirely in the browser, so a course can adopt it without provisioning servers or purchasing anything. Data and AI skills are moving faster than most curricula can follow, and the demand for these skills is showing up in both hiring and learner behavior. LinkedIn named Databricks one of its Top 10 Skills on the Rise for 2026, while Udemy included Databricks among its 100 Fastest-Growing Global Skills. Two very different signals pointing in the same direction: knowing how to work with modern data and AI platforms is increasingly valuable. For a student, that can be the difference between “I've studied distributed computing” and “I've built a data pipeline on the platform your team uses.” For an instructor, it means making an existing course more directly connected to how data and AI work gets done in industry, without fully redesigning the curriculum. The barriers that often make industry platforms difficult to bring into the classroom, including cost, licensing, and IT provisioning, are solved by Databricks Free Edition; a permanently free account with no credit card, no cloud contract, and nothing to install. That matters because the two usual barriers to teaching with industry tools are cost and setup, and Free Edition removes both. It’s designed specifically for learning and non-commercial use, and is available to students and educators globally. What is Databricks Free Edition? A no-cost, perpetually free version of the Databricks Data + AI Platform, built for students, hobbyists, and aspiring data and AI professionals. It runs in the browser with no cloud contract and no credit card required to sign up, on smaller compute sizes under fair-use limits. It is not for production or commercial use. (Source: databricks.com/learn/free-edition) Databricks also has deep roots in academia. It was founded by the UC Berkeley professors and PhD students who created Apache Spark™, and open source is still at the center of what we build - Delta Lake, MLflow, and Unity Catalog are developed with global communities under vendor-neutral foundations (the Linux Foundation, LF AI & Data, and the Apache Software Foundation), and Databricks recently open sourced Omnigent, a meta-harness for AI agents. For educators, that means the skills students build are rooted in industry-wide open standards, not a single proprietary tool. Because Free Edition is the real platform rather than a simplified sandbox, the skills transfer directly. A student who writes a Spark job, runs a SQL query, deploys a model, or builds an agent in Free Edition is using the same tools professionals use in production. There's no "now unlearn the training tool and learn the real one" step later. One environment can serve as a statistics lab, a database course, a business-analytics class, and an AI capstone - which cuts the number of tools students and instructors have to learn. This table maps common courses to the tools that might fit your current curriculum. Across these surfaces, Genie Code, the platform's agentic coding and data assistant, helps students generate, explain, and debug code and take on multi-step tasks autonomously, reflecting how work is increasingly done. Distribute through your existing LMS or a GitHub repository. Export the assignment notebook as an .ipynb file and share it with any datasets or instructions; students import a copy into their Free Edition workspace, complete it, and export the finished notebook for submission. For group assignments, students can share a notebook and collaborate in real time. Three options for datasets too large for GitHub or a local download: (1) host the dataset in cloud storage students connect to; (2) use Open Sharing to share the dataset from your Free Edition workspace directly into each student's workspace; or (3) pick a free dataset from Databricks Marketplace that students access natively inside the platform. Yes. Databricks is built for collaboration — with real-time co-authoring, comments, and tagging, students can work together and invite you into their notebooks to troubleshoot or give feedback. Databricks Free Edition is designed for up to five people to share an account for a group project. See how to set up collaboration in Databricks Free Edition . Free Edition runs on smaller compute sizes under fair-use limits. If a workspace exceeds its quota, its compute pauses for the rest of the day and resumes the next day. Hitting a limit mid-assignment is rare and never permanent. Furthermore, you and your students can double your available daily credit up to three times per year, so students can always keep working during crunch periods and exams. The best way to ensure a smooth experience is to test each assignment in Free Edition ahead of time to catch any step that needs significant compute. Yes - it's perpetually free, with no cloud contract and no credit card required to sign up. It's built for learning and explicitly not for production or commercial use, which fits a classroom well. Credits reset daily, so students start each day fresh. A good place to start is anywhere you currently use a cloud-based notebook environment. Sign up for Databricks Free Edition yourself and take the Databricks Fundamentals course; once you're comfortable, assign both to your students and see how the self-paced courses fit your existing curriculum.
