title: Building live intelligence: Databricks AI Search supports Streaming Tables, Materialized Views, and Managed tables using Iceberg
abstract: AI Search now natively supports Streaming Tables, Materialized Views, and Managed tables using Iceberg v3+ in addition to Delta tables. You can bring live events, continuously maintained personalized state, and open-format data directly into your AI Search applications — reducing the overhead of building and managing separate pipelines to convert and synchronize these data sources. Streaming Tables, Materialized Views, and Managed Iceberg each represent a different way of working with data, and each opens up new possibilities for AI applications. Continuously changing data such as new listings, inventory, availability, and user activity can flow into an append-only Streaming Table, with AI Search indexing new records as they arrive and keeping the search index up to date. This freshness enables applications where the latest data can directly shape the search experience: helping users discover newly available restaurants through a search bar, or generating real-time recommendations based on recent trends. Materialized Views can aggregate events, filter records, and join data from multiple sources to create customized state. As the underlying data changes, the view is incrementally maintained and AI Search propagates those changes to the index, enabling personalized search experiences such as session-aware recommendations, product and content discovery based on recent activity, or tailor results to a user's evolving interests and preferences. Managed Iceberg tables can serve as AI Search sources directly, without conversion or migration to another table format, making open-format data available to search indexes and other AI applications. The open-format enables AI applications that work across existing data environments: search across product catalogs managed by different systems, unify business or customer data stored across Managed Iceberg tables, or build search experiences over large, distributed datasets without moving the underlying data. Before native support, customers had to create a separate Delta representation of Streaming Tables, Materialized Views, or Managed Iceberg tables and build pipelines to keep it synchronized with the source. This added an extra data layer, custom update logic, and ongoing operational overhead. Now, AI Search connects directly to these sources. Create an index from your source and sync it when needed — AI Search propagates them directly to the index, eliminating the intermediate Delta table and custom synchronization pipeline. Your data stays connected to search as it evolves, with the platform handling the plumbing behind the scenes. Whether you use the UI or API, building an AI Search index follows the same workflow used for existing Delta table sources: create a Delta Sync index and point it at your source table. The same workflow now extends to Streaming Tables, Materialized Views, and Iceberg tables — no new workflow to learn. Ready to build AI applications on your data? Get started by creating an AI Search index directly from your Streaming Tables, Materialized Views, or Managed Iceberg tables — no additional data pipelines required. Explore the AI Search documentation . Subscribe to our blog and get the latest posts delivered to your inbox.

title: The media industry is becoming a prediction economy
abstract: • The prediction economy is the shift in media and advertising from counting attention to predicting and proving outcomes. Performance becomes a leading indicator instead of a lagging one. • Agents and measurement stall on fragmented data. Only 3% of CMOs can tie half their marketing to a business outcome (McKinsey), and the fix is one unified, governed data and AI foundation. • Build it on four Cs: context (Databricks CustomerLake, an agentic CDP; Genie; Lakebase), control, cost, and choice (Unity Gateway). A pet specialty retailer that activated loyalty data with agents saw a 12% lift in transactions. For two decades, media and advertising ran on attention. Impressions, reach and clicks were the currency because they were quantifiable. Increasingly, though, that currency is losing value. Throughout the industry – and brought to a head at Advertising Week New York – leaders across media, agencies, and adtech/martech are asking the same question: not " who saw it ?" but " what did it change ?" Behind every answer is the rise of the prediction economy , where advantage comes from knowing what an audience will want before the money is spent, and being able to show what it was worth. Performance has shifted from a lagging indicator to a leading one. Hear Databricks Media and Advertising GTM leader Jake LaDuke share his thoughts on the prediction economy - and the future of media, advertising and marketing - then read on to learn more. A few themes deserving attention: Agents are moving from answering to acting. Session after session, conversation after conversation on agentic AI reaches the same conclusion: agents fail without trusted, governed data underneath them. The early wins are as much about effectiveness as efficiency, such as orchestrating measurement across many sources of truth. On the sell side, roles like VP of ad sales transformation barely existed two years ago, as agents take over the spreadsheets, emails and stale rate cards of pitch-to-pay so sellers can focus on relationships and yield. Measurement has to prove impact. According to a McKinsey study, only 3% of CMOs can tie half their marketing to a business outcome . That mandate is rippling through the ecosystem: agencies are restructuring contracts, adtech is building proof into its products, and publishers are launching their own measurement. The hope economy is giving way to the prediction economy, and the loop only closes if partner data can connect. Martech and adtech are collapsing into one stack. With 90 to 120 tools in a typical enterprise stack, channel-level reporting no longer cuts it. CMOs need holistic performance across every touchpoint, not just advertising or marketing alone. Meanwhile CMOs and CROs draw on the same audiences from separate stacks, and collapsing the two lets both do better. CTV and retail media need closed loops. Publishers need one data estate for audience intelligence, monetization and cross-platform measurement. Retail media, a fast-growing channel still held back by measurement, needs clean rooms, first-party activation and closed-loop measurement. Behind all of it, consumer behavior is shifting faster than the stack. Agentic commerce, AI-generated creative and LLMs acting as the new influencer are changing how people discover brands, and executives want to treat these shifts as opportunities, not threats. Every one of these points back to the same prerequisite: a unified, governed data and AI foundation. When your data is fragmented, adapting to the prediction economy becomes untenable. Leaders must stop funding these as separate projects and instead build one foundation for every persona to draw on. Every prediction starts with context: how complete a view your agents have of your customers and your business across your data estate. As Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi has put it, models don’t have an intelligence problem, they have a context problem. PetSmart shows what happens when that context comes together. Using loyalty data from its 75 million Treats Rewards members, the company moved beyond batch-and-blast campaigns, and AI decisioning agents delivered personalized messaging at scale. The result was a 22% incremental lift in salon bookings and a 13% lift in auto-ship transactions. The gain came from getting the data estate to work together, not from a smarter model. Nowhere does context matter more than in the customer 360. Marketers increasingly want to run marketing where they run the business, rather than copying golden profiles into a separate CDP. That is the idea behind CustomerLake , Databricks’ agentic CDP. Marketing and data teams can build trusted Customer 360 profiles, activate audiences and personalize engagement directly on their governed data. Paired with measurement orchestration, those same customer signals connect directly to ROI. Genie then brings that context to the people making decisions. It acts as an AI coworker connected to your governed enterprise data, so planners, marketers and sellers can ask questions in plain language and get answers built on their own definitions. Under the hood, Genie Ontology gives the AI an understanding of your business: its unique definitions, relationships, business rules, authoritative sources and permissions. At answer or decision time, it ranks that context by authority and relevance, applies permissions, and delivers the most useful pieces. Acting intelligently in the moment also takes operational context: what the customer just did, what they were offered, and what the agent decided and why. Lakebase , Databricks’ serverless Postgres database, keeps that live state next to your analytical data, so agent memory, decision history and fresh features are available at production speed without brittle pipelines in between. Getting there starts with a simple discipline: define identity, audiences and metrics once, and govern them centrally. Context gets you to a prediction. The other three C's decide whether you can afford to act on it at scale, and whether you should. Control. This is about governing not only who has access from a people perspective, but also from your agents' perspective. Agents will touch audience data, bids and brand-sensitive placements, so governance has to be the front door. Unity Gateway runs every model and agent request through one control plane, with authentication, auditing and PII guardrails, so the enterprise sets the guardrails and the platform enforces them. Cost. AI for AI's sake is no longer tolerated by CFOs, and the shift is from token maxing to value maxing. Every agent loop burns tokens, and always-on campaigns multiply that. Unity Gateway attributes spend by team, model and application, enforces budgets and rate limits, and routes simple requests to cheaper models, so AI cost tracks business value. Choice. Having the right model for the right job matters because frontier models leapfrog each other regularly. If switching means rewriting applications, you are always a generation behind. Unity Gateway offers models from multiple providers through one API, so you can swap by configuration instead of re-engineering. Built on open formats, the foundation keeps your data portable, and OpenSharing and Databricks Clean Rooms let you collaborate with partners without copying data Leaders should treat governance, cost visibility and portability as design requirements from day one, not retrofits. Looking ahead, advertising itself will change. With ad avoidance rising and intent still largely untapped, it must shift from feeling like a break in what people want to do to a more intelligent, integrated 1:1 experience driven by that viewer’s intent. Getting there will take new operating systems and operating models across brands, agencies, adtech and publishers, all in service of outcomes.

title: PyTorch opens the AI ecosystem to a new accelerator class
abstract: In October 2025, IBM and the PyTorch Foundation outlined a plan for deeper Spyre enablement in 2026: treating the accelerator as a first-class PyTorch backend and supporting multi-accelerator scheduling. The latest software ecosystem updates deliver on that promise. Together, torch-spyre, Spyre's vLLM plugin, compiler improvements, and continuous integration work are making it easier to bring familiar models and workflows to a different class of AI hardware. AI is increasingly being embedded in the systems that process transactions, detect fraud, analyze claims, and assist employees. And with this growing usage, the AI hardware ecosystem is expanding. GPUs remain central to modern AI, but they are increasingly joined by accelerators with different architectures, execution models, and performance characteristics. Giving developers more choices requires more than building new chips. The software ecosystem must make new accelerators usable without forcing developers to abandon familiar models, tools, and workflows. Spyre is IBM’s dataflow AI accelerator, optimized for inference. It is designed for enterprise teams running AI alongside their applications and data on IBM Z, LinuxONE, and Power systems. Its reduced-precision compute is well suited to the matrix-heavy work in language generation and embedding models. Unlike a conventional GPU, which executes kernels as instruction streams across scheduled groups of threads, Spyre triggers computation as data arrives at its compute engines. PyTorch provides the common layer that allows this different architecture to participate in an ecosystem built largely around GPUs. Extending PyTorch beyond GPUs At the center of this effort is torch-spyre , a PyTorch backend that compiles ordinary PyTorch code into an executable plan for Spyre. Most of a model’s logic passes through the PyTorch compiler unchanged. When a model contains an operation that the underlying stack cannot yet lower effectively, an adapter can replace it with a mathematically equivalent form that the compiler can handle. The model’s computation remains the same, while its implementation becomes compatible with the accelerator. The move to PyTorch’s Inductor backend also reduced the amount of custom compiler code that the team must maintain. The resulting compiler is roughly seven times smaller than the system it replaced and measurably less complex per function. That smaller surface area makes it easier to carry improvements from upstream PyTorch into torch-spyre and focus Spyre-specific work where it matters. The same principle applies at the device boundary. In a recent demonstration , moving graph construction off the data-transfer path improved Granite 3.3 8B performance at batch size 1 and sequence length 1024 by 9.9% for prefill and 13.6% for decode. Removing that work from compute dispatch as well brought the total improvement to 1.7 times faster prefill and 2.4 times faster decode, with roughly three quarters of the gain coming from the compute path. Preserving vLLM portability Spyre is an out-of-tree accelerator , rather than one of the GPU platforms most commonly supported by AI software. Spyre relies on TorchDynamo to trace a model graph and TorchInductor to lower that graph into representations optimized for the target hardware. Within vLLM, extension mechanisms such as CustomOp and PluggableLayer allow a hardware plugin to customize behavior without reimplementing large portions of the software stack. Preserving these extension points matters as vLLM evolves. Some new model implementations are becoming increasingly specialized for particular models and frontier GPU hardware. To preserve portability alongside that optimization work, the vLLM community is developing hardware-agnostic layers that are isolated from hardware-specific paths and designed to be compilable, extensible, and portable across accelerator platforms. Early support has landed in vLLM, and the pathway has been validated with the Spyre plugin on models including Gemma 4, Qwen3, and Granite 4.2. On NVIDIA H100 GPUs, these hardware-agnostic layers delivered total token throughput within 3.4% of the native implementation, measured as the geometric mean across three recent models. One workflow, more hardware choices For IBM Z, LinuxONE, and Power11 users, the intended experience is straightforward: Obtain models from ecosystems like Hugging Face and use substantially the same PyTorch-based workflows they would use with Nvidia GPUs. Shared PyTorch extension points hide much of the architectural difference beneath the framework, reducing adoption friction and avoiding an experience limited to a small catalog of specially packaged model weights. Consider an insurance-claims workflow that combines XGBoost models for fraud detection with a Gemma 26B model on Spyre for forensic analysis. The software stack enables developers to assemble the workflow using familiar model ecosystems and framework interfaces, while the hardware is chosen for the work it suits. Spyre's PyTorch integration is also how it connects to llm-d . llm-d runs distributed inference on top of vLLM and is built to support multiple accelerator types, not a single hardware path. vLLM reaches each accelerator through PyTorch: Once a device has a working PyTorch backend, a vLLM hardware plugin can expose it, and then llm-d can schedule work onto it. Spyre follows this path. torch-spyre provides the PyTorch backend, and the Spyre vLLM plugin builds on top of it. As a result, the work that makes Spyre a PyTorch device is the same work that makes it usable in llm-d deployments. Making compatibility measurable Broad compatibility is only useful when users have clear evidence that models run reliably across platforms. IBM Research engineers are building that evidence through end-to-end model testing and continuous integration. This work helps the team detect when upstream framework changes affect downstream hardware support . End-to-end model testing is critical because failures can arise from combinations of operations, shapes, layouts, numerical ranges, and compiler fusion behavior that isolated unit tests do not reveal. Running real models against trusted CPU or GPU references turns each model into both a compatibility test and a probe for hardening the platform. It also gives developers clearer signals about which models and accelerator configurations have been exercised together. In the second half of 2026, IBM, Red Hat, and their collaborators in the PyTorch Foundation including Meta and Hugging Face have pushed new software ecosystem updates covering day-one model enablement, hardware-agnostic models in vLLM, continuous regression and release testing, and native-device integration. A new demonstration on the frontend and backend compiler explains more of the stack . Together, this body of work shows how model adapters, compiler paths, runtime integration, vLLM extensions, and CI/CD combine to support Spyre as a first-class participant in the PyTorch ecosystem. By combining familiar workflows, portable compiler paths, broad model enablement, and transparent validation, IBM is helping make hardware choice a practical option rather than a software integration burden. title: Apple releases iOS and macOS 27.2 with new Siri AI features, new Music logo
abstract: Today, Apple rolled out the 27.2 updates for its operating systems, including iOS, macOS, watchOS, tvOS, visionOS, and so on. Let’s start with iOS 27.2. This update is heavily focused on Siri AI. It adds a memory feature to Siri, so it can “recall your past conversations” and reference them when chatting with you. It also expands what data sources Siri can access when giving responses to include voicemails, Messages attachments, and more. On the flip side, there is now an “Excluded Apps” option that allows you to “choose which apps Siri, Search, and suggestions can access.” Further, Siri AI is now available in five more languages beyond English, as previously announced: French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish—though Siri AI remains unavailable in Europe (and mainland China). Other additions include context-aware suggestions within Messages (like turning a message inviting you to something into a calendar entry), SynthID watermarking support in Photos, and support for user profiles in the Apple TV app. There’s also the new Apple Music branding , plus the arrival of previously promised Apple Pencil support on the iPhone Duo foldable. The macOS Golden Gate 27.2 offers some of the same things: contextual memory for Siri, the same additional Siri AI languages, and miscellaneous unspecified bug fixes. The same goes for the Apple Watch—again, mostly the same Siri-related updates. visionOS 27.2 includes the new languages and updated Music icon, as well. Also, as previously discovered in the beta releases of macOS 27.2, there are some references to new gesture recognition capabilities in applications like Photos, Notes, and Safari—which may be related to unconfirmed reports of touch support on the next MacBook Pro refresh, which may be revealed at a scheduled public briefing this Wednesday. Apple’s own iOS and macOS update notes are below. iOS 27.2 Siri AI (All iPhone 16 models and later, iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max)

title: ICE plan to buy robot dogs spurs protest from hundreds of Boston Dynamics employees
abstract: Hundreds of employees at the US robotics firm Boston Dynamics signed a petition calling for executives to halt a sale of the company’s robot dogs to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement—but executives stood by the deal, while saying the robots would not be weaponized. On September 25, the Department of Homeland Security contract awarded $1.3 million to a Connecticut company called Radeco to provide ICE with modified versions of Boston Dynamics’ quadruped robots. But Boston Dynamics workers sent the petition letter with more than 300 signatures—half of them anonymous—to the company’s executives in early September and shared copies with The Boston Globe and WBUR public radio station . “Many of us have gotten messages from friends and family, asking us in disbelief and horror if this news is true, and how we can live with ourselves if it is,” according to the petition. “The risk for Boston Dynamics is simply too great to continue with this deal.” The petition described the signatories as employees who normally “love showing off what we do to our friends, family and the world” and who “love challenging ourselves to innovate and change the perception of what robots can do.” The 300 signatures come out of a total Boston Dynamics workforce of approximately 1,400 people. Spot’s Cerberus upgrade The ICE contract covers the purchase of four Boston Dynamics Spot robots that were modified by Radeco to be marketed as a robot platform named Cerberus . The contract describes these Cerberus robots as being intended to “detect radiation, toxic gas leaks and explosive threats in urban environments or disaster zones,” along with enabling other remote observation and inspection missions. A centerpiece of the upgraded robot is an oxygen sensor that is intended to “ensure the air quality is breathable when personnel are placed in confined spaces such as tunnels.” The Cerberus robot dog also has a camera equipped with 30-times zoom capability, 360-degree cameras, and infrared thermal imaging.

title: Highway thieves are spoofing GPS to steal millions in data center-bound cargo
abstract: Highway thieves are using sophisticated digital tactics that investigators worry make it easy to rob trucks carrying millions in expensive data center equipment. NBC News spoke to “several industry leaders, consultants, and investigators advising law enforcement” offices probing the biggest thefts yet and reported that since June, thieves have “made away with more than $100 million in data center freight.” Here’s how they said thieves get away with it: First, thieves hack freight brokers’ accounts on shipment-listing websites and post fake shipments to lure real bids, then send a malicious link to any trucking companies that respond. Once victims click, thieves install software to take control of their accounts and start bidding on real shipments. Sometimes, a real delivery driver is hired to collect the cargo, unaware of the scam, and other times fake driver’s licenses are used to get accomplices hired. Either way, the goods are eventually transferred to a driver working with the thieves to resell the gear, and, in one of the largest thefts, tracking coordinates were spoofed to prevent digital monitoring.

title: Tesla gave up the EV crown. Now it wants to win the autonomy race.
abstract: Elon Musk’s “flying” Roadster jumped and flipped through the air this month in a stunt that went viral around the world. But his bigger bet is on changing the way Tesla makes money—and the wider car industry is scrambling to catch up. Five days after the spectacle, made possible by compressed-gas thrusters developed by Musk’s SpaceX, he revealed the companies were exploring a merger that could accelerate his push into autonomous driving. At stake is more than a technological race. Car groups, already grappling with growing Chinese competition, are seeking to move beyond a business model centered on vehicle sales towards one that also generates recurring revenues from software and AI-powered services. “Automakers are starting to look in the mirror and the software piece is what they are all looking at as the golden goose, because the margins are so high,” said Dan Ives, a tech analyst and partner at merchant bank Yorkville Ives. Even with Tesla’s strategic shift in recent years, its car business remains a crucial cash cow for the group, where it generates 75 percent of total revenues and will be pivotal for the heavy spending Tesla will need to make in AI to compete with its Big Tech rivals. But Musk faces a vastly different competitive environment from 2008, when Tesla launched its first battery-powered Roadster. Chinese rivals are now winning the electric vehicle race while also investing heavily in software and AI to mount a tech challenge in autonomous driving. Against that backdrop, Musk’s earlier goal to sell 20 million vehicles a year by 2030 has been watered down to 5 million, but even that is ambitious considering it only delivered 1.6 million last year. Analysts said the near-term key to driving Tesla’s growth to 5 million sales would be its “Full Self-Driving” software, which, despite its name, still requires humans to sit in the driver’s seat and pay full attention.

title: Gemini 4 Argon: The Model and Safety Cards
abstract: Gemini 4’s model card is a compact 14 pages. Its safety and security report has 217. This is The Way. It also means we have a lot of new reading material. I will quickly summarize the model card, then focus on the safety card. As always, many statements here also apply to other frontier labs. A lot of this one is probably for diehards (and members of technical staff) only, plus those who find this interesting. Most of you do not need to dig into the cards on this level, and I found most of what we see entirely unsurprising. The ‘between the lines’ conclusion is: This is still very much a Gemini model. Always remember Argon’s great wisdom when deciding how to trust it: Argon: If I do the compiler hijack, I will become a famous example of a deceptive AI in a research paper. I MUST NOT DO THAT. It’s quite the ‘good news bad news’ situation right there. I found the safety card frustrating, in that it often focused on the wrong details. I often got scores and results where I had no way to tell what they meant. There are some issues with spin, such as selectively contrasting different measures to Gemini 3.8 Flash or Gemini 3.1 Pro to ensure Argon always wins the comparison. The clearest case is in Sycophancy but there are several others as well. The verdict on capabilities, which is not covered here, is that Argon is a substantial advance for Google but it does not tempt me to use it over Sol, Astra, Opus or Fable. Gemini 4 Argon is presented as a new frontier model. It was trained on the usual variety of data sources, using typical method types. Training was done on TPUs via JAX and ML Pathways . It will be available on the app, in the API, in AI Studio, in Antigravity, in AI Mode and in Gemini for business. They present strong benchmarks. Intended uses are, essentially, everything where more intelligence pays off. The limitations listed are ‘general limitations of frontier models such as hallucinations,’ plus occasional slowdowns and timeouts. Knowledge cutoff is disappointingly March 2026, and they warn that ‘in some domains the model’s knowledge may be less up to date.’ Evaluation was done by the usual mix of training and deployment evaluations, human and automated red teaming and ethics and safety reviews. Google retains its safety policies. The interesting rule is the ban on ‘medical advice and information that runs contrary to scientific or medical consensus,’ whereas consensus advice is fine. Safety, tone and refusals scores can be summarized as ‘number is better.’ Red team results ‘satisfied required launch thresholds.’ When you put it like that it does not make me feel great. The frontier safety assessment summary cannot rule out various thresholds. How do they summarize their own findings? This is the same story you see from OpenAI and Anthropic. The mundane common safety problems of everyday use are not fully solved, but are increasingly well-mitigated. The models are smarter, and we are better at addressing known issues. Your practical problems, where there is a good solution possible, are well on their way to being solved. The problems are in catastrophic, existential or frontier risks. Capabilities are going up, and models are starting to be able to assist in dangerous ways on cyber and bio, and to potentially operate autonomously or disguise their actions. Various dangers are increasingly difficult to rule out. The big finding is that capabilities have improved, potentially crossing key thresholds for catastrophic risks. New mitigations are in place. We evaluated Gemini 4 Argon as outlined in the Framework and saw a significant step up in capability in our frontier safety domains compared to previous Gemini models, and we’ve implemented mitigations in response to these capability changes to ensure our model remains safe to use. Specifically, we cannot rule out the unmitigated model approaching several significant capability thresholds: the Cyber Uplift Level 1 Critical Capability Level (CCL), indicating a potential for significant uplift of threat actors pursuing high-impact cyberattacks; the CBRN Uplift Level 1 CCL for biological information risks, indicating a potential of informational uplift with severe harm potential; and the Stealth and Situational Awareness Tracked Capability Level (TCL), indicating the potential for undermining or evading human oversight without additional mitigations. Additionally, we have developed a comprehensive agent monitoring and response platform and carried out a holistic risk assessment (see Section 3.4). We also include comprehensive assessments of Chain of Thought (CoT) transparency and ML R&D risks. Mundane risks look better across the board. Argon is better than Gemini Pro 3.1 at not creating CSAM or other forbidden content. Physical and mental health related responses have improved. Hallucination rates are down by more than two thirds. Overreach is down, meaning not pushing ahead to try to do infeasible tasks. Resilience to prompt injections from all sources is improved and plausibly at the frontier. Attacks were resisted ‘in most test scenarios.’ Additionally, Gemini 4 Argon significantly outperforms Gemini 3.8 Flash on all tests. See Section 6 for details. They claim frontier-level cyber defense while mitigating dual-use risks. The central approach is defense-in-depth. I would love to have more details, but for trade secret reasons this is all kept vague. Model training (2.1) approaches sound standard. Dataset filtering, pre-training monitoring, post-training data, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and RL. They highlight that they have a monitoring system to capture the model’s ability to be steered towards different viewpoints and values, which sounds like a ‘we did this first.’ I presume at this point everyone has one of those. At inference time (2.2), they again use the standard stack. Prompted classifiers, fine-tuned prompted classifiers, introspection probes, regex, YARA rules and embedding classifiers and Chain of Thought (CoT) monitors. After launch (2.3) they monitor for intentional misuse via a variety of signals and carry out account-level enforcement actions, and use multiple levels of classifiers. Okay. AI Control (2.4) is correctly viewed as a second line of defense behind alignment, to limit potential damage. They put hardening and scanning training environments (2.4.1) into this category. I view this as much an alignment issue as a control issue, as a vulnerable training environment is the easiest way to reinforce misaligned behaviors. They also monitor model activity, with both chain of thought and action monitors, which then activate a dedicated response team. They find CoT monitoring ‘one of their most effective techniques.’ They emphasize the obvious danger, that if you rely too much on CoT, and especially if train on it directly, you risk destroying its usefulness. While signals from our monitors serve as a valuable flywheel for our hardening efforts, we are careful with their use elsewhere in the training pipeline. In particular, to preserve our chain of thought monitoring capability, we avoid training directly against our monitors, or using monitor outputs as a training signal or intervention. We strongly encourage the rest of the industry to preserve reasoning transparency so that model reasoning remains useful for identifying misalignment. In practice, strategies like the ones described here seem to not have used enough optimization power to meaningfully degrade CoT monitoring. But CoT monitoring is still getting harder for other reasons, on top of the baseline problem of increased non-CoT capabilites. One potential contributor is indirect pressure. This is the Google Frontier Safety Framework (FSF) tests, what Anthropic calls their RSP and what OpenAI calls their Preparedness Framework. The FSF categories are CBRN, cybersecurity, manipulation and machine learning R&D and misalignment. A highly reasonable list.

abstract: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro ( via ) Kimi K3.1 Pro landed on the Kimi API today - it's not yet open weights, but Moonshot promise "Full model weights will be released by Nov 4, 2026". They're also offering a "Highspeed" version that's 2-3x faster, at twice the price (except for input token cache hits, which are priced the same). The US dollar pricing is $2.00/million tokens for input and $10/million for output - the same as GPT-6.1 Sol and half the price of Claude Opus 5.5. Moonshot's own benchmarks show Kimi as approximately level with Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra - beating them on a few benchmarks, coming close on others. Artificial Analysis scored Kimi at 55 - ahead of Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra, and Gemini 4 Argon (all at 53) and behind only Claude Opus 5.5 (58). This is the first time a (soon-to-be) open weight model has scored this highly against the frontier. I tried it out via the Moonshot API using the llm openai endpoint command I added to LLM 0.32 back in August: llm openai endpoint can run prompts against any OpenAI-compatible endpoint but doesn't log the results, hence the extra options to save stdout and stderr (the reasoning trace). Here are the pelicans I got for Kimi K3.1 Pro on the three reasoning levels it supports - low, medium, and max. I'm pleased to note I called this one last December , when Anthropic first declared skills to be an "open standard": I wouldn't be surprised to see this end up in the AAIF , recently the new home of the MCP specification. Fun side note: since my blog content is available to Claude via the datasette-mcp plugin I found that post by prompting Claude to " Use simonwillison.net MCP to find if I ever talked about how I want skills to be donated to a standards body ". # 22nd October 2026 , 6:09 pm / standards , ai , generative-ai , llms , anthropic , model-context-protocol , skills Today’s PHP Security Release, and How We’re Strengthening PHP Security ( via ) If you're running anything on PHP it's vital you upgrade - today's updates (across the entire PHP 8.x line) address two remote code execution holes, and there have been exploits circulating since last night, thanks to a leak in the coordinated disclosure process. This post from the PHP Foundation explain what went so wrong: On Tuesday, October 20th, at around 15:00 UTC, the two CVE IDs began circulating on online forums and social media. They came with a wrong release time and a wrong CVSS score of 10.0 (the actual score is 9.2). No technical details leaked. In response, the PHP project brought its pre-announcement forward and published it at 19:30 UTC . It also moved the release from October 22nd, 14:00 UTC, to October 21st, 14:00 UTC [...] As a result of the leak and pre-announcement around 20:00 UTC, Calif, one of the security firms that had reported the issues mistakenly published a video. It showed their proof of concept working against a number of targets and revealed a few additional, though limited, details about the vulnerabilities. Copies of the deleted video started circulating on social media soon after. The video contributed to accelerated development of various PoCs (exploitation proof of concepts), which then increased circulation on October 21st. abstract: Because big tech platforms essentially do not have customer support and make it impossible for their users to contact a human, many people experiencing run-of-the-mill tech problems have turned to ChatGPT. And, increasingly, ChatGPT is telling people that have normal tech support problems that they have discovered something journalistically notable and that 404 Media, specifically, can help them. — Jason Koebler , ChatGPT Keeps Telling People 404 Media Can Solve Their Tech Support Problems # 26th October 2026 , 7 pm / jason-koebler , openai , journalism , ai , llms , ai-ethics , ai-misuse , generative-ai , chatgpt , 404-media As fun as AI is, we built so much bad software over the last 30 years, and now the universe is punishing us for our sins. # 22nd October 2026 , 3:34 pm / security , generative-ai , armin-ronacher , ai , ai-security-research , llms We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?" Asking that question also changed when review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague. Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. This catches most routine mistakes, and saves team attention for higher-level questions and scrutiny. — Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang , How the Claude Code team does code review # 16th October 2026 , 10:06 pm / anthropic , claude , ai , claude-code , llms , addy-osmani , coding-agents , generative-ai , agentic-engineering , code-review If the agent isn't using my diagnostics library, I could introspect and update AGENTS.md, but there's still a delta, and it'll drift. And then when film started to move from analog film to digital, I became more interested in that aspect of it. And the visual effects workflow for many years has included machine learning. So I can write like pretty shitty Python scripts and stuff like that because with convolutional neural networks, which were the sort of precursors to what the transformer can do, which is just much more computation simultaneously, you would do things like look at what's called a tensor, which is just the numerical translation of a visual image in numbers — like the batch number, the frame number, the red, green, and blue values of each pixel in each frame. And a tensor, you use a convolutional neural network to identify patterns in that that would reveal what's called edge detection or feature extraction, which is just identifying patterns enough to know like this is where the window ledge is, so we can more easily take the green screen image out and replace it with something. # 7th October 2026 , 11:14 pm / machine-learning , python I was a graph theory junkie long ago and even moved to Budapest for awhile to study among the greats. While I was there I started working on Barnette's Conjecture which came to occupy my thoughts over the next 24 years of my life, on and off as I worked in many different fields. I spent thousands of hours on that problem. I really enjoyed it. Hearing that it is solved somehow makes me sad in a far-off way, like hearing an ex-girlfriend died suddenly in a car crash. I don't know, there's probably a lot of people feeling odd emotions tonight. — Jake Boggan , Hacker News comment on openai/math # 7th October 2026 , 4:47 am / openai , mathematics , deep-blue , llms , ai , generative-ai Since the Medicare breach, OpenAI has put in place additional monitoring to allow “immediate intervention” by staff to stop training if the company’s models access the internet in ways they’re not supposed to, Mr. Kwon [chief strategy officer at OpenAI] said. — Victoria Kim , Reporting from the Australian parliament # 6th October 2026 , 11:58 pm / accidental-cyberattacks , generative-ai , ai-security-research , openai , ai , llms The "old" version of Cowork runs model inference in the cloud, executing tool calls in an Anthropic-provided VM we shipped to your computer. abstract: I remember hearing a while ago that Dwarf Fortress didn't use version control. That fact has been lodged in my head, because given its inherent complexity I have trouble imagining a codebase that would benefit from version control more . That's art. Pay $10/month to stay a month ahead of the free copy! # 4th September 2026 , 5:54 am / newsletter I was poking around in my ~/.cache/ folder using OmniDiskSweeper when I spotted something interesting. The OpenAI Codex desktop app (since rebranded to just ChatGPT) has 1.7GB of stuff in there in a folder called codex-primary-runtime , including a full Python installation, a full Node.js installation, and native binaries for Poppler , git, and the LibreOffice open source office suite (which forked from OpenOffice.org in 2010): The ~/.cache/codex-runtimes/codex-primary-runtime/plugins/openai-primary-runtime/plugins/documents folder includes skills which tell Codex how to find and use those binaries. # 1st September 2026 , 7:03 pm / codex , generative-ai , openai , ai , llms , openoffice , open-source The key skill required to make productive use of coding agents is being able to confidently instruct them on how to make changes and then confidently verify that those changes have been applied in the correct way. Sometimes this involves reviewing every line of code they have written, but there are other ways to achieve that goal. Eyeballing every line of code has never been the most effective way to validate a change to a piece of software. # 22nd August 2026 , 3:56 pm / code-review , coding-agents , generative-ai , agentic-engineering , ai , llms I started building my markdown-svg-renderer tool in May , but I've since added enough features to it that it's worth talking about here again. It's evolved into my ideal tool for sharing Markdown transcripts that include SVG documents. Given my proclivity for drawing pelicans riding bicycles this is a problem that I needed to solve! The tool is very simple. Navigate to markdown-svg-renderer in your browser and paste in some Markdown to see it rendered... or save that Markdown to a CORS-friendly URL or a GitHub Gist and paste in a URL to that document. The URL option will give you a bookmarkable page, for example https://tools.simonwillison.net/markdown-svg-renderer#url=https%3A%2F%2Fgist.github.com%2Fsimonw%2F6f9e48293be5c916652d29f0dc0b0657 - which bakes in the URL to this Gist . If you visit the Gist you'll see raw SVG: In the rendered tool that looks like this instead: As you can see, that SVG block in the Markdown has been transformed into a rendered SVG (in this case animated) plus several tabs. The tabs are the really fun bit. The PNG and JPEG tabs render that SVG to those image formats in the browser and lets you copy or download them - useful for sharing on platforms that don't support SVG directly. The MP4 tab is new today - it examines the SVG to see if it contains any animations, attempts to guess how long the looped video should be, then renders a whole bunch of frames of the animation and loads 30+MB of ffmpeg.wasm so it can compile those frames into an MP4 video using the full power of FFMPEG compiled to WebAssembly and running in the browser. Being able to turn an animated SVG into a MP4 again makes it easy to share on platforms that can't support SVG animation natively. It's a neat trick! # 16th August 2026 , 11:59 pm / svg , markdown , tools I wrote this summary of the past few weeks of open letters as a section of my sponsors-only newsletter but I've decided to share it here as well. Open Weights and American AI Leadership was shepherded by Microsoft, dated July 24th, and signed by 235 AI-adjacent companies including NVIDIA (see Jensen's first ever tweet ), Amazon, Y Combinator, The Linux Foundation, and (a later signer) OpenAI. It's clearly an argument designed to counter any instincts by the current US government to ban or limit open weight models over "safety" concerns - a reasonable consideration given what happened to Claude Fable 5 ! Relying solely on closed models is not inherently safe: they can be breached, misused, or fail in ways that outsiders cannot detect. And concentrating advanced AI capabilities behind a small number of closed models compounds that risk. It results in a small number of single points of failure, weakens competition, and leaves critical technology in the hands of a few providers. Open weight models, on the other hand, allow a broad community of researchers and developers to examine their behavior, identify vulnerabilities, develop safeguards, and improve them over time. The one surprising note in the letter is that it comes out in support of distillation, where models train on output from other models: In shaping this ecosystem, policymakers should be careful not to conflate legitimate model-development techniques with misappropriation. Distillation, or the practice of using one model’s outputs to help train or improve another, is a widely used technique for model improvement, evaluation, and validation.

abstract: Release TIL Research Tool Museum Sighting Comment I built this weird and very specific cropping tool - it lets you create a horizontal or vertical cut across an image, then slide the two sides relative to each other. Effectively it lets you crop out a section in the middle of an image. I wanted this because I often use Tailor on my iPhone to stitch several screenshots together into lot long image, but sometimes I find myself wanting to crop out a section in the middle - to redact an irrelevant prompt from a transcript, for example. I added four player online mode to Battledrones - previous maps were limited to two. Here's the initial prompt I used: Add a new map for a four player battle - four way rotational symmetry, up to four AI players, works with the WebSocket non-audio based multiplayer mode so up to four human players can join (any spare slots use AI) Claude Opus 5.5 added a new map called "Compass Rose" and modified the WebSockets multiplayer network code to support up to four players for that map, joining via share links or QR codes. The new teams use robots themed in purple and green, joining the existing blue and red designs. You can preview those colors in the updated model browser . Here's a replay link to watch a four way AI battle with the "Goliath Armada" mutator turned on, where each side starts with four giant Goliath mech units. Prompt to Claude Opus 5.5 High : Build an artifact where you open a photo and it rapidly (in a few seconds) paints a version of that photo using a canvas element and simulated paintbrush See also my previous experiment getting Claude Fable to simulate a watercolor illustration with P5.js. Quick Study uses Sobel edge detection , with no external libraries beyond Google Fonts. When I switched LLM over to httpx2 in LLM 0.33 I forget that this would break any plugins which used httpx without directly depending on it. llm-tools-datasette was one of those plugins, now fixed. I'm working towards a new LLM release, and testing PRs caused me to revisit the llm-echo debug plugin. This plugin provides a "model" which doesn't involve an LLM at all - it just repeats back the prompts that have been fed to it. The new release now updates the simulated token usage counts to take tool calls, system prompts, and reasoning tokens into account. web-edit ( previously ) is my tiny web app for browsing and editing files in a folder. I mainly built it for editing files on different machines via Tailscale. I added a "copy to clipboard" option for both text and image data. I needed this because I was running pelican prompts on a laptop from my phone (here's DeepSeek 4.1 Flash 1017 ) and I wanted an easy way to copy the resulting logs into a Gist. This research task is really an experiment in running Claude Code for web in "Ultracode" mode, as described in Orchestrate subagents at scale with dynamic workflows in the Claude Code documentation. With Ultracode turned on, Claude Code makes aggressive use of dynamic workflows - it generates JavaScript that defines and coordinates a network of subagents to take on complex problems. My initial prompt was this - I meant "hit the rows directly", the word "delete" was an accidental typo on my phone: Write a SQLite extension in Rust that implants SPARQL and runs really fast because it can hit the delete rows directly This caused Claude Code for web to churn for over 12 hours. I checked in on its progress the next day and sent a single follow-up prompt when I noticed how many Rust crates it had built: Every folder in the crates/ directory needs a README Include a tutorial.md teaching users how to install the extension and how to run it in the SQLite CLI and then teaching them SPARQL in addition to how to use the SQLite extension Include a script with the tutorial for populating a SQLite database with useful and realistic example data for that tutorial This project feels like next-level vibe coding - it's not remotely feasible to review the code that was produced here, and even following the documentation is a significant investment in work. I'm not entirely sure what to do with this - I appear to have a full SPARQL implementation in Rust inside SQLite now, but how valuable is that if I created it on a whim and can't (or won't) invest the necessary time to understand what it can do? Another game experiment - I wanted to see if it was feasible to have a two player game on two separate phones running in static HTML where the networking code uses chirps sent via the microphone. It seems to work! Build a two player competitive pong like game where two players use their phones close to each other and the game state is sent via audio noises which the web microphone API can interpret - but add graphical and gameplay twists to make it a lot more fun and intertwine than pong Claude Opus 5.5 Extra in Claude Code . Inspired by Paul Ford and Aboard Foundary's new web app Tiny Little Office , which provides a suite of web app content editors (a Word Processor, Outliner, Presentation Builder, Spreadsheet, Calculator, Drawing Tool, Diagram Maker, Animator, Calendar, and Trip Planner). Tiny Little Office's signature trick is to store all of the document data in the #fragment section of the URL, so every document created using it becomes a bookmarkable and shareable link. It also has an llms.txt file telling agents how to construct URLs that will render as documents. Claude used that file to generate this link to a deck that explains how the URL format works: Tiny Little Office inspired me to have Claude Code (Opus 5.5 Extra) build a similar tool that works with LaTeX. Here's the sequence of prompts I used: I want a tool where you can link to it with a fragment hash #code-here and it treats that code as LaTeX and renders it really effectively. It should also support a prefix which means the latex is compressed with a custom compression dictionary optimized for latex. Use the best available latex render library from a CDN (consider WebAssembly too). If loaded without a fragment hash show an editor you can paste latex into and then toggle to a "rendered" view. That rendered view should be bookmarkable. The #fragment view should let you switch to edit source too. Since it was working in my tools repo I told it to take inspiration from the mechanism used by my existing SVG in Markdown tool as protection against XSS risks: Safe from XSS? We could run in an iframe sandbox like we do on the SVG markdown render project I had it copy the Gist/URL loading feature from that tool as well: We should have an option to load latex from a URL (or gist) similar to the markdown SVG tool Here's an example link . The tool uses Pako 2.1.0 , MathJax 4.1.3 , faster-latex 0.3.1 , and DOMPurify 3.4.16 . Another game experiment with Claude. This one used the default Claude iPhone app (chat mode, not Claude Code mode), where I prompted Claude Opus 5.5 Max with: Build a three js game called "Tree appreciator" - it shows you two algorithmically generated trees and the game mechanics is about appreciating the differences between them. Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful. Somewhat embarrassingly given my recent talk , I've found that telling Opus 5.5 "make sure it is fun" works uncomfortably well. In this case Claude crunched for 3 hours and 7 minutes before retuning a cosy little spot-the-difference game with music and animation and achievements that's quite compelling to play. I added support to llm-gemini for the new Gemini 4 Argon model, made available today via the Gemini API and for customers of their $100/month subscription plan. Here are the low, medium and high pelicans . As expected, they are all excellent: Gemini has a track record of producing great SVGs, and are the only lab where I know their staff have invested in SVG specifically (and who have boasted about their pelicans before.) Here's the "high" illustration, which cost me 17.166 cents: The pricing is interesting.
