title: Apollo says AI has delivered 'zero financial payoff' outside the tech industry
abstract:
One of the world's largest investment firms isn't bullish on AI. Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images 2026-10-25T16:02:08.173Z Read in app This story is available exclusively to Business Insider subscribers. Become an Insider and start reading now. Have an account? Log in . One of the world's largest investment firms says that only tech companies are getting a share of the AI pie . In an economic analysis published on Saturday, Apollo Global Management said that while the Magnificent Seven — a group of established tech companies that includes Nvidia and Meta — are seeing revenue growth during the AI boom, this growth isn't being shared by other industries. "Mainstream corporate America is pulling back and starting to view token spending not as a source of growth but as a cost center that weighs on margins," Torsten Slok, a partner and chief economist at Apollo, said in the report. "The technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech." In a series of graphs, Slok measured three main metrics that have boomed for tech companies but not for regular companies: revenue per worker, profit margins, and productivity growth. Since 2022, revenue per employee figures have skyrocketed for tech companies — rising from $550,000 to nearly $800,000 today. Meanwhile, that figure hasn't changed much for everyone else in the S&P 500, lingering around $550,000 for the last seven years. Similarly, while profit margins soared among tech companies since 2022, they've stagnated at about 10% for everyone else. And across the economy, AI hasn't yet dramatically increased productivity growth as some AI optimists have predicted. Apollo's research portends a dark shadow over a US economy throwing massive amounts of dough toward AI tools and companies, whose leaders have promised that an " age of abundance ," where people won't have to work as much, will soon be upon us. "The question looking ahead is whether, even as models become commoditized, mainstream corporate America can turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins," Slok said. title: A 10-year-old CNN outperforms frontier LLMs for skin cancer diagnosis
abstract:
This is a melanoma. Figure 1. Invasive melanoma on the ear, under 0.8 mm thick. Both LLMs called it a seborrhoeic keratosis and said it could be discharged. The CNN called it a melanoma. Clinical photograph on the left, dermoscopic image on the right. Images: MILK10k , MILK study team, CC BY-NC. I showed these two images - a clinical photograph and a dermoscopic (skin microscope) image - to GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1, two of the most capable AI models available in October 2026. Both said it was a seborrhoeic keratosis, a harmless warty growth, and that the patient could be discharged. I then showed them to fine-tuned version of Inception v3, a convolutional neural network (CNN) first published by Google in 2015 and fine-tuned here on public dermatology images. The CNN got the right answer based on the dermoscopy view. It was one of 200 biopsy-proven lesions I gave to all three. The CNN named the right diagnosis (out of 6 possiblities) for 125 of them (62%). The two frontier LLMs named it for 84 and 85 (42%). A ten-year-old network, fine-tuned for about twenty minutes, beat both of them at recognising skin cancer. The test # The lesions come from MILK10k , a public dataset released through the International Skin Imaging Collaboration in 2025, in which each lesion is photographed twice: a clinical close-up and a dermoscopic image taken through the illuminated magnifying lens dermatologists use. I drew 200 lesions at random, all confirmed by histopathology: 100 that should not be discharged: 30 melanomas, 25 basal cell carcinomas, 25 squamous cell carcinomas (including Bowen’s disease) and 20 actinic keratoses. 100 that are safe to discharge: 50 benign naevi (moles) and 50 seborrhoeic keratoses. Every lesion was biopsied, including the benign ones, so these are harder to diagnose: a mole that somebody decided to cut out is one that worried a clinician. Basal cell carcinoma on the trunk of a 75-year-old man. All three models answered correctly. Invasive melanoma under 0.8 mm thick, with very little pigment. GPT-6 Astra called it a basal cell carcinoma with 95% confidence. Claude Fable 5.1 and the CNN called it a melanoma. Seborrhoeic keratosis on the leg. Both LLMs called it an actinic keratosis and the CNN a squamous cell carcinoma: all three were wrong, though all three would have kept it rather than discharge it. Figure 2. Three more of the 200 test lesions. Clinical photograph on the left, dermoscopic image on the right. Images: MILK10k , MILK study team, CC BY-NC. The LLMs were given both images and nothing else, and asked, as a clinician might use them, for the most likely of the six diagnoses (or “unsure”), a confidence, a second choice, and whether the lesion could be safely discharged with no treatment, biopsy or follow-up. Both models got the same prompt at default settings, and neither refused a case. The CNN is deliberately not state of the art. I used Inception v3 pretrained on everyday photographs and then fine-tuned all layers on 68,011 dermoscopic and clinical images from the ISIC Archive on a single H100 GPU. These 200 test lesions, and every other photograph of the same lesion or patient, were removed from its data (including the validation set) before training, so it had never seen them, and they were not used to choose the model or set its threshold. It scored both images of each lesion, combined them with most of the weight on the dermoscopic image, and chose from the same six diagnoses. You can try the CNN yourself . Remarkably the model is small enough to run entirely in a phone browser using WebGPU. Nothing is uploaded, and its random sample button draws from these same 200 lesions. title: Fixing Tool-Call Accuracy in vLLM
abstract:
When I use an open-weight model, I see results that are nowhere close to what the quality benchmarks indicate. Tool call accuracy is an important part of serving open-weight models. When your tool calls aren’t accurate, the model builds up on nonsensical context. This leads to low quality results, particularly for agentic workloads where multi-turn sessions are common. Sadly, many providers and widely-used inference engines don’t fully pass tool-call accuracy tests . For example, when we served Kimi K2.6 with vLLM version 0.28, we got the expected tool call schema only 92% of the time. In other words, 2 out of every 25 attempted tool calls failed. Fortunately, vLLM recently added support for constrained decoding , a technique to guarantee schema-adherence. This feature has then been released as a server-side flag in vLLM 0.31. By enabling it, you can get to 100% schema accuracy with the newer Kimi and DeepSeek models. In this blog post, we first describe tool call schema accuracy and why it’s important in serving agentic workloads. We then talk about constrained decoding and how it fixes the schema accuracy problem. You can enable an LLM to call an external tool in two steps: (1) inform the AI model about the existence of externally available tool calls and (2) provide the model with instructions on how to output structured tool-calls. For example, when connecting OpenCode to Kimi, OpenCode sends Kimi a JSON array describing available tools. One of the tools in this list is webfetch , which fetches Web page contents: The inference engine then wraps this JSON description in LLM-specific tokens before passing it into the LLM, to match how the LLM was trained to recognize tool declarations. When serving Kimi, this looks something like: The JSON object describing the tool (or function , in the JSON above) includes the tool’s parameters, their types, which of the parameters are required, etc. This is known as the tool’s schema . For an agent harness (e.g., OpenCode) to successfully execute a tool call generated by the LLM, the call must follow the rules specified in its schema. Then, when a user asks to fetch a Web page via their agent harness, the LLM may output the following tokens: These tokens are parsed by the inference server’s parser, extracting the LLM-specific tokens and turning the call into a JSON object such as: This is then sent back to your harness (OpenCode, in our example), which runs its webfetch tool and sends its output back to the model. For a tool-call to succeed, the call must adhere to the tool’s schema. The simple approach to tool calling is to let the model generate tool calls freely and trust that the model’s training is sufficient to generate correct calls. This is similar to how we trust the model to generate syntactically correct prose. The simple approach works most of the time because modern models are good at following structured patterns. But success “most of the time” implies that many tool calls can still fail, resulting in context window pollution due to error messages, lower model performance, and increased cost due to the agent having to retry the call one or more times. To avoid such experiences when using Kimi, Moonshot AI published their K2VV ToolCall benchmark. This benchmark lets providers verify that they serve Kimi with the same quality as the original, including its default behavior of only generating valid tool calls. K2VV ToolCall’s workload consists of 2000 requests selected to evaluate when the LLM generates tool calls and whether the generated tool calls are syntactically correct (i.e., adhere to the provided schema). The benchmark allows analyzing the model’s quality by quantifying two metrics: trigger similarity and schema accuracy . Trigger similarity considers when the service decides to trigger a tool call, and how similar its decisions are to Moonshot AI’s own service. Schema accuracy quantifies the fraction of tool-calls that adhere to the tool’s schema and can therefore be invoked successfully. For example, when tool-call accuracy is 50%, half of the tool calls generated by the model are malformed. Schema accuracy usually falls short due to the probabilistic nature of language models. A model generates tokens based on likelihood. It is not running a compiler or type checker. Even with a clear prompt, it can still produce malformed tool calls. This can be caused by, for example, a mismatch between the model’s training data and the current inference harness. Models are trained on many tool-calling datasets, each with its own tools, schemas, and conventions. As a result, a model may generate a tool or field name that it has seen during the training, even if it does not exist in the current production environment. For example, it may generate search_web when the available tool is web_search , or use city_name when the active schema expects location . An LLM computes for each token the probability that it is the next in the sequence. It then selects the next token by performing a weighted sample. Constrained decoding avoids malformed tool calls by preventing models from sampling tokens that would result in a syntactically invalid tool call. When using constrained decoding, instead of letting the model sampling tokens freely and validating the result afterward, the inference engine guides generation step by step. At each step, only valid tokens are allowed. Which tokens are allowed is determined by the provided tool schema. vLLM implements this using structural tags from the XGrammar library . The snippet below shows an excerpt of how XGrammar implements constrained decoding in Kimi K2.6. It defines the valid structure of a tool call, including where the call begins, where the index appears, where the arguments begin, and where schema-constrained JSON must be generated. You can find the full implementation here . With this definition, generation must follow a valid path: Begin tool call → Tool name → Tool call index → Begin arguments → Schema-constrained JSON → End tool call Invalid paths are blocked during generation. For example, when generation reaches the tool-call index phase, the engine restricts sampling to integer tokens and masks out everything else. The figure below, reproduced from XGrammar’s article, provides a good visualization of how invalid tokens are masked. Source: Dong, Yixin, et al. "XGrammar: Flexible and efficient structured generation engine for large language models." Proceedings of Machine Learning and Systems 7 (2025). [ link ] This changes schema accuracy from a best-effort approach to a runtime guarantee. The model still decides which token to generate, but now the token is selected from a restricted and syntactically-correct set. Notably, this runtime enforcement adds negligible performance overhead. By precomputing token masks for each phase, and applying them efficiently on the GPU during generation, XGrammar guarantees correct tool calls without trading off significant performance. Moonshot AI recommends constrained decoding to be turned on and its own API behaves as such. So we initially added constrained decoding in our fork of vLLM. After vLLM added this feature in v0.25, we switched to using this feature from upstream for Kimi and DeepSeek. Unfortunately not long after, we found out that our tool-call accuracy score dropped back to 91%! After analyzing the problem, we confirmed that vLLM’s implementation of constrained decoding was still correct. Instead, we found that vLLM changed its default behavior for requests that do not explicitly turn constrained decoding on. This is primarily because vLLM is designed to support a wide range of models. Supporting constrained decoding is a per-model task and problems fall into three camps: Due to these issues, vLLM maintainers reported seeing problems with several models after constrained decoding was enabled.

title: Eunice is almost here
abstract:
William Gibson's Agency (2020) is a mind-bending science fiction novel. Without getting lost in its intricate plot, one storyline takes place in an alternate San Francisco in 2017, where a young woman named Verity is hired to test an experimental AI assistant called Eunice. At one point, we encounter this extraordinary exchange: Verity: "Where'd you get this? It's wrong." Eunice: "This no-name account, in Zurich. Part of me knew it was there, how to get it, how to get it here. Plenty more, but if I tried it again, they'd be on us." Verity: "When did you have time to do any of that?" Eunice: "Started when we were looking out the window. Before we left, up to the park, it was already points." Eunice: "Frequent flyer. There's a global market, buy or sell. Hard to track..." Verity looked at the green bag. Verity: "You did this since I turned you on?" Gibson published Agency nearly three years before ChatGPT's release, and six years before the emergence of today's increasingly autononomous AI agents. We now have GPT-Live and emerging models like Block's Dessa , bringing us remarkably human-like full-duplex conversations. Meanwhile, OpenAI's Dots and Meta's Muse are introducing 24/7 agents capable of independently pursuing goals, taking action, and working in the background. What makes Eunice remarkable isn't just that she can talk, it's that she's doing so much else while talking. The pieces are coming together. As always, Gibson was right on the money. Eunice is almost here.

title: Removing Next.js Got My Blog to 100 on Every Lighthouse Category
abstract:
Removing Next.js Got My Blog to 100 on Every Lighthouse Category K korindiehacker Author 2026-10-26 9 min read English My blog just scored a perfect 100 on every Lighthouse category. I love blogging. I wanted to build a blog that’s light, fast, free of clutter, able to run multiple blogs, and fully accessible on top of that. And finally, at long last, I’ve more or less pulled it off. It was quite a tedious process. Ugh… and I even had to remove Next.js, the framework I’d been using most. It was far, far more painful than I expected. I’d like to share the journey of improving performance while building this blog. Why did I decide to build my own blog? When you think of blogs, a few names come to mind. Medium, Blogger, Ghost… But none of them satisfied me. Medium and Blogger are bloated with features, and their actual performance wasn’t satisfying either. Blogger Medium Truly horrifying. Hmm…… And there was another problem: it’s a hassle to work directly with the markup and raw code we all love (Markdown, HTML, CSS). For the record, all performance measurements were taken with pagespeed.web.dev . Of course, there are plenty of alternatives: WordPress, Ghost, Hugo. I didn’t like WordPress’s plugin hell. Ghost has to be self-hosted (there’s ghost.org too, but it’s way too expensive…), and every version upgrade broke something in the editor, so keeping it up to date was a chore. Hugo is the best of the bunch, but in the end, setting it up is still a hassle. Looking back, I guess what I really wanted was SaaS. The one I liked most was Bear Blog. Great performance. I love its product philosophy, too. But its extreme minimalism was a downside for me. The editor UX didn’t work for me, either. If it at least let me add AdSense and attach images for free, I probably would’ve just used Bear Blog. As fast as Bear Blog, but with a bit more functionality and better usability. That’s the blog I wanted to build. Oh, and if you’re curious, you can check it out at bloffy.co . Anyway. Enough about me. Let me share how I actually improved the performance. Let’s hit 100 on Lighthouse Performance. Obviously, caching is a must. It goes without saying that caching is essential. Get caching right and performance improves dramatically. And Next.js makes caching really convenient.
There’s ISR , and it also extends fetch with a next option for caching . Handy. Using these well alone gets you a long way on performance. Unfortunately, though, our site can be reached from anywhere in the world. Why is that unfortunate? Within the same region, caching makes things fast, but visitors from other regions still end up eating the network latency. No, silly. That’s what a CDN is for. Yes. That’s why we use a CDN. And if you deploy a Next.js app to Vercel, you get a CDN out of the box. I don’t dislike Vercel; it’s incredibly convenient. But the Pro plan is pricey right from the start, there’s the serverless cold start problem, and the dependency on the Vercel ecosystem isn’t something you can ignore either. So why not use a different CDN service? Cloudflare, for example. I honestly think Cloudflare is a genuinely nice company. You can run large-scale infrastructure and most apps on it for free. But then I figured I didn’t really need Next.js’s caching anymore. Having to invalidate two caches every time I publish a post makes things a pain to manage. In short, for a static website, I figured a CDN alone is enough. And that’s reason number one why I didn’t need Next.js. Image optimization. Images these days run over 10MB. Serve those on the web as-is and your performance will go completely off the rails. Optimizing images is quite a hassle. You have to resize per device, compress, and then handle the CDN on top of that. On a previous project, I had a serverless function (AWS Lambda) compress and resize images whenever one landed in storage (S3), and I put CloudFront in front as the CDN. It was a pretty reasonable setup for tailoring things exactly the way I wanted. But it’s also a setup that needs a fair amount of upkeep. So this time I went with Cloudflare’s Image Transformations . Even on the free tier you get 5,000 images, so I use it without a second thought. At this point I sound like a Cloudflare sales rep. I’m just an ordinary solo developer. Ta-da. Here’s the Next.js blog’s performance after all that caching and image optimization. For reference, this was Next.js 16.1.6. Pretty high scores. But this isn’t enough. We want 100. A clean, no-asterisks 100. So I dug into what the problem was. It said a substantial amount of legacy JavaScript was found, and it wasn’t code I wrote. It came from the framework runtime that Next.js ships in its bundle. But this page is a static page with zero interaction. Every page is pre-rendered with ISR, and I thought I’d followed the Next.js guidelines well. So as an experiment, I ripped out every client component the app had, left only server components, and measured again. The score didn’t budge. At first I suspected hydration , but once I dug in, the problem wasn’t hydration alone. The cause was the client runtime that Next.js always ships, even for static pages. Even with only server components, the runtime chunks, hydration, and the RSC payload for the router all stay. That’s because next/link and next/image are themselves client components ( 'use client' ), so having just those two is enough to pull in the runtime and trigger hydration. So what if I strip out next/link and next/image too? The App Router’s own runtime, the router and error boundaries, still remains. There’s no official way to get it down to zero; the only option was a hack: stripping the scripts out of the rendered HTML. That’s when it hit me: “If I’m going to do that, why am I even using Next.js?” And then, the unused code. You can see that the bulk of the JavaScript is code that isn’t needed. Unused code alone comes to 230,460 bytes. That’s not good.
Most static websites don’t need JavaScript at all. Unused JavaScript is needed even less. This is where I really agonized. Is dropping Next.js for the sake of 100 points the right call? I’d spent a lot of time building the public-facing web app. Let’s remove Next.js. In the end, for the quality of the blog (even if it’s just 5 points), I decided to rip Next.js out entirely. My judgment was that I wouldn’t need Next.js’s excess features in the long run either. I considered going fully vanilla, but I didn’t want to give up the productivity and infrastructure benefits of a framework. I needed to find the right one. I chose Hono . I liked its technical philosophy. “Fast and simple” was exactly the solution I needed most, and JSX support was a bonus. The migration cost didn’t look too big, either. Ta-da. Finally, 100. Tada. And just like that, 100 across the board. Go ahead and run the very page you’re reading right now through pagespeed.web.dev . There’s no JavaScript, and unused code dropped sharply to 407 bytes. As a bonus, build time went down by about 40% too. Oh, why is SEO at 69? That site was built for testing, and it deliberately blocks search indexing. That’s why it’s 69. By the way, if you score 100 on everything in DevTools, Lighthouse actually sets off fireworks for you. 🎉🎉 Hono vs. Next.js Performance Next.js Performance (server components only) Hono Performance The long task that runs before anything is rendered on screen took 309.3ms on Next.js, and when I built the same page with Hono, it took 68.01ms. That’s roughly a 78% improvement. Does your static site really need Next.js? Is a JS payload, hydration included, really doing a static site any good? I don’t think so. It leaves behind unnecessary JavaScript, so in most cases I think it’s simply not needed. That said, for an interaction-heavy app, I think Next.js can be a great framework. In fact, the management app for this very blog is built with Next.js! P.S. This blog runs on Bloffy, the blogging platform I’m building.

(189 points, 121 comments on Hacker News)

title: PaperPilot – Zero-Cloud, Pure-Rust PDF Engine with WASM and MCP
abstract:
PaperPilot PDF tools for your AI agent — and for you. Pure Rust. Runs locally. Files never leave your machine. Try it in your browser → · Download · Roadmap PaperPilot is a PDF and document toolkit written in Rust. The same engine runs as: Surface Use it for MCP server Give Codex, Claude Code, Kimi Code, Pi, Claude Desktop, Cursor, or any MCP client the ability to merge, split, OCR, and compress PDFs CLI Batch and scripted workflows Browser (WASM) Zero-install tools; files are processed in browser memory, nothing is uploaded Desktop app Tauri + Svelte GUI with viewer, markup, and diff Local REST API Call it from Python, Node, or n8n at localhost:7823 No Chromium, no C++ runtime, no cloud calls. Quick start 1. Use it with your coding agent (MCP) Codex, Claude Code, Kimi Code, and current Pi releases connect to the same local
stdio server. See the coding agent setup guide for each
client's configuration and verification steps. Builds from this source can also
print ready-to-merge configuration: paperpilot-mcp --client-config codex # Also: claude-code, kimi-code, pi, claude-desktop, cursor Download paperpilot-mcp from Releases , then add it to claude_desktop_config.json : { "mcpServers" : { "paperpilot" : { "command" : " /path/to/paperpilot-mcp " } }
} Restart Claude and try: "Merge these two PDFs and compress the result." 2. Use the CLI # Merge paperpilot merge --inputs doc1.pdf doc2.pdf --output merged.pdf # Compress paperpilot compress --input in.pdf --quality 75 --output compressed.pdf # Rotate pages 1, 3–5 by 90° paperpilot rotate --input in.pdf --pages 1,3-5 --angle 90 --output out.pdf 3. Use it in the browser Go to usepaperpilot.com . Open your browser's Network tab while you work — you'll see no file uploads. 4. Build from source git clone https://github.com/KrushnaVardhanReddy/PaperPilot.git cd PaperPilot
cargo build --release -p paperpilot-cli -p paperpilot-mcp -p paperpilot-gateway Desktop app: cd apps/desktop && pnpm install && pnpm tauri dev Requires Rust 1.75+, Node.js, and pnpm. What it can do today (v0.6) Organize: merge, split, rotate, delete pages, reorder pages, extract pages, booklet imposition, N-up grid Optimize: compress Extract: plain text, OCR (pure-Rust PaddleOCR via rten ) Security: watermark, validate signatures, remove signatures, PII scan, deep sanitize Office data: Excel → JSON, Excel → CSV Coming next (see ROADMAP.md ): v0.7: PDF ↔ Markdown / HTML / JSON v0.8: PDF → Word / Excel / PowerPoint v0.9: encrypt, decrypt, sign, redact, forms, annotations v1.0: render, flatten, repair, compare, PDF/A, Bates numbering Why another PDF tool? Private by default. Everything runs locally or in your browser tab. Agent-ready. MCP support is first-class, not an afterthought. One engine, many surfaces. CLI, MCP, REST, WASM, and desktop share the same Rust core, so behavior is consistent. Small and dependency-light. Pure Rust, built on lopdf , pdf_oxide , rten , and friends. Benchmarks Run cargo bench --workspace to reproduce. Methodology and results: SYSTEM_BENCHMARK_REPORT.md . Architecture Desktop (Tauri) · CLI · REST (Axum) · MCP (stdio) · WASM (browser / edge) │ Rust core workspace paperpilot-core · paperpilot-pdf · paperpilot-nlp · paperpilot-gateway paperpilot-mcp · paperpilot-wasm · paperpilot-storage Embed in your own site < div id =" paperpilot-widget " > </ div > Local REST API paperpilot serve --port 7823
curl -X POST http://localhost:7823/api/v1/pdf/merge \ -H " Content-Type: application/json " \ -d ' {"inputs": ["a.pdf", "b.pdf"], "output": "out.pdf"} ' Swagger docs at http://localhost:7823/docs . Contributing Issues and PRs are welcome. Good first contributions: bug reports with a sample PDF, new tool requests, and docs fixes. License Community Edition (this repo): Apache 2.0 . It includes the CLI, MCP server, REST gateway, WASM engine, and desktop app. An Enterprise Edition (SSO, RBAC, audit logs, DLP) is developed separately.

title: Steal My Bitcoin CTF PoC
abstract:
sponsored with ❤️ by Steal My Bitcoin CTF proof of concept One live PHP callback against the Steal My Bitcoin challenge, start to finish, in a single standard-library Python file. This README explains stealmybitcoin_poc.py , a single-file Python reproduction of the request sequence used in my Steal My Bitcoin CTF run. It uses only Python's standard library. The script builds the requests itself, checks each leak before moving on, and records the HTTP bytes from a new run. This can probably be done easier without all the extra debug crap and as in my John Hammond video about the Steam Local Privilege Escalation I discovered, you could probably clean up this ugly PoC. Note ⚠️ Honestly please clean it up or make your own better version that isn't crumpled by Sol. ⚠️ Everything below is written against the Docker lab , not the live challenge. The lab is a local Alpine PHP 8.4.26 CLI server behind nginx, which is the same build and worker model the offsets were calibrated on. Stand it up in a minute and the whole chain runs end to end on your own machine. The live run that actually solved the challenge is kept as a historical note at the bottom . stage what goes out what comes back ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 0 health GET /php-version.php -> PHP 8.4.26 confirmed 1 heap leak 249,042 B producer + 8 x 6,672 B -> 256 B cookie (OOM poisons a worker) └─ Zend chunk base 2 code leak 251,557 B producer + 8 x 92,388 B -> 16 B cookie (OOM poisons a worker) └─ zval_ptr_dtor 3 callback 368,812 B POST -> forged HashTable runs (fake HashTable + command) └─ zif_system(cmd) ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 20 HTTP requests at most. No looping, no retries. The short version A small multipart upload makes PHP chew through far more memory than the wire size suggests. When it runs out of memory partway through session upload-progress parsing, PHP leaves stale state behind in a worker that then gets reused. Shape the follow-up requests right and bytes fall out through session cookies. I read those as a heap address and a PHP code address. With both addresses, a final request drops a forged PHP structure where cleanup will find it, and cleanup calls zif_system , PHP's handler for system . That command sends back a fresh proof marker and one print-flag result over the connection that is still open. Why two addresses? The OS randomizes where PHP's code and heap land, independently. The heap leak tells the script where to put the forged structure, the code leak tells it where the function it wants to call actually lives. Addresses from an earlier worker or an earlier run are not safe substitutes, and every time I tried it the attempt just failed. Contents The lab Start here What each request does 1. How a small producer reaches the memory limit 2. How the heap address is recovered 3. How the PHP code address is recovered 4. How the final request reaches system Reading the result How often it actually works The live run that solved it Jargon, briefly Thanks The lab The offsets in this PoC are calibrated for Alpine PHP 8.4.26 running the built-in CLI server with four workers . The lab reproduces exactly that, behind nginx, on loopback. Important The build matters more than the version string. A Debian php:8.4.26-fpm stack reports the same PHP/8.4.26 but has a different binary layout, so the code-pointer fingerprint will never match and the run aborts at the code-leak stage. Use the Alpine image below. Three small files. Put them in an empty directory: public/php-version.php (the health endpoint, and the only page the PoC needs) Fatal error: Allowed memory size of 134217728 bytes exhausted (tried to allocate 131072 bytes) in Unknown on line 0
1ef0e73d8615157a uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root),0(root),1(bin),2(daemon),3(sys),4(adm),6(disk),10(wheel),11(floppy),20(dialout),26(tape),27(video) 0ec066e8b91457c7c19b5612f3e2ded7f117df08f402693669c1ffc2cfc24942 /usr/local/bin/print-flag LOCAL_DUMMY_WIF_NEVER_USE The PHP fatal, then the nonce this run generated, then id , then the hash of the binary it resolved, then the dummy flag. Exit status is 0 on a verified run and 1 on anything else. Warning The producer deliberately walks PHP into its memory limit. Only run this somewhere that behaviour is authorized. The script will only talk to the challenge endpoint or a loopback lab URL, and anything else aborts before a packet goes out. One run means one health GET, up to two leak batches, and at most one final request. No looping, no retries. Every multipart body stays under 1 MiB, though each leak batch pipelines nine separate requests down one connection. Flag What it does --url Lab endpoint, or the challenge. Required to do anything. --output-dir Where to write the run's evidence. Defaults to poc-run- . What each request does Step What goes out, what should come back Why Health One ordinary GET /php-version.php must return HTTP 200, PHP 8.4.26 , and X-Powered-By: PHP/8.4.26 . Keeps the memory-limit payload away from a changed or unhealthy endpoint. Heap leak One 249,042-byte multipart producer, then eight pipelined 6,672-byte consumers. title: Where the Romans Fought (interactive map)
abstract:
Pick a period, or drag the year slider to see the battles of any 25 years; Play runs through them from the founding of Rome. Each dot is a place, its area the number of battles there, and its slices the opponents, starting at 12 o'clock and running clockwise in the order of the legend; grey is civil war. Diamonds are sea battles; dashed rings are battles placed only within their region, in the colour of the most frequent opponent; triangles at the edge point to Caledonia, Nubia and Arabia. Nearby dots merge as you zoom out and split as you zoom in. Hover or tap a dot for its battles; select it to list them with their full records. The Roman record in the 1,469 battles with a known result. The Roman states are counted together; the 236 civil-war battles and the 4 with unknown results are left out. A battle with several opponents counts against each of them, and once in the total. Select a row to list its battles. The Empire includes the western and eastern courts of 395–480 and the restored empire of 1261–1453; the other successor states are counted on their own. Germans, Goths, Gauls and the Greek cities are many peoples or cities under one name; the note of each battle names them. Traditional battles are counted as the sources tell them: they are most of the early Republic's record, which modern historians doubt. Select a row for the full record: date, place, sides, commanders, the Roman army and its languages, the sources, and for doubtful entries the reason. Results give the winner first; the coloured edge marks a Roman win (blue), draw (grey) or defeat (orange). Traditional marks a battle known only from a tradition that modern historians doubt; borderline an entry that may not meet the rules, kept with the reason (hover the label to read it). A hollow marker means that only the region of the battle is known. The images of the set, made for X: the map, Italy with Rome and Latium, the Balkans, Anatolia and the East with Constantinople, the win-draw-loss tables, and the full list in fourteen parts. A named land or sea battle in which a Roman force fought, as a principal belligerent or as a distinct allied force: one with its own name in the ancient and medieval historians or the standard modern works, or in English Wikipedia's battle lists and campaign boxes. Sieges count when there was real fighting (assaults, sorties, relief battles); a distinctly named battle inside a siege is its own entry. Left out: unnamed skirmishes, massacres without a battle, captures and surrenders without fighting, and legends. When in doubt an entry is kept and marked borderline, with the reason: 649 entries, most of them minor. The Roman Kingdom, the Republic and the Empire, West and East as one state (the western court to 480, the eastern throughout), and after 1204 every Roman successor state: Nicaea and the empire it restored at Constantinople (1261–1453), Epirus, Thessalonica (1224–46), Trebizond (1204–1461), the Morea (1349–1460) and Theodoro in the Crimea (to 1475). Client kings and allies (Pergamon, Rhodes, the Numidian kings, the Ghassanids, the federates) are not Rome; Romans in foreign service do not make a battle Roman. The battles of the kings and the early Republic are included as the ancient historians tell them, and 94 battles known only from a tradition that modern historians doubt are marked traditional, each with the reason. Most are the battles of 753–391 BCE: they rest on Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus and Plutarch, who wrote centuries later from the annalists, and Livy himself says that most records of early Rome perished when the Gauls burnt the city (6.1). Others are victories that Livy took from annalists who invented or inflated them (the Scipios in Spain, 215–214 BCE), and a few medieval battles known only from much later chronicles (the early Ottoman traditions of 1284–1303). Battles with Roman forces on both sides, 236 in all, are mapped and listed, in grey, with the factions (Caesar and the Pompeians, Constantine and Maxentius, John VI Kantakouzenos and the regency), but not scored. Foreign armies in a Roman civil war count as allies. Palmyra under Zenobia is counted as an opponent; the battles of the Gallic emperors are civil wars. Each battle takes the colour of its main opponent: Greeks, Persians and the East, peoples of Italy (Latins, Etruscans, Samnites, the Italian allies, the slave revolts), Carthage and Africa (with Numidia, Mauretania and the Moors), Western Europeans, Balkan peoples and Slavs (Illyrians, Thracians, Dacians, Bulgaria, Serbia, the Rus'), steppe peoples, Seljuks and Ottomans, and Arabs (the caliphates and emirates, the Fatimids and Hamdanids); grey for civil wars. Each place is drawn as a small pie: its area grows with the number of battles there, and the slices give the number against each opponent. The victor is the side that won on the battlefield: it held the field, routed the enemy, took the city or destroyed the fleet; strategic outcomes and disagreements between the sources are in the notes. In a siege the besieger wins if the place fell and the defender if the siege was raised. A draw is an indecisive battle, or one that both sides claimed with no clear verdict from modern scholarship. For every battle the research recorded who fought on the Roman side: the contingents as the sources give them (legions and allies, themes and tagmata, federates and mercenaries), their main languages, and an estimate of the share of Greek speakers, with its basis and a confidence. Where the sources say nothing, the estimate rests on where that army was recruited in that period, and the record says so: 1,061 of the 1,709 estimates are of low confidence. Twenty-one research batches by period, each following the same written rules and citing its sources battle by battle; then twelve coverage and fact-check passes against the Wikipedia lists and war articles, which added 123 battles, corrected 129 fields and removed 7 entries (listed under Left out); then checks of names, of possible doubles and of every position against the present-day country. Positions: 586 known, 812 approximate, 311 only within their region. The 18 images were made for X in the house style of the series, 3200 × 1800 pixels: the overview map with the number of battles per 20 years, Italy with Rome and Latium, the Balkans, Anatolia and the East with Constantinople, the win-draw-loss tables, and the list in fourteen parts. Every battle with its date, war, place, coordinates, sides, allies, commanders, result, the Roman state, the Roman army (contingents, languages, an estimate of the share of Greek speakers, with its basis and confidence), the reasons for doubt, sources and notes: as a CSV table, as JSON, or as a spreadsheet with the record tables and the entries left out; and the record alone as CSV. Sources, cited battle by battle: Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Polybius, Plutarch, Appian, Caesar, Cassius Dio, Tacitus, Josephus, Ammianus Marcellinus, Zosimus, Procopius, Agathias, Theophylact Simocatta, Theophanes, Leo the Deacon, Skylitzes, Attaleiates, Anna Komnene, Kinnamos, Choniates, Akropolites, Pachymeres, Gregoras, Kantakouzenos, Sphrantzes, Chalkokondyles, Panaretos and the Arabic and Ottoman chroniclers, among others; for what counts as a battle, the battle lists, war articles and campaign boxes of English Wikipedia and the standard modern works (the Cambridge Ancient History, Goldsworthy, Haldon, Treadgold, Bartusis, the Oxford Dictionary of Late Antiquity and Kazhdan's Oxford dictionary of the medieval empire). Map: Natural Earth; today's borders dashed. Where the rules left room for judgement, this is how it was settled. The map, the record and the list follow the call shown; the alternative is given so that readers can weigh it.

title: RadarAgent: Agentic Tool Utilization for Radar-to-Language Understanding
abstract: MmWave radar senses human motion without recording appearance or identity, which makes it attractive for privacy-aware applications. However, its raw point clouds and signal-level features are hard for people to read. Existing radar-language models make such data queryable by training a radar tokenizer aligned to a language model, at the cost of specialized pipelines, paired data, and architecture-specific engineering. We present RadarAgent, an agentic framework that exposes radar processing as callable tools and lets a foundation model reason over them to describe motion in natural language, with no radar-token pretraining. In HumanML3D-style motion captioning, it exceeds the Radar-LLM baseline on key semantic metrics across several backbones, improving ROUGE-L from 36.0 to 39.6 and BERTScore from 83.3 to 90.7, and tool calling clearly outperforms flat feature prompting.

title: Huni: A Networked Testbed for Real-time Human and Generative AI Interaction
abstract: Real-time audio/video-based interaction between humans and generative AI (GenAI) systems is now widely deployed in mainstream applications such as OpenAI ChatGPT and Google Gemini. Unlike traditional human-to-human realtime communication, human-GenAI interaction introduces fundamental challenges for today's network infrastructure. However, systematically evaluating different design factors remains difficult in the absence of controlled and reproducible experimental platforms that can isolate key components for human-GenAI interaction. In this paper, we present Huni, a networked testbed for real-time human-GenAI interaction. Huni provides end-to-end control over the interaction pipeline, such as transmission paradigms (e.g., WebRTC, QUIC/HTTP-3, and Media over QUIC), adaptation algorithms (e.g., congestion control and bitrate adaptation), network conditions (e.g., bandwidth, round-trip time, and packet loss), and GenAI processing logic. We demonstrate the usability of Huni through two case studies: (i) comparing call setup time across different WebRTC and QUIC-based schemes, and (ii) evaluating the performance of multiple congestion control algorithms under diverse network conditions. We hope Huni can facilitate future research on real-time human-GenAI interaction.

title: NPUGen: NPU as KV Generator for Stable Long-Context Mobile LLM Inference
abstract: As on-device large language model (LLM) applications like mobile agents become increasingly popular, long-context inference has become a key challenge. The key-value (KV) cache is the foundation of efficient autoregressive decoding, but its memory footprint grows rapidly with context length, often exceeding the memory limits of mobile devices. Existing KV cache management methods, such as compression and storage offloading, often lead to performance degradation or unpredictable stall latency. We find that in the prevalent CPU/GPU-decoding mobile pipelines, the NPU remains largely idle during decoding and can recompute missing KV cache more efficiently than storage offloading. We therefore propose NPUGen, whose KV recomputation engine generates missing KV cache on the idle NPU via a prefill-like forward pass, avoiding unstable storage I/O, CPU intervention, and unnecessary data movement. NPUGen further introduces a hidden-state anchor mechanism that eliminates redundant prefix recomputation, and turns KV recomputation into a schedulable background service to cope with resource contention and guarantee foreground QoS. Experiments on smartphones with Qualcomm SoCs across multiple long-context tasks show that NPUGen significantly reduces decoding latency and fluctuations, providing fast and stable long-context inference on resource-constrained mobile devices.

title: WiP: A New Sense for Agents to Understand Human Behavior through mmWave
abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel in processing text, vision, and audio, they remain blind to human behaviors in everyday physical environments. Millimeter-wave (mmWave) sensing offers a privacy-preserving, device-free perceptual channel. As LLMs cannot inherently process radar modalities, the core challenge is how to convert continuous radar observations into tokens that an LLM can understand without losing human kinematics. To address this bottleneck, we present mmMind, an interactive cognitive agent driven by pose-guided kinematic tokenization. By leveraging 3D human pose to supervise a spatial-temporal radar encoder, mmMind generates continuous tokens that faithfully preserve intricate posture transitions and physical kinematics. A lightweight projector then maps these tokens directly into the LLM's embedding space, unlocking multi-turn contextual interaction and spatial-temporal reasoning. Evaluations on a 17.9-hour real-world dataset demonstrate substantial improvements over baselines in radar captioning and physical question answering.

title: WIP: AMAS: An Android Macro Action System for Efficient LLM Mobile Agents
abstract: Recent advances in LLMs have enabled mobile agents that can automate user tasks through natural language interaction with app interfaces. However, current agents execute tasks as sequences of basic UI actions (taps, swipes), incurring extra latency, token cost, and accumulating error risks. Motivated by this, we propose AMAS, an Android Macro Action System that constructs reusable, system-grounded macro actions by identifying system-level application entry transitions that directly jump to task-relevant, app-specific screens. Results show that AMAS reduces agent's average LLM calls by 23.22%, LLM latency by 26.38%, and token cost by 21.9%, while having a 6.0% gain on success rate. Further coverage analysis shows that AMAS constructs 184 stable and distinct macro actions across the 20 benchmark apps, averaging 9.2 per app. At the task level, AMAS provides every task with at least one macro action, and 54.3% of tasks coverage. These results demonstrate that system-level macro actions can provide broad coverage while improving both the efficiency and reliability of LLM-based mobile agents.

title: Real-Time RAN Observability at the Far Edge: AI on the Fronthaul
abstract: Operational RAN observability is reported every 5 to 15 minutes, averaging over as many as 1.8 million slots. Resolution is only half the problem: the quantities that explain a physical-layer fault, such as the beamforming weights the DU computed and the elements each layer actually drove, are not counted at all. Neither limit will cope with 6G integrated sensing, non-terrestrial networks, and ever-larger MIMO arrays. The 7.2x fronthaul split puts a standardized, tappable boundary in the middle of every modern base station; we argue it is the right place to obtain real-time observability, and that the analysis must run at the far edge, because the evidence is transient: it crosses the wire once, cannot be averaged down without losing the fault, and is not recoverable afterwards at any resolution. From passive captures, with no vendor-supplied instrumentation and no cooperation from either the DU or the radio supplier, we recover DU-side scheduling behavior and radio-side execution, including the per-beam and per-layer beamforming weights carried on the C-plane, separating measured quantities from those conditioned on an array hypothesis. On that extraction we ground an eleven-agent platform in which a language model only interprets measurements. Across three independent capture labs covering 4T4R, 32T32R, and 64T64R radios, a fourth lab read over the M-plane, and a dataset of 87 distinct captures, one unmodified code path recovered per-layer weights and revealed three faults nobody was looking for, two of them on the DU side, including a pair of effectively un-beamformed layers for which no alarm currently exists. A separate root-cause diagnosis was confirmed by the repair that followed.

title: Resource-Constrained Lifelogging: A Utility-Based Replacement Policy for Video Understanding
abstract: Lifelogging on personal mobile devices allows users to interact with their past experiences through Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) hosted on edge servers. However, offloading continuous lifelog data streams is severely constrained by limited edge storage. In this work, we present an end-to-end edge-offloaded lifelogging system featuring a utility-based replacement policy to manage multimodal databases under strict storage constraints. To preserve semantically valuable data, we propose diversity- and variance-based utility functions to quantify lifelogs' representativeness, formulating the replacement decisions as a multiple-choice knapsack optimization problem. We evaluate our system under multiple real-world storage constraints using an egocentric video dataset for video question answering, simulating interactive discussions between users and MLLM-powered AI assistants. Experimental results demonstrate that our utility-based replacement policies: (i) boost accuracy by 102.5% on average (by 135% at most) compared to the First-In-First-Out (FIFO) baseline, (ii) achieve at least 78.2% relative coverage compared to unlimited storage, and (iii) incur merely 1.96% communication overhead and 0.03% computation overhead. This work facilitates scalable, long-term digital memory for AI assistants, paving the way for resource-efficient immersive communication services.

title: Demo: Multi-Device Cuffless Blood Pressure Monitoring via PPG-to-ECG Generation
abstract: Cuffless blood pressure (BP) monitoring is central to managing cardiovascular diseases, and is commonly based on photoplethysmography (PPG) or electrocardiography (ECG). ECG delivers better BP accuracy, but straps and patches make it impractical for daily use; PPG is already present on the rings and watches people wear all day, yet carries far less cardiac information. We bridge the two by generating ECG from PPG: a diffusion model performs a selective, ECG-targeted generative process conditioned on PPG, using a QRS-adaptive forward process together with scale- and frequency-alignment modules that constrain R-peak position, amplitude range and heart rate. This demo runs that pipeline live on heterogeneous commodity wearables—two smart rings (Circular Ring, OmniRing), a smart watch (Mi Band 4) and our own PPG wristband. Attendees wear the device of their choice, watch an ECG being synthesized from their own PPG in real time, and compare the resulting estimate against an Omron cuff, shown alongside a signal-quality index and the running error against the cuff.

title: When Not to Diagnose: Evaluating Evidence-Sufficiency Recognition in ECG Multimodal Language Models with ECGTrustBench
abstract: Mobile electrocardiogram (ECG) capture routes photographed or scanned 12-lead images to an AI model or a clinician, yet missing leads, calibration loss, or photographic degradation can remove diagnosis-critical evidence while the tracing remains visually readable. A condition-aware evidence-sufficiency check is therefore needed to flag unusable captures for recapture or clinician review before diagnosis. Existing ECG multimodal large language model (MLLM) evaluations cannot support this, as they assume every question is answerable. We introduce ECGTrustBench, which evaluates evidence-sufficiency recognition as answerable-versus-insufficient QA over 3,300 image-question pairs, with corruption criteria unanimously approved by three licensed clinicians. Across ECG-specific, medical-domain, general-domain, and proprietary MLLMs, we find a consistent gap between answering and abstaining: ECG-specific models reach up to 77.3% clean accuracy yet abstain on at most 10% of evidence-deficient cases, while proprietary models achieve recognition up to 82%. Overall, current models respond more to visible degradation than to missing diagnostic evidence, highlighting a critical gap for evidence-sufficiency gating.

title: SpatialMind: Spatially Aware On-Device Embodied AI via Viewpoint Integration
abstract: On-device embodied AI allows local processing of visual data and prompt responses to user requests. Applying embodied AI to more complex domains requires spatial cognition, to properly comprehend the 3D environment and geometric relations between objects. However, existing vision-language models (VLMs) are weak in spatial cognition due to their limitations to 2D image understandings. In this paper, we present SpatialMind, a new on-device embodied AI technique that bridges the gap between 2D visual inputs and 3D physical reality, by injecting 3D spatial knowledge into on-device VLMs in a sparse form of 2D allocentric spatial memory. This memory is constructed by systematically aligning cross-frame visual features to a unified global viewpoint, and we prune the scope of on-device computation to maximize the compute efficiency in memory construction and VLM reasoning. Experiment results in diverse indoor environments show that SpatialMind greatly enhances the performance of spatially aware on-device embodied AI tasks, with high adaptability, robustness and compute efficiency.

title: Demo: MobileClaw: A Notification-Driven, Human-Gated Mobile LLM Agent
abstract: Smartphone assistants built on large language models (LLMs) today either drive an application's screen display or wait to be asked through chatting; neither is integrated into the event stream produced by the mobile OS and user-installed applications. We demonstrate MobileClaw, an Android system component that attaches an external LLM to the OS notification channel. A background service captures every posted notification and asks the model for recommended further actions; an interactive front end carries out the user's requests through built-in skills, operated through OS API calls rather than screen automation. The model is treated as an untrusted component: nothing it decides takes effect unless the user confirms it. Notification text and everything the app reads from the device pass a sanitizer before they leave the phone, and privileged operations run in a separate process behind an allowlist it re-checks itself. Demo attendees may fire synthetic or real notifications, manipulate local resources on the device, approve or reject suggested actions, and watch the model's reasoning trace in real time.

title: Educating Humans, Training Machines: From Doing to Becoming in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping higher education. Generative AI systems can summarize texts, generate written work, provide feedback, assist in problem solving, and support increasingly complex cognitive activities across disciplines. While these technologies create significant opportunities for teaching and learning, they also challenge long-standing assumptions about the relationship between academic task performance and evidence of learning. This paper argues that the central challenge for higher education is not simply integrating artificial intelligence into the classroom but reconsidering the purpose of education through a shift from task-oriented learning focused on “doing” toward developmental learning centered on “becoming.” Drawing upon Bloom’s Taxonomy, experiential learning, transformative learning, situated learning and research on human–AI collaboration, this paper develops a conceptual framework for examining the changing relationship between cognitive task performance and learner development in AI-augmented educational environments. Rather than assigning lower-order cognition to artificial intelligence and higher-order cognition exclusively to humans, the framework recognizes that AI can support activity across cognitive levels while distinguishing successful task performance from the intellectual development of the learner. The paper argues that the educational value of AI ultimately depends on whether its use contributes to the development of judgment, agency, reflection, ethical responsibility, creativity, and intellectual identity. Implications for curriculum design, assessment, faculty development, and institutional policy are discussed.

title: WiP: RadTomDop: Physics-Guided Diffusion Reconstruction for X-Band Doppler Radio Tomography in Device-Free Indoor Localization
abstract: RadTomDop presents a device-free indoor localization system that couples compact 10.585 GHz reflective Doppler probes with radio-tomographic spatial reconstruction. The distributed probes acquire motion-induced perturbations of reflected X-band signals and forward synchronized measurements through an embedded CAN/Ethernet pipeline. To recover indoor activity from sparse and cluttered measurements, RadTomDop introduces a Doppler-conditioned physics-guided diffusion reconstruction module instead of conventional smooth inverse reconstruction. The model enforces consistency with the calibrated RTI forward operator while learning plausible room-constrained activity patterns. This end-to-end prototype transforms reflected-wave measurements into interpretable activity maps and object trajectories, enabling privacy-preserving indoor detection and tracking without tags, wearables, or active transmitters.

title: WiP: GuardedMobile: Runtime Verification for LLM-Based Mobile GUI Agents in High-Stakes App Workflows
abstract: The next failure mode for mobile GUI agents is not a bad answer in a chat window; it is a bad tap on a phone. In high-stakes app workflows, one tap can submit a form, upload identity, disclose private data, accept terms, change account state, or authorize payment. This paper presents GuardedMobile, a lightweight runtime verifier that mediates proposed mobile GUI actions before app execution. We introduce MobileRiskBench-WiP, a trace-based benchmark of 52 workflows, including 12 ambiguous stress cases with misleading button labels and weak confirmation screens. Across three LLM-like agents and action-noise levels of 0.00, 0.10, and 0.20, Full GuardedMobile-Stress reduces unsafe workflow rate by about 95% and risk-weighted failure by about 95%, while retaining 86.5% task completion. The result is preliminary: stress tests show a safety-completion tradeoff, including clarification requests, delay, false positives, and residual unsafe actions.

title: GUARD-EYE: Guiding User Awareness with Real-time Detection for EYe health and Engagement
abstract: Digital Eye Strain (DES) is a prevalent health issue caused by extended screen usage, improper viewing distances and poor ambient lighting. Current preventative measures rely on static timers and lack the environmental context necessary for personalized intervention. We introduce GUARD-EYE, a context-aware wearable smart-headset system designed to actively monitor and mitigate DES risk factors using the sensor capabilities of modern smart glasses. The system uses a depth sensor, visible light cameras, and edge-based YOLO object detection to dynamically determine viewing distance, ambient lighting, and digital screen usage. We propose a heuristic eye strain risk model that leverages these sensor streams to calculate a real-time fatigue score and trigger audiovisual feedback during extended unsafe conditions. In addition, the system integrates Large Language Model (LLM)-generated contextual insights to deliver more personalized, dynamic behavioral feedback based on viewing data. To compare intervention strategies across diverse scenarios, we introduce a novel LLM-based user simulation framework1. Across three modeled compliance personas, the exploratory simulation produced a lower fatigue burden index for contextual alerts (5.12/10) than for the no-alert baseline (6.74/10), suggesting that context-aware intervention policies warrant further evaluation with human participants.

title: Separating Safety from Preference in Clinical LLM Evaluation
abstract: Conversational AI increasingly answers patients' rehabilitation questions, but a fluent, well-liked answer can still be clinically unsafe, and preference-only evaluation hides this by collapsing many judgments into one winner. We ran a human-centered evaluation of the mRehab Advisory Agent with two cohorts in distinct roles: six domain experts rate clinical safety and correctness, and three end users rate helpfulness, affect, and clarity, alongside blinded best-to-worst rankings exported as provenance-rich records. In a 200-question pilot (435 ranked triples), raters ranked the agent first most often (53.3%; p < 0.001), yet it led on affect and clarity, not helpfulness, and drew the lowest expert safety rate (88.8% vs. 93.7% for two GPT-4.1 mini comparators). That gap traced to a single expert with near-zero agreement, so it points to rater calibration rather than an unsafe agent, and catching it depended on recording safety separately from preference. As these agents take on more patient guidance, the gap between what sounds good and what is safe will only grow, and evaluations that keep both signals will matter more than leaderboards that report one.

title: Sparsity-Aware Scheduling for Efficient MoE-Based LLM Serving on Edge Servers
abstract: To support real-time and domain-customized edge intelligent applications, LLMs are increasingly deployed on edge computing servers. However, we observe that current MoE-based LLM serving systems, inherited from the cloud-based architectures, face a critical sparsity-vanishing problem when serving at the edge: tokens within an input batch often activate a large fraction of experts, which incurs significant I/O overhead from frequent expert swapping between CPU and GPU memory, ultimately degrading system throughput. In this work, we propose Saber, a sparsity-aware scheduling framework optimized for efficient MoE-based LLM serving on edge servers. The core idea of Saber is to introduce a group-level batching strategy that dynamically identifies requests with similar activated experts, and coalesces them to construct sparsity-preserving input batches. To ensure efficient online execution, activation patterns are precomputed and clustered offline, enabling fast request grouping through a lightweight classifier at runtime. Additionally, Saber incorporates a utility-driven priority scheduling mechanism to maximize inference throughput while maintaining low latency by intelligently adjusting group priorities. Experiments on representative MoE-based LLMs demonstrate that Saber significantly outperforms existing sparsity-agnostic schedulers, achieving up to 3.8× lower batch execution time and 3.27× higher throughput at comparable latency levels.

title: WiP: Beyond Tokenization: Structure-Aware Attention and Hybrid Backbone for Wireless Foundation Models
abstract: Plume showed that protocol-aware tokenization lets a compact 140M-parameter model rival frontier LLMs on 802.11 trace understanding [6]; Plume-2 showed that architecture and scale move the needle, yet tokenization still dominates [7]. This work asks the next question: does the training architecture itself matter? We study two architecture-level levers that do not touch the tokenizer. First, a structure-aware attention bias A = QKT + b, where b injects packet-trace geometry from the existing separator tokens. Second, a hybrid Mamba/attention backbone that interleaves linear-time state-space layers with a few dense global attention layers [4, 5]. On five real-world failure categories, the five configurations span 96.1–98.6% Top-1 accuracy. Mamba and the reduced-attention hybrid achieve 1.7× and 1.5× the Transformer's forward-pass throughput while trailing its accuracy by 2.1 and 0.6 points, respectively. In our preliminary single-run results, the structure bias improves Top-1 by 0.4 points on the Transformer and 0.8 points on the hybrid. The biased hybrid reaches 98.4% Top-1 at 13.8k tok/s, slightly exceeding the Transformer baseline's 98.2% while providing 1.48× its throughput. These results suggest that architecture is primarily an efficiency lever and that packet-relative bias can recover the hybrid's accuracy.

title: Demo: A Propagation-Theory and Knowledge-Enhanced Intent-Driven Platform for 6G Network Twinning
abstract: For sixth-generation (6G) communication systems, network digital twins have become a cornerstone for planning, design, and optimization across terrestrial, low-altitude, and non-terrestrial domains. To enable rapid large-area network planning and twinning from multisource heterogeneous data, this demo proposes a propagation-theory and knowledge-enhanced intent-driven platform (PKIP), in which a wireless propagation knowledge-enhanced radio foundation model and large language model-driven intent understanding are jointly incorporated. The proposed PKIP reconstructs the radio propagation environment and visualizes natural-language intent as dynamically evolving trends of communication key performance indicators in response to variations of the real network. Two demos are showcased: intent-driven regional coverage twinning and intent-driven low-altitude route twinning. PKIP supports 6G network planning, design validation, and optimization-parameter acquisition, achieving errors below 5 dB and a 91.3% latency reduction.

title: Demo: ChannelAgent: Agent-Driven One-Click Digital Twin Channel Generation for AI-Native 6G
abstract: Digital twin is emerging as a key enabler for the intelligent design, analysis, and operation of artificial intelligence (AI)-native sixth-generation (6G) networks. Digital twin channel (DTC) extends this paradigm to wireless communication by providing high-fidelity, real-time representations of the physical wireless channels. However, DTC generation faces key challenges in channel task parsing, ubiquitous environment construction, and real-time channel twinning. This demo presents ChannelAgent, the first agent-driven platform for one-click DTC generation. By combining agent-driven task orchestration, an environment generation large language model (EnvGen LLM), and high-performance electromagnetic computation, ChannelAgent forms an end-to-end workflow of task parsing, intelligent scheduling, environment reconstruction, and channel twinning. The prototype completes each electromagnetic propagation computation within 50 ms with a mean absolute path loss error below 5 dB, enabling high-fidelity and real-time DTC generation across diverse 6G environments.

title: Poster: Exploiting Side-Channel Leakage in AI Glasses
abstract: AI glasses increasingly connect first-person perception with cloud-based LLMs and VLMs, enabling real-time context-aware assistance. However, this cloud-connected design may expose privacy-sensitive information through encrypted network traffic metadata. In this work, we present AISeeU, a preliminary study of network side channels in LLM-powered AI glasses. We consider a passive observer who monitors packet timing, size, direction, and burst patterns without decrypting traffic or compromising the device. Using network traces collected from Ray-Ban Meta glasses, we show that traffic metadata contains structured patterns that can reveal sensitive information about user prompts and model responses. Our findings highlight a new privacy risk in wearable AI systems.

title: Experience: Agentic Security Analysis of 5G Protocol Interactions
abstract: This paper reports our three-year experience building 5GAudit, an LLM-based agentic framework for discovering vulnerabilities in 5G protocol interactions. We review the evolution of 5GAudit through successive redesigns, each driven by fundamental deficiencies uncovered in real deployment. We refine 5GAudit to enable it to conduct agentic cross-protocol/domain/system analysis, perform automatic verifier-in-the-loop validations of vulnerabilities, and go beyond predefined threat models by leveraging CWE (Common Weakness Enumeration) theory to enumerate new vulnerability patterns. Our system successfully discovers 42 0-day vulnerabilities of 5G protocol interactions in open-source 5G software, 20 of which have been assigned CVE numbers to date. We demonstrate 5GAudit as an example to share our lessons learned on applying LLM-based agents to 5G-specific security analysis with the community.
